title: PSI record PSI-142 (PSI-142) — Objectives
text:
PSI-142 — Quantitative Studies of Cool Flame Transitions at Radiation / Stretch Extinction Using Counterflow Flames (PSI-142). Ground Investigation; platform: Not Applicable; hardware: Principal Investigator Laboratory Hardware; period 2016-08-01 to 2021-07-31.
Objectives: By using the Flame Extinguishment (FLEX) experimental data from the Physical Sciences Informatics (PSI) system of combustion science, the purpose of this grant was to conduct new simulations and ground-based experiments using ozone-sensitized counterflow flames to:
 1) Develop a new diagram of the flammability limits of diffusional cool flames affected by radiation, diffusion, and convection.
 2) Bridge the knowledge gap between the flammability limits and extinction limits of hot flames and cool flames.
 3) Verify the phenomena observed on the ISS flame extinguishment experiments.
 4) Obtain new, quantitative data of extinction limit, flame temperature, and species distribution for the validation of kinetic and radiation models involving cool flames.
 5) Extend the cool flame experiments from the original ISS droplet experiments to a more general ground-based combustion system involving radiation, diffusion, convection, and low-temperature chemistry while maintaining a one-dimensional geometry.

title: PSI record PSI-142 (PSI-142) — Approach
text:
PSI-142 — Quantitative Studies of Cool Flame Transitions at Radiation / Stretch Extinction Using Counterflow Flames (PSI-142). Ground Investigation; platform: Not Applicable; hardware: Principal Investigator Laboratory Hardware; period 2016-08-01 to 2021-07-31.
Approach: Using the experimental conditions of FLEX flight, a comparative studies of the oxygen concentration effects on the extinction limits of cool flames was conducted using three different numerical modeling schemes, (a) spark-assisted flame propagation of a n-heptane/air mixture, (b) one dimensional freely-propagating dimethyl ether (DME) flames using an arc-length continuation method and (c) simulated cool flame regimes and burning limits at elevated pressure (up to 20 atm) using DME/air mixtures.

Specific research details are outlined in the publication, ''Dynamics of cool flames'' [https://doi.org/10.1016/j.pecs.2019.100787]; '' Understanding Cool Flames and Warm Flames'', [https://doi.org/10.1016/j.proci.2020.09.019] and ''Study of the low-temperature reactivity of large n-alkanes through cool diffusion flame extinction'', [https://doi.org/10.1016/j.combustflame.2017.01.028].

title: PSI record PSI-142 (PSI-142) — Hypothesis
text:
PSI-142 — Quantitative Studies of Cool Flame Transitions at Radiation / Stretch Extinction Using Counterflow Flames (PSI-142). Ground Investigation; platform: Not Applicable; hardware: Principal Investigator Laboratory Hardware; period 2016-08-01 to 2021-07-31.
Hypothesis: This investigation attempts to answer the critical question as to what conditions causes the hot flames transfer to cool flames and how the cool flame flammable region is related to hot flame flammability limit and extinction limit. The investigation hypothesizes that factors such as oxygen concentration, dilution, pressure, diffusion, and convection transport processes affect the cool flame transition.

title: PSI record PSI-142 (PSI-142) — Research impacts / Earth benefits
text:
PSI-142 — Quantitative Studies of Cool Flame Transitions at Radiation / Stretch Extinction Using Counterflow Flames (PSI-142). Ground Investigation; platform: Not Applicable; hardware: Principal Investigator Laboratory Hardware; period 2016-08-01 to 2021-07-31.
Research impacts / Earth benefits: Obtaining a fundamental understanding of the warm diffusion flame is particularly relevant to combustion in highly turbulent flow fields and in microgravity environments, owing to the possibility of long residence times. The results showed that the warm flame has a double reaction zone structure and plays a critical role in the transition between cool flames and hot flames. At elevated pressures, it was found that the flammable region of warm flames and cool flames expands due to the increase in low-temperature and intermediate-temperature reactivity with pressure. Since many real engines operate in the 20-40 atm pressure range, therefore, cool flames and warm flames are relevant and important flame regimes for high-pressure near-limit combustion applications. These calculations from this investigation will serve to advance the understanding of near-limit flame dynamics and provide guidance for experimental observation of different flame regimes.

title: PSI record PSI-62 (PSI-62) — Objectives
text:
PSI-62 — Concurrent Flame Spread Modeling using Flamelet Generated Manifolds in Microgravity with Comparison to BASS Experiments using Two-Color Tomography (PSI-62). Ground Investigation; platform: n/a; hardware: n/a; period 2019-05-01 to 2021-04-30.
Objectives: The objective of this research was to develop and validate new flamelet generated manifold (FGM) modeling techniques for concurrent flame spread in microgravity. Concurrent flame spread presented one of the greatest modeling challenges in combustion science due to the intricate coupling between heat transfer, mass transport, and chemical kinetics near the solid-vapor interface. Traditional modeling strategies often relied on hybridized turbulence and chemistry models that were not fully consistent and failed to capture important intermediate reaction pathways.
To overcome these shortcomings, this PSI grant advanced the use of an unsteady flamelet generated manifold (UFGM) framework that reduced the complexity of reacting systems by mapping them into lower-dimensional manifolds. The research aimed to leverage this methodology to simulate solid fuel combustion processes with high fidelity, using the NASA Burning and Suppression of Solids (BASS and BASS-II) experiments as benchmarks. Ultimately, the long-term goal was to enable accurate prediction of flammability limits for spacecraft materials and to provide a tool that could also serve as a subgrid-scale model in large-eddy simulations of fires, supporting spacecraft safety and hazard mitigation.

title: PSI record PSI-62 (PSI-62) — Approach
text:
PSI-62 — Concurrent Flame Spread Modeling using Flamelet Generated Manifolds in Microgravity with Comparison to BASS Experiments using Two-Color Tomography (PSI-62). Ground Investigation; platform: n/a; hardware: n/a; period 2019-05-01 to 2021-04-30.
Approach: The approach combined high-resolution computational modeling with experimental validation to study concurrent flame spread in microgravity. A previously developed computational framework was employed to run fully coupled simulations of fluid–solid responses, focusing on materials subject to charring and ablation. Within this framework, the unsteady FGM method was implemented and tested on various BASS geometries, including flat sheets, spheres, and rod-shaped polymethyl methacrylate (PMMA) samples, as well as wax cylinders.
Experimental imagery found in PSI from the BASS and BASS-II investigations was post-processed using newly developed two-color tomography methods with DSLR cameras, enabling 3D reconstructions of soot and temperature fields for direct comparison to model predictions. The evaluation metrics included flame geometry, temperature distribution, soot volume fraction, and flame spread rate, with special emphasis on reproducing the “Goldilocks” flammability zone reported by Olson and Ferkul. Comparative analyses were also carried out with a parallel NSF-supported terrestrial flame spread project, ensuring that the predictive capabilities of the UFGM approach were assessed across both microgravity and normal-gravity conditions.

title: PSI record PSI-62 (PSI-62) — Hypothesis
text:
PSI-62 — Concurrent Flame Spread Modeling using Flamelet Generated Manifolds in Microgravity with Comparison to BASS Experiments using Two-Color Tomography (PSI-62). Ground Investigation; platform: n/a; hardware: n/a; period 2019-05-01 to 2021-04-30.
Hypothesis: The unsteady flamelet generated manifold (UFGM) approach was believed to be able to accurately reproduce concurrent flame spread in microgravity, including phenomena such as the “Goldilocks” flammability zone, by coupling near-wall thermal, mass transport, and chemical processes with far-field flow dynamics.

title: PSI record PSI-62 (PSI-62) — Research impacts / Earth benefits
text:
PSI-62 — Concurrent Flame Spread Modeling using Flamelet Generated Manifolds in Microgravity with Comparison to BASS Experiments using Two-Color Tomography (PSI-62). Ground Investigation; platform: n/a; hardware: n/a; period 2019-05-01 to 2021-04-30.
Research impacts / Earth benefits: This research provides predictive tools for screening new materials’ flammability limits, which can lead to the design of safer spacecrafts. The development of Large Eddy Simulation subgrid models is expected to improve hazard assessment capabilities critical for managing fire risks during long-duration space missions and within confined spacecraft habitats. On Earth, these advancements could improve combustion modeling by deepening our understanding of coupled thermal, chemical, and flow processes, which betters fire safety standards. The computational methods being refined have the potential to enable more effective fire prevention and mitigation strategies and foster innovations in diagnostics and simulations applicable across a variety of combustion scenarios. Overall, this research can contribute significantly to safer human exploration in space and improvements to fire safety protocols on Earth.

title: PSI record PSI-60 (PSI-60) — Objectives
text:
PSI-60 — Computational and Experimental Analysis of SPICE Data Sets (PSI-60). Ground Investigation; platform: n/a; hardware: n/a; period 2019-06-05 to 2022-08-29.
Objectives: This ground investigation sought to increase understanding of the issues that control the large discrepancy between soot formation in 1g and in 0g flames. The objective of this investigation was to integrate computational and experimental methods to derive temperature distributions and soot volume fractions from the Smoke Point in Coflow Experiment (SPICE) data available in PSI. By analyzing over 1600 raw DSLR images and incorporating advanced soot models, the study sought to improve understanding of soot formation, oxidation, radiative re-absorption, and aggregate growth in heavily sooting flames. The work further aimed to reconcile microgravity and normal gravity flame behavior, identify key physical and chemical processes influencing smoke point development, and provide a framework for evaluating model parameter sensitivity.

title: PSI record PSI-60 (PSI-60) — Approach
text:
PSI-60 — Computational and Experimental Analysis of SPICE Data Sets (PSI-60). Ground Investigation; platform: n/a; hardware: n/a; period 2019-06-05 to 2022-08-29.
Approach: The approach was to combine image processing, experimental diagnostics, and detailed soot modeling. Raw Nikon NEF images were decoded into three color channels and analyzed using color-ratio pyrometry to extract soot temperature fields. Absolute light calibration from SPICE was then used to calculate soot volume fractions. For computational modeling, a coupled flow–species–soot system was implemented, modified to include radiation re-absorption and discrete-sectional aggregate formation. Simulations were performed for both Yale and ACME burner configurations under normal and microgravity conditions. Comparisons between experimental data and computed results guided sensitivity analyses of soot evolution parameters, including the effects of radiation, scattering, boundary conditions, and heat transfer to the burner structure.

title: PSI record PSI-60 (PSI-60) — Hypothesis
text:
PSI-60 — Computational and Experimental Analysis of SPICE Data Sets (PSI-60). Ground Investigation; platform: n/a; hardware: n/a; period 2019-06-05 to 2022-08-29.
Hypothesis: Microgravity conditions would produce longer, more diffuse flames with lower temperatures and increased soot concentrations compared to normal gravity, and that careful integration of experimental temperature fields into the simulations would reduce discrepancies between measured and predicted soot distributions.

title: PSI record PSI-60 (PSI-60) — Research impacts / Earth benefits
text:
PSI-60 — Computational and Experimental Analysis of SPICE Data Sets (PSI-60). Ground Investigation; platform: n/a; hardware: n/a; period 2019-06-05 to 2022-08-29.
Research impacts / Earth benefits: This study sought to enhance understanding of soot formation, flame structure, and radiative transport under microgravity and normal gravity, improving predictive models for combustion in both spacecraft and terrestrial systems. For space applications, the results support safer fire detection, suppression, and cleaner combustion technologies critical for long-duration missions. On Earth, the insights help reduce pollutant emissions, optimize combustion efficiency, and inform the design of cleaner energy and industrial systems.

title: PSI record PSI-26 (BASS) — Objectives
text:
BASS — Burning and Suppression of Solids (PSI-26). Microgravity Investigation; platform: International Space Station (ISS); hardware: Microgravity Science Glovebox; period 2009-10-01 to 2013-06-30.
Objectives: The two main objectives for BASS are to:
 1.) Begin to bridge the gap between the normal gravity NASA-STD-6001 Test#1 method, ground-based microgravity tests, and actual material flammability in microgravity. The relation between these can be investigated by observing flames burning for the longer times available in flight. Practical, realistic (thicker) fuels in typical geometries will be examined, including wake flames which have characteristics of a fire burning behind another object (for example, a fire burning in tight area which may not be easily accessible).
 2.) Assess the effectiveness of an inert, gaseous extinguishing agent (similar to that used on ISS) in putting out flames over different materials, geometries, preheating, and flow.

title: PSI record PSI-26 (BASS) — Approach
text:
BASS — Burning and Suppression of Solids (PSI-26). Microgravity Investigation; platform: International Space Station (ISS); hardware: Microgravity Science Glovebox; period 2009-10-01 to 2013-06-30.
Approach: The experiment was conducted aboard the International Space Station (ISS) inside the Microgravity Glove Box (MSG). Custom-made fabric samples consisting of 75% cotton and 25% fiberglass (by mass) measuring were used as a fuel source as well as Nomex fabric and Ultem. A Kanthal wire (29-gage)igniter was used to initiate combustion at one end of the fabric. Airflow was controlled using a variable speed fan, with airflow speeds reaching as high as 40 cm/s. The airflow was directed along the fuel surface in either the opposed or concurrent direction.

This investigation explored two primary air flow configurations; concurrent-flow and opposed-flow. With concurrent-flow air flows in the same direction as the flame spread and in opposed-flow air flows in the opposite direction of flame spread. Flames were observed in the top and edge profiles and data was collected on flame size, shape, color, spread rate, and potential flame quenching. The samples were placed in a small flow duct (76 mm x 76 mm cross section) that allowed for airflow across the fabric. Other sample shapes were utilized as well including spheres and cylinders.

title: PSI record PSI-26 (BASS) — Hypothesis
text:
BASS — Burning and Suppression of Solids (PSI-26). Microgravity Investigation; platform: International Space Station (ISS); hardware: Microgravity Science Glovebox; period 2009-10-01 to 2013-06-30.
Hypothesis: BASS experiments were based on the hypothesis that materials in microgravity, with adequate ventilation, burn as well if not better than the same material in normal gravity with other conditions being identical (pressure, oxygen concentration, temperature, etc.) To test this hypothesis with any but the thinnest materials requires extended microgravity time – longer than available in drop towers or parabolic aircraft.

title: PSI record PSI-26 (BASS) — Research impacts / Earth benefits
text:
BASS — Burning and Suppression of Solids (PSI-26). Microgravity Investigation; platform: International Space Station (ISS); hardware: Microgravity Science Glovebox; period 2009-10-01 to 2013-06-30.
Research impacts / Earth benefits: Current NASA spacecraft materials selection is based on a standard test method (NASA–STD–6001 Test 1) that segregates material based on 1-g behavior without consideration of low gravity effects. A critical element of this understanding is the radiative heat emission from the flame. These results are used in first order models and predictions of heat release in spacecraft fires and as a means to extend heat release data from tests like the NASA cone calorimeter test (NASA–STD–6001 Test 2) to a performance-based material selection process. Using nitrogen as a flame suppressant in microgravity provides a direct link to current and planned extinguishment techniques.
BASS results provide essential guidance to ground-based microgravity combustion research efforts. Detailed combustion models are validated using the simpler flow environment afforded by tests in microgravity. Once validated, they can be used to build more complex combustion models needed to capture the important details of flames burning in normal gravity. These models have wide applicability to the general understanding of many terrestrial combustion problems and will guide novel spacecraft design and ensure the safety of future crewed missions.

title: PSI record PSI-106 (SLICE) — Objectives
text:
SLICE — Structure and Liftoff In Combustion Experiment (PSI-106). Microgravity Investigation; platform: International Space Station (ISS); hardware: n/a; period ? to ?.
Objectives: Objective: The objective of this investigation is to better understand the structure and stability of laminar diffusion flames in microgravity.

Specific objectives of this investigation were:
1. To investigate the structure of laminar diffusion flames in microgravity to understand the stabilizing mechanisms at the flames base.
2. Determine the liftoff velocity limits for different fuels and burner diameters.
3. Evaluate the impact of fuel dilution with nitrogen on soot formation and flame stability.
4. Quantify the effects of microgravity on flame length and radiative heat loss compared to normal gravity conditions.
5. Validate numerical models for flame dynamics, soot production, and thermal radiation in non-premixed flames.

title: PSI record PSI-106 (SLICE) — Approach
text:
SLICE — Structure and Liftoff In Combustion Experiment (PSI-106). Microgravity Investigation; platform: International Space Station (ISS); hardware: n/a; period ? to ?.
Approach: The SLICE apparatus consisted of a fan-driven flow duct, exchangeable burner tubes, and integrated sensors to measure flow rates and temperature. This setup used several fuels such as methane, ethylene, and nitrogen-diluted mixtures. Flames were then manually ignited and observed under controlled coflow air conditions. A high resolution camera captured still images while sensor data was overlaid on these images. Calibration tests for airflow velocity, soot measurement, and the fans were conducted to ensure the accuracy of the results. More than 4,000 high-resolution images were captured across 13 testing experiments. Data was then analyzed to correlate flame structure with stability with flow dynamics and fuel properties.

title: PSI record PSI-106 (SLICE) — Hypothesis
text:
SLICE — Structure and Liftoff In Combustion Experiment (PSI-106). Microgravity Investigation; platform: International Space Station (ISS); hardware: n/a; period ? to ?.
Hypothesis: The hypothesis is that the structure and stability of laminar diffusion flames in microgravity are significantly influenced by burner diameter, coflow velocity, and fuel composition and are fundamentally different than flames observed on Earth.

title: PSI record PSI-98 (SAFFIRE-I) — Objectives
text:
SAFFIRE-I — Spacecraft Fire Safety Experiment-I (PSI-98). Microgravity Investigation; platform: International Space Station (ISS); hardware: Saffire 1 enclosure in Cygnus; period 2001-03-02 to 2008-02-28.
Objectives: The objectives of this investigation were to:
(1) determine how rapidly a large scale fire grows in low-gravity and (2) investigate the low-g flammability limits compared to those obtained in NASA’s normal
gravity material flammability screening test.

title: PSI record PSI-98 (SAFFIRE-I) — Approach
text:
SAFFIRE-I — Spacecraft Fire Safety Experiment-I (PSI-98). Microgravity Investigation; platform: International Space Station (ISS); hardware: Saffire 1 enclosure in Cygnus; period 2001-03-02 to 2008-02-28.
Approach: The Saffire-1 experiments was performed on the Orbital Science’s Cygnus resupply vehicle after it deberthed from the ISS. The sample material for Saffire-I is a composite fabric called Sibal consisting of cotton on a fiberglass substrate (75% cotton, 25% fiberglass by weight). It has been used in many space experiments because it burns like cotton but maintains structural integrity after the cotton is consumed. The sample was approximately 0.94 meters long and 0.4 meters wide, simulating a large piece of flammable fabric. The Saffire-1 flight unit had a sample card installed in the middle of a large flow duct. Air is drawn through the flow duct by fans located at the top of the duct with flow straighteners at the bottom of the experiment module. Saffire-I was conducted at an air flow velocity of 20 cm/s. Once the sample was ignited flame images were captured using two cameras. In addition, thermocouples provided flow, flame, and plume temperatures, two radiometers recorded flame radiation, solid state sensors were used to measure pressure, CO2 and O2 mole faction, and two anemometer tracked flow velocity. All data was compressed, and subsequently downlinked.

title: PSI record PSI-98 (SAFFIRE-I) — Hypothesis
text:
SAFFIRE-I — Spacecraft Fire Safety Experiment-I (PSI-98). Microgravity Investigation; platform: International Space Station (ISS); hardware: Saffire 1 enclosure in Cygnus; period 2001-03-02 to 2008-02-28.
Hypothesis: This investigation hypothesizes that due to large differences between fire behavior in normal and reduced gravity, the use of terrestrial fires and fire standards to design spacecraft fire safety systems presents an inherent risk to the vehicle because of the significant level of uncertainty. While this approach has been successful thus far, the uncertainty and risk will increase as exploration missions venture further from earth with considerably longer transit times for a safe return. There is a significant lack of microgravity data available for spacecraft designers on which to base their fire safety designs and procedures. To address this knowledge gap, this investigation proposed to conduct large-scale fire safety experiments in an expendable spacecraft without risk to a crew.

title: PSI record PSI-98 (SAFFIRE-I) — Research impacts / Earth benefits
text:
SAFFIRE-I — Spacecraft Fire Safety Experiment-I (PSI-98). Microgravity Investigation; platform: International Space Station (ISS); hardware: Saffire 1 enclosure in Cygnus; period 2001-03-02 to 2008-02-28.
Research impacts / Earth benefits: The Saffire-I experiment provides a new way to study a realistic fire on an exploration vehicle, which has not been possible in the past because the risks are too high. Instruments on an unmanned cargo vessel measure oxygen, carbon dioxide, heat, pressure and flame growth, and two video cameras provide views of the flame. Results determine microgravity flammability limits for several spacecraft materials, help to validate NASA’s material selection criteria, and how microgravity and limited oxygen affect flame size. The investigation is crucial for the safety of current and future space missions. Studying fire in small, sealed environments such as the Cygnus cargo supply vehicle benefits fire safety and prevention efforts on Earth, including inside mines, airplanes, or submarines.

title: PSI record PSI-117 (PSI-117) — Objectives
text:
PSI-117 — Effect of External Thermo-Convective Perturbation on Cool Flame Dynamics: A Multidimensional Multi-Physics CFD Analysis (PSI-117). Ground Investigation; platform: n/a; hardware: n/a; period 2017-02-15 to 2022-02-14.
Objectives: The objective of this ground investigation was to use flight data obtained from PSI through NASA’s Flame Extinguishment Experiment (FLEX) to quantify how externally imposed thermal and convective perturbations regulated the dynamics and ultimate fate of already established droplet cool flames, and to explain run-to-run variability by isolating the roles of deliberate heating and unintentional drift-induced convection. Focusing on both small and large droplets, the work mapped stability windows for ignition, sustained oscillation, transitions to hot ignition and warm-flame behavior, and extinction under microgravity. By leveraging and extending the FLEX data in the PSI, this study produced reusable models and sensitivity analyses that coupled low-temperature chemistry with transport and radiative effects.

title: PSI record PSI-117 (PSI-117) — Approach
text:
PSI-117 — Effect of External Thermo-Convective Perturbation on Cool Flame Dynamics: A Multidimensional Multi-Physics CFD Analysis (PSI-117). Ground Investigation; platform: n/a; hardware: n/a; period 2017-02-15 to 2022-02-14.
Approach: OpenFOAM was used to develop a 3-D CFD model of n-alkane droplet cool flames in microgravity, coupling variable-density Navier–Stokes flow with low-temperature combustion chemistry, coupled heat and mass transfer, and radiation. Model fidelity was established against ISS FLEX measurements, after which controlled simulations examined three forcing modes (i) convection alone to mimic droplet drift, (ii) imposed heat flux, and (iii) combined convection plus heating applied to both large (1–4 mm) and sub-millimeter (~0.5 mm) droplets.

To accelerate progress, the study began with simplified chemistry and transitioned to reduced mechanisms for parameter sweeps over forcing amplitude and frequency, ambient composition (including ozone-assisted cases), and pressure. From each case, predictive observables were extracted (ignition delay, oscillation frequency and amplitude, stand-off and extinction diameters), and were used to construct stability maps that delineated conditions for cool-flame onset, persistence, and quenching. These maps were reconciled with FLEX observations and were used to guide next-generation test matrices for both large- and small-droplet experiments.

title: PSI record PSI-117 (PSI-117) — Hypothesis
text:
PSI-117 — Effect of External Thermo-Convective Perturbation on Cool Flame Dynamics: A Multidimensional Multi-Physics CFD Analysis (PSI-117). Ground Investigation; platform: n/a; hardware: n/a; period 2017-02-15 to 2022-02-14.
Hypothesis: External thermo-convective perturbations (imposed temperature gradients, non-uniform heating, oscillatory/shear inflow) were expected to govern cool-flame ignition, oscillation, transition to hot ignition, and extinction by shifting residence time and scalar dissipation. In microgravity, where buoyancy was suppressed, this forcing was anticipated to dominate transport. A multidimensional, multi-physics CFD model was used to map perturbation-dependent stability boundaries and predict observables for comparison with FLEX data.

title: PSI record PSI-117 (PSI-117) — Research impacts / Earth benefits
text:
PSI-117 — Effect of External Thermo-Convective Perturbation on Cool Flame Dynamics: A Multidimensional Multi-Physics CFD Analysis (PSI-117). Ground Investigation; platform: n/a; hardware: n/a; period 2017-02-15 to 2022-02-14.
Research impacts / Earth benefits: Space Benefits: Potential to improve spacecraft fire-safety modeling by resolving cool-flame/extinction behavior in microgravity; leverages FLEX to define safer operating envelopes/materials.
Earth Benefits: Advances low-temperature combustion understanding relevant to engine knock, efficiency, and emissions; delivers validated CFD tools transferrable to practical combustors.

title: PSI record PSI-115 (PSI-115) — Objectives
text:
PSI-115 — Utilization of the Smoke Aerosol Measurement Experiment Data for Advanced Modeling and Simulation of Smoke Generation in Micro-Gravity (PSI-115). Ground Investigation; platform: Not Applicable; hardware: n/a; period 2017-01-30 to 2019-12-31.
Objectives: The objective of this investigation was to use numerical simulation to explore the influence of gravity on pyrolysis smoke growth from a fundamental perspective. The intention of this effort is to quantify the differences between microgravity and Earth gravity smoke, and to identify the fluid dynamic mechanisms that cause the differences.

title: PSI record PSI-115 (PSI-115) — Approach
text:
PSI-115 — Utilization of the Smoke Aerosol Measurement Experiment Data for Advanced Modeling and Simulation of Smoke Generation in Micro-Gravity (PSI-115). Ground Investigation; platform: Not Applicable; hardware: n/a; period 2017-01-30 to 2019-12-31.
Approach: The formation and growth of dibutyl-phthalate (DBP) particles in Earth gravity and microgravity environments was simulated. Direct numerical simulation via a Navier-Stokes nodal approach was utlilized. The smoke originates from pyrolysis vapor expelled from a heated sample in a geometry similar to that considered in the SAME experiments. This study considered two cross-flow velocities of sufficiently low speed that buoyancy cannot be neglected in the presence of gravity. Simulations are presented to assess the dependence of particle size distributions on thermophoresis, particle settling, and flow geometry. The final report for this investigation introduces the simulation and modeling methodology, followed by a description of the flow geometry and the parameter space under consideration.The differences in the wake geometry attributable to buoyancy for the lower of two flow speeds was examined. Instantaneous scalar fields were used to describe particle accumulation and growth in the buoyant and non-buoyant wakes that form downstream of the hot vapor source.

title: PSI record PSI-115 (PSI-115) — Hypothesis
text:
PSI-115 — Utilization of the Smoke Aerosol Measurement Experiment Data for Advanced Modeling and Simulation of Smoke Generation in Micro-Gravity (PSI-115). Ground Investigation; platform: Not Applicable; hardware: n/a; period 2017-01-30 to 2019-12-31.
Hypothesis: Without buoyancy, mixing and heat transfer are reduced, the time-temperature history of the combustion vapors (or particle precursors) and particle trajectories are significantly altered, changing the composition of the smoke. The chemical composition of the burning material also affects the characteristics of the smoke generated.

title: PSI record PSI-115 (PSI-115) — Research impacts / Earth benefits
text:
PSI-115 — Utilization of the Smoke Aerosol Measurement Experiment Data for Advanced Modeling and Simulation of Smoke Generation in Micro-Gravity (PSI-115). Ground Investigation; platform: Not Applicable; hardware: n/a; period 2017-01-30 to 2019-12-31.
Research impacts / Earth benefits: Models and tools that characterize particles generated as smoke can be used to ascertain how temperature, gravity, and material properties affect the smoke produced. This would directly lead to better smoke detection devices and prevent fires that can lead to loss of materiel and loss of life.

title: PSI record PSI-47 (DAFT / DAFT-2) — Objectives
text:
DAFT / DAFT-2 — Dust and Aerosol Measurement Feasibility Test / Dust and Aerosol Measurement Feasibility Test-2 (PSI-47). Microgravity Investigation; platform: International Space Station (ISS); hardware: TSI P-Trak; period 2003-03-01 to 2009-06-01.
Objectives: The focus of DAFT / DAFT-2 was to mitigate the risk for the Smoke Aerosol Measurement Experiment (SAME). SAME relied on a commercially available condensate nuclei counter, the TSI P-Trak, to quantify smoke aerosols in a microgravity environment, however there were concerns that th P-Trak would not be reliable in microgravity as it relies on gravity to recycle isopropyl alcohol used in the measurement process.
DAFT / DAFT-2 tests that a modified P-Trak particulate counter would be accurate in microgravity.

Summarized objectives include:
 1) Demonstrate the Functionality of the Modified TSI P-Trak in Microgravity
 2) Compare the TSI P-Trak Performance against the DustTrak control
 3) Create and Analyze Aerosol Standards in Microgravity
 4) Ensure the reliability of future aerosol experiments

title: PSI record PSI-47 (DAFT / DAFT-2) — Approach
text:
DAFT / DAFT-2 — Dust and Aerosol Measurement Feasibility Test / Dust and Aerosol Measurement Feasibility Test-2 (PSI-47). Microgravity Investigation; platform: International Space Station (ISS); hardware: TSI P-Trak; period 2003-03-01 to 2009-06-01.
Approach: The experimental approach consists of the following components:

 1) Modification of Instrumentation: TSI P-Trak was modified for use in microgravity by redesigning the condenser tube to use capillary forces for recycling isopropyl alcohol and removing the mercury switch responsible for detecting instrument orientation.
 2) Aerosol Generation: Arizona Red Dust (ARD) was chosen as an aerosol standard due to its ease of dispersion. The ARD was aerosolized with GN2 to create particle samples. The aerosol was contained within 15-liter Mylar bags.
 3) On-Orbit Testing: The modified P-Trak gathered data from counting aerosol particles and these data were compared to the DustTrak CNC specifically designed to work in microgravity.

title: PSI record PSI-47 (DAFT / DAFT-2) — Hypothesis
text:
DAFT / DAFT-2 — Dust and Aerosol Measurement Feasibility Test / Dust and Aerosol Measurement Feasibility Test-2 (PSI-47). Microgravity Investigation; platform: International Space Station (ISS); hardware: TSI P-Trak; period 2003-03-01 to 2009-06-01.
Hypothesis: The TSI P-Trak operates by condensing isopropanol around aerosol particulates that are subsequently laser counted. It was hypothesized that the P-Trak would not work in microgravity due to two potential failure modes that exist. 1) the system would clog or become obscured by isopropanol, and 2) the internal air-flow dynamics of the optics chamber of the device will cause an over counting of particulates.

The TSI P-Trak was modified for microgravity use via using capillary action to recycle the isopropanol. Therefore, there are two basic hypotheses:
 1) that the P-Trak, as modified for use in SAME, would function normally in microgravity.
 2) that the aerosol created and filtered per the experiment design would be within the measurement capabilities of the test devices.

title: PSI record PSI-47 (DAFT / DAFT-2) — Research impacts / Earth benefits
text:
DAFT / DAFT-2 — Dust and Aerosol Measurement Feasibility Test / Dust and Aerosol Measurement Feasibility Test-2 (PSI-47). Microgravity Investigation; platform: International Space Station (ISS); hardware: TSI P-Trak; period 2003-03-01 to 2009-06-01.
Research impacts / Earth benefits: Extended duration space flight missions with larger vessels will require fire detection systems with increased reliability and sensitivity. This research will impact the development of novel fire and smoke detection systems for the International Space Station and future spacecrafts. Additionally, the successful adaptation of the TSI P-Trak for microgravity can inform the design of instruments for use in other challenging Earth environments, such as submarines or underwater laboratories where accurate detection of smoke can save lives.

title: PSI record PSI-100 (SAFFIRE-III) — Objectives
text:
SAFFIRE-III — Spacecraft Fire Experiment-III (PSI-100). Microgravity Investigation; platform: International Space Station (ISS); hardware: Saffire III enclosure in Cygnus; period 2017-04-18 to ?.
Objectives: The objectives of this investigation were to:
(1) determine how rapidly a large scale fire grows in low-gravity and (2) investigate the low-g flammability limits compared to those obtained in NASA’s normal gravity material flammability screening test.

title: PSI record PSI-100 (SAFFIRE-III) — Approach
text:
SAFFIRE-III — Spacecraft Fire Experiment-III (PSI-100). Microgravity Investigation; platform: International Space Station (ISS); hardware: Saffire III enclosure in Cygnus; period 2017-04-18 to ?.
Approach: The Saffire-III experiments were performed on the Orbital Science’s Cygnus resupply vehicle after it deberthed from the ISS. As a follow on to the Saffire 1 investigation, the Saffire III investigation also used SIBAL as the sample material. However, the experiments were conducted at a flow velocity of 30 cm/s compared to 20 cm/s during Saffire I. The flow was either concurrent or opposed. Once the sample was ignited flame images were captured using two cameras. In addition, thermocouples provided flow, flame, and plume temperatures, two radiometers recorded flame radiation, solid state sensors were used to measure pressure, CO2 and O2 mole faction, and two anemometer tracked flow velocity. All data was compressed, and subsequently downlinked. Details related to samples and experimental parameters are provided in the Experimental Details file in the Science document folder.

title: PSI record PSI-100 (SAFFIRE-III) — Hypothesis
text:
SAFFIRE-III — Spacecraft Fire Experiment-III (PSI-100). Microgravity Investigation; platform: International Space Station (ISS); hardware: Saffire III enclosure in Cygnus; period 2017-04-18 to ?.
Hypothesis: This investigation hypothesizes that due to large differences between fire behavior in normal and reduced gravity, the use of terrestrial fires and fire standards to design spacecraft fire safety systems presents an inherent risk to the vehicle because of the significant level of uncertainty. While this approach has been successful thus far, the uncertainty and risk will increase as exploration missions venture further from earth with considerably longer transit times for a safe return. There is a significant lack of microgravity data available for spacecraft designers on which to base their fire safety designs and procedures. To address this knowledge gap, this investigation proposed to conduct large-scale fire safety experiments in an expendable spacecraft without risk to a crew.

title: PSI record PSI-100 (SAFFIRE-III) — Research impacts / Earth benefits
text:
SAFFIRE-III — Spacecraft Fire Experiment-III (PSI-100). Microgravity Investigation; platform: International Space Station (ISS); hardware: Saffire III enclosure in Cygnus; period 2017-04-18 to ?.
Research impacts / Earth benefits: The Saffire-I experiment provides a new way to study a realistic fire on an exploration vehicle, which has not been possible in the past because the risks are too high. Instruments on an unmanned cargo vessel measure oxygen, carbon dioxide, heat, pressure and flame growth, and two video cameras provide views of the flame. Results determine microgravity flammability limits for several spacecraft materials, help to validate NASA’s material selection criteria, and how microgravity and limited oxygen affect flame size. The investigation is crucial for the safety of current and future space missions. Studying fire in small, sealed environments such as the Cygnus cargo supply vehicle benefits fire safety and prevention efforts on Earth, including inside mines, airplanes, or submarines.

title: PSI record PSI-39 (CFI) — Objectives
text:
CFI — Cool Flames Investigation (PSI-39). Microgravity Investigation; platform: International Space Station (ISS); hardware: Multi-User Droplet Combustion Apparatus (MDCA)  Combustion Integrated Rack (CIR); period 2020-10-01 to 2021-10-20.
Objectives: The objectives of this investigation are to:
 1) Examine the combustion behavior of n-dodecane and mixtures of n-dodecane/iso-dodecane at pressures ranging from 0.25 atm to 5 atm.
 2) Analyze the effects of helium dilution on cool flame behavior.
 3) Examine the behavior of combustion characteristics.
 4) Investigate the relationship between droplet size, pressure, and flame extinction, and (5) understand the consequence of soot formation during cool flame combustion.

title: PSI record PSI-39 (CFI) — Approach
text:
CFI — Cool Flames Investigation (PSI-39). Microgravity Investigation; platform: International Space Station (ISS); hardware: Multi-User Droplet Combustion Apparatus (MDCA)  Combustion Integrated Rack (CIR); period 2020-10-01 to 2021-10-20.
Approach: The Combustion Integrated Rack (CIR) contains the Multi-User Droplet Combustion Apparatus (MDCA) which facilitates the controlled combustion of fuel droplets. A system of gas bottles and fuel syringes delivers the desired gas mixture to the combustion chamber ranging from 0.25 to 0.5 atm. Droplets of fuel are dispensed and suspended between hypodermic needles or tethered using silicon-carbide fibers. A hot-wire igniter is positioned near the droplet for ignition. After ignition the wire is retracted. Fuels observed include n-dodecane, farnesane, and mixtures of n-dodecane/iso-dodecane. Fuels diluted with molecular oxygen, atomic nitrogen, and helium to study the influence on flame extinction and dynamics. Flames were observed with a black-and-white camera for droplet size measurements. A UV camera was used for capturing the OH* radical emissions and flame size. Other high resolution cameras were used for monitoring and documentation. Narrow-band and wide-band radiometers for analyzed flame radiation.

title: PSI record PSI-39 (CFI) — Hypothesis
text:
CFI — Cool Flames Investigation (PSI-39). Microgravity Investigation; platform: International Space Station (ISS); hardware: Multi-User Droplet Combustion Apparatus (MDCA)  Combustion Integrated Rack (CIR); period 2020-10-01 to 2021-10-20.
Hypothesis: Flame combustion of liquid hydrocarbon fuels such as n-dodecane, n-dodecane/iso-dodecane mixtures, and faresane in microgravity can provide insights into low-temperature chemical kinetics, revealing critical parameters like droplet extinction diameters and flame dynamics that are not observable on Earth.

title: PSI record PSI-39 (CFI) — Research impacts / Earth benefits
text:
CFI — Cool Flames Investigation (PSI-39). Microgravity Investigation; platform: International Space Station (ISS); hardware: Multi-User Droplet Combustion Apparatus (MDCA)  Combustion Integrated Rack (CIR); period 2020-10-01 to 2021-10-20.
Research impacts / Earth benefits: A basic understanding of cool flames is important for understanding ignition phenomena of practical fuels and fuel additives. Cool flames play a key role in the development and selection of new fuels and the design of advanced engines such as clean, high-efficiency Homogeneous Charge Compression Ignition (HCCI) engines. The research will also help combustion chemists to develop new computational models to compute combustion performance in for many practical applications on earth, including an understanding of how cool flame reactivity determines octane and cetane number for fuels in spark ignition and diesel engines.
Cool Flames Investigation (CFI) will provide critical validation for complex chemical kinetic mechanisms, advance the understanding of flame dynamics and instabilities in low-temperature combustion, and support the design of safer spacecraft systems by refining knowledge of combustion in microgravity environments.

title: PSI record PSI-102 (SAME) — Objectives
text:
SAME — Smoke and Aerosol Measurement Experiment (PSI-102). Microgravity Investigation; platform: International Space Station (ISS); hardware: Comparitive Soot Diagnostic Hardware; period 2001-03-02 to 2008-02-28.
Objectives: One of the major goals of this investigation was to quantify the sizes that the liquid smoke particulate achieves in low gravity and to relate the droplet size distribution to the smoke generation and smoke transport conditions in the experiment. A numerical code was to be developed to predict the smoke droplet growth as a function of the fuel pyrolysis rate, the thermodynamic properties of the pyrolysis vapor, and the flow environment.

title: PSI record PSI-102 (SAME) — Approach
text:
SAME — Smoke and Aerosol Measurement Experiment (PSI-102). Microgravity Investigation; platform: International Space Station (ISS); hardware: Comparitive Soot Diagnostic Hardware; period 2001-03-02 to 2008-02-28.
Approach: The crew installed the near field hardware in the Glovebox, attached the Far Field Box to the Glovebox, and positioned the video cameras. The operator then ran the self diagnostic procedures on the two smoke detectors and activated the video cameras, turned on the igniter for a predefined period of time (15 to 60 seconds), and initiated the thermophoretic soot samplers to sample the smoke. The actual duration of each combustion event was typically 2 minutes. After flight, the particulate collected on the thermophoretic probes were analyzed using a Transmission Electron microscope (TEM) to determine primary and aggregate particle dimensions. The remains of the samples were weighed to determine their mass loss. The digital data was transcribed from the video record and analyzed to determine the response of the detectors. Once the flight mass loss rates were determined, 1-g operation conditions to produce the same loss were determined.The measurements were made using smoke generated by overheated spacecraft materials where variables such as the sample temperature, flow field, and particle aging time were more rigorously controlled.

title: PSI record PSI-102 (SAME) — Hypothesis
text:
SAME — Smoke and Aerosol Measurement Experiment (PSI-102). Microgravity Investigation; platform: International Space Station (ISS); hardware: Comparitive Soot Diagnostic Hardware; period 2001-03-02 to 2008-02-28.
Hypothesis: The three hypotheses that motivated this investigation:
In a μg environment, with the absence of the strong buoyancy-induced flows, smoke particle growth from a pyrolyzing/smoldering source, as a result of nucleation, condensation, and coagulation, will lead to larger particles compared to those produced in 1g. The formation of the larger particles is favored by the expected higher vapor concentration and smoke residence times near the source due to the reduced velocities and mixing at μg conditions. In particular, it is hypothesized that liquid aerosol smokes produced in microgravity will exhibit substantially larger droplet sizes than under the same conditions in normal gravity (with a corresponding decrease in the particle number density for the same mass of smoke). The change in the size distribution and number density will, in turn, affect the response of the smoke detectors and possibly result in some detectors not producing an alarm when exposed to this smoke.

title: PSI record PSI-102 (SAME) — Research impacts / Earth benefits
text:
SAME — Smoke and Aerosol Measurement Experiment (PSI-102). Microgravity Investigation; platform: International Space Station (ISS); hardware: Comparitive Soot Diagnostic Hardware; period 2001-03-02 to 2008-02-28.
Research impacts / Earth benefits: The SAME experiment will provide technology for an advanced fire detector for future spacecraft that will be used for long duration missions. SAME will provide quantitative data on the sensitivity of these detectors to reduced gravity smokes that will allow evaluation of the adequacy of these existing technologies using relevant data. The current Fire Prevention, Detection, and Suppression (FPDS) program plan allows for the re-evaluation of future sensor technology, to allow new technology and capability to be utilized. The results from SAME are needed to provide the reduced gravity baseline data against which future detection technology developments can be evaluated.The smoke detectors developed from the results of SAME can also be useful in other extreme environments on Earth, such as submarines or underwater laboratories. Accurate detection of smoke in these environments can save lives.

title: PSI record PSI-159 (ACME CFI-G) — Objectives
text:
ACME CFI-G — Advanced Combustion via Microgravity Experiments / Cool Flames Investigation with Gases (PSI-159). Microgravity Investigation; platform: International Space Station (ISS); hardware: ACME  Combustion Integrated Rack (CIR); period ? to ?.
Objectives: 1. Plan and support flight testing on the International Space Station (ISS).
2. Determine the conditions for which cool diffusion flames occur for propane, n-butane, and n-pentane; normal and inverse flames; and a broad range of Zst, Tad, and fluent flow rate.
3. Support the flight tests with advanced CFD simulations.
4. Identify or develop a chemical kinetics mechanism that yields good agreement between the CFD predictions and the ISS measurements.
5. Disseminate the results as widely as possible.

title: PSI record PSI-159 (ACME CFI-G) — Approach
text:
ACME CFI-G — Advanced Combustion via Microgravity Experiments / Cool Flames Investigation with Gases (PSI-159). Microgravity Investigation; platform: International Space Station (ISS); hardware: ACME  Combustion Integrated Rack (CIR); period ? to ?.
Approach: Perform spherical diffusion flame tests aboard the International Space Station. Consider multiple fuels, a range of reactant dilutions, flow rates, and pressures for normal and inverse convection directions. Observe the flames with a broad suite of cameras, radiometers, photomultiplier tubes, and thermocouples.

title: PSI record PSI-159 (ACME CFI-G) — Hypothesis
text:
ACME CFI-G — Advanced Combustion via Microgravity Experiments / Cool Flames Investigation with Gases (PSI-159). Microgravity Investigation; platform: International Space Station (ISS); hardware: ACME  Combustion Integrated Rack (CIR); period ? to ?.
Hypothesis: The hypotheses of this research are that testing aboard the ISS can demonstrate the following for the first time, contributing to an improved understanding of cool flame kinetics.
 1. Steady-state cool diffusion flames on spherical porous burners.
 2. Cool diffusion flames burning propane, n-butane, and n-pentane.
 3. Cool diffusion flames for a wide range of Zst, Tad, and pressures.
 4. Inverse cool diffusion flames.
 5. Cool diffusion flames for which a decrease in fluent flow rate will cause extinction, whereas an increase will cause a transition to a hot diffusion flame, with oscillation possible between hot and cool flames.

title: PSI record PSI-159 (ACME CFI-G) — Research impacts / Earth benefits
text:
ACME CFI-G — Advanced Combustion via Microgravity Experiments / Cool Flames Investigation with Gases (PSI-159). Microgravity Investigation; platform: International Space Station (ISS); hardware: ACME  Combustion Integrated Rack (CIR); period ? to ?.
Research impacts / Earth benefits: Combustion provides 86% of the world’s energy and an even higher fraction of the energy used for transportation. The internal combustion engines used for transportation generally have thermal efficiencies of 38% or lower because of thermal losses. These efficiencies may increase to 60% if future engines can take advantage of ultra-lean combustion. However, this progress is being impeded by the limited understanding of the chemistry of cool flames. Research into cool diffusion flames (whose peak temperatures are 500 – 1000 K) has grown exponentially since they were discovered in 2012. The measurements performed for this project will help to test and advance cool flame kinetics mechanisms. This should facilitate the development of more efficient internal combustion engines.

title: PSI record PSI-101 (SAME-R) — Objectives
text:
SAME-R — Smoke Aerosol Measurement Experiment-Reflight (PSI-101). Microgravity Investigation; platform: International Space Station (ISS); hardware: Comparitive Soot Diagnostic Hardware; Refer to final report; period 2010-07-01 to 2010-09-30.
Objectives: Similar to the original SAME investigation, the primary objective of the SAME-R investigation was to quantify the sizes that the liquid smoke particulate achieves in low gravity and to relate the droplet size distribution to the smoke generation and smoke transport conditions in the experiment. One of the problems encountered during the SAME investigation was that after the thermal precipitators were returned to the ground, it was found that all the TEM grids were severely contaminated with some unidentified foreign particles, making these grids unusable although some of them showed shapes of certain types of smoke particles. Based on that experience the SAME-R investigation employed several modification covering new materials, extended operating conditions, and diagnostic equipments.

title: PSI record PSI-101 (SAME-R) — Approach
text:
SAME-R — Smoke Aerosol Measurement Experiment-Reflight (PSI-101). Microgravity Investigation; platform: International Space Station (ISS); hardware: Comparitive Soot Diagnostic Hardware; Refer to final report; period 2010-07-01 to 2010-09-30.
Approach: SAME-R utilized the SAME hardware used on-orbit. Based on the experience gained from SAME, SAME-R included the following modifications: 1) a new test material,
Pyrell®, an intumescent fire-retardant foam by Foamex, was introduced to replace DBP samples, 2) test conditions were broadened including higher heating temperatures and no-flow during sample heating time, and 3) a new instrument, M-pass, developed in-house GRC, was used to replace one of the two Commercial Diagnostic Enclosures that includes a DustTrak and an ionization detector used in SAME. SAME-R flight tests were conducted from July 16, to September 9, 2010, successfully completing 66 test points. After SAME-R flight tests, three major post–flight ground tests were performed to improve data reduction process and to validate the lognormal distribution assumption, the key to the moment method employed by SAME and SAME-R.

title: PSI record PSI-101 (SAME-R) — Hypothesis
text:
SAME-R — Smoke Aerosol Measurement Experiment-Reflight (PSI-101). Microgravity Investigation; platform: International Space Station (ISS); hardware: Comparitive Soot Diagnostic Hardware; Refer to final report; period 2010-07-01 to 2010-09-30.
Hypothesis: The three hypotheses that motivated the original SAME investigation is also applicable for the reflight SAME-R investigation:
In a μg environment, with the absence of the strong buoyancy-induced flows, smoke particle growth from a pyrolyzing/smoldering source, as a result of nucleation, condensation, and coagulation, will lead to larger particles compared to those produced in 1g. The formation of the larger particles is favored by the expected higher vapor concentration and smoke residence times near the source due to the reduced velocities and mixing at μg conditions. In particular, it is hypothesized that liquid aerosol smokes produced in microgravity will exhibit substantially larger droplet sizes than under the same conditions in normal gravity (with a corresponding decrease in the particle number density for the same mass of smoke). The change in the size distribution and number density will, in turn, affect the response of the smoke detectors and possibly result in some detectors not producing an alarm when exposed to this smoke.

title: PSI record PSI-101 (SAME-R) — Research impacts / Earth benefits
text:
SAME-R — Smoke Aerosol Measurement Experiment-Reflight (PSI-101). Microgravity Investigation; platform: International Space Station (ISS); hardware: Comparitive Soot Diagnostic Hardware; Refer to final report; period 2010-07-01 to 2010-09-30.
Research impacts / Earth benefits: Along with the results from the original SAME investigation, the results from SAME-R can lead to technology for an advanced fire detector for future spacecraft that will be used for long duration missions. SAME will provide quantitative data on the sensitivity of these detectors to reduced gravity smokes that will allow evaluation of the adequacy of these existing technologies using relevant data. The current Fire Prevention, Detection, and Suppression (FPDS) program plan allows for the re-evaluation of future sensor technology, to allow new technology and capability to be utilized. The results from SAME are needed to provide the reduced gravity baseline data against which future detection technology developments can be evaluated. The smoke detectors developed from the results of SAME can also be useful in other extreme environments on Earth, such as submarines or underwater laboratories. Accurate detection of smoke in these environments can save lives.

title: PSI record PSI-25 (BASS-II) — Objectives
text:
BASS-II — Burning and Suppression of Solids - II (PSI-25). Microgravity Investigation; platform: International Space Station (ISS); hardware: Microgravity Science Glovebox (MSG); period 2010-01-01 to 2022-12-31.
Objectives: BASS-II results contribute to the combustion computational models used in the design of fire detection and suppression systems in microgravity and on Earth.
Objectives Include:
 1) Study the ignition, flame growth, flame spread, and extinction limits for solid fuels burning in low-velocity forced flows in microgravity.
 2) Begin to bridge the gap between the normal gravity NASA-STD-6001 Test #1 method, ground-based microgravity tests, and actual material flammability in microgravity.
 3) Provide SoFIE PIs with preliminary data to refine Science Requirements.
 4) Practical, realistic (thicker) fuels in typical geometries will be examined, including slabs, cylinders, and spherical sections.

The primary variables include:
 • Forced flow velocity (speed and direction)
 • Ambient oxygen concentration (via working volume nitrogen vitiation)
 • Sample geometry (rods, spherical section, slabs, films, and fabric sheets

title: PSI record PSI-25 (BASS-II) — Approach
text:
BASS-II — Burning and Suppression of Solids - II (PSI-25). Microgravity Investigation; platform: International Space Station (ISS); hardware: Microgravity Science Glovebox (MSG); period 2010-01-01 to 2022-12-31.
Approach: To summarize, BASS-II's approach, microgravity combustion tests were performed aboard the International Space Station. Active crew support for real-time “lab partner” operations. The wind tunnel was installed in the Microgravity Science Glovebox which supplied power, imaging, and a level of containment. Fuel samples were mounted inside a small wind tunnel which could impose airflow speeds up to 40 cm/s. Main variables are airflow speed and oxygen concentration (oxygen varied below 21% by adding nitrogen). Flame appearance, flame growth, and spread rates were determined in both the opposed and concurrent flow.

title: PSI record PSI-25 (BASS-II) — Hypothesis
text:
BASS-II — Burning and Suppression of Solids - II (PSI-25). Microgravity Investigation; platform: International Space Station (ISS); hardware: Microgravity Science Glovebox (MSG); period 2010-01-01 to 2022-12-31.
Hypothesis: BASS–II tests the hypothesis that materials in microgravity, with adequate ventilation, burn as well if not better than the same material in normal gravity with other conditions being identical (pressure, O2
concentration, temperature, etc.). NASA tests and controls materials from a flammability perspective using an upward burning test in normal gravity, which is considered to be the worst-case geometry for
flammability of the material on Earth. However, it may not be conservative for flammability in space. Testing at constant O2 mole fractions permits studying flame spread and extinction at low and high flow speed. We are interested in finding the fundamental limit for a given material.

title: PSI record PSI-25 (BASS-II) — Research impacts / Earth benefits
text:
BASS-II — Burning and Suppression of Solids - II (PSI-25). Microgravity Investigation; platform: International Space Station (ISS); hardware: Microgravity Science Glovebox (MSG); period 2010-01-01 to 2022-12-31.
Research impacts / Earth benefits: A primary goal of BASS-II is improved spacecraft fire safety, improved understanding of combustion in space and how to avoid it. If you’re on a mission far from Earth, a fire can be catastrophic. BASS-II helps engineers select the safest materials and improve firefighting methods on future space missions. In outer space, fuels burn as oval balls rather than with an upward pointed cone flame as they do on Earth. This simpler combustion process enables researchers to evaluate computer models of fuel burning. These models can then be used to more accurately study flames on Earth, such as in wildfires, building fires, energy recapture from waste recycling, and other combustion problems.

title: PSI record PSI-99 (SAFFIRE-II) — Objectives
text:
SAFFIRE-II — Spacecraft Fire Experiment-II (PSI-99). Microgravity Investigation; platform: Cygnus Spacecraft; hardware: Cygnus Pressurized Cargo Module  SAFFIRE; period 2016-09-30 to 2017-04-01.
Objectives: The objectives of SAFFIRE-II are to determine how rapidly a large scale fire grows in low-gravity and to investigate the low-g flammability limits compared to those obtained in NASA’s normal gravity material flammability screening test.

title: PSI record PSI-99 (SAFFIRE-II) — Approach
text:
SAFFIRE-II — Spacecraft Fire Experiment-II (PSI-99). Microgravity Investigation; platform: Cygnus Spacecraft; hardware: Cygnus Pressurized Cargo Module  SAFFIRE; period 2016-09-30 to 2017-04-01.
Approach: The Saffire-II experiment was performed on the Orbital Science’s Cygnus resupply vehicle after it deberthed from the ISS. As a follow on to the Saffire-I investigation, the Saffire-II investigation added more samples including SIBAL, silicone, structure PMMA, flat PMMA, and PMMA with Nomex. The Saffire-1I flight unit had a sample card installed in the middle of a large flow duct. Air is drawn through the flow duct by fans located at the top of the duct with flow straighteners at the bottom of the experiment module. Saffire-II has a sample card that contains 9 samples, each 5 cm x 29 cm. Depending on the sample material, the Saffire-II was conducted at an air flow velocity of either 20 or 30 cm/s, the flow being either concurrent or opposed. Once the sample was ignited flame images were captured using two cameras. In addition, thermocouples provided flow, flame, and plume temperatures, two radiometers recorded flame radiation, solid state sensors were used to measure pressure, CO2 and O2 mole faction, and two anemometer tracked flow velocity. All data was compressed, and subsequently downlinked. Details related to samples and experimental parameters are provided in the Experimental Details file in the Science document folder.

title: PSI record PSI-99 (SAFFIRE-II) — Hypothesis
text:
SAFFIRE-II — Spacecraft Fire Experiment-II (PSI-99). Microgravity Investigation; platform: Cygnus Spacecraft; hardware: Cygnus Pressurized Cargo Module  SAFFIRE; period 2016-09-30 to 2017-04-01.
Hypothesis: This investigation hypothesizes that due to large differences between fire behavior in normal and reduced gravity, the use of terrestrial fires and fire standards to design spacecraft fire safety systems presents an inherent risk to the vehicle because of the significant level of uncertainty. While this approach has been successful thus far, the uncertainty and risk will increase as exploration missions venture further from earth with considerably longer transit times for a safe return. There is a significant lack of microgravity data available for spacecraft designers on which to base their fire safety designs and procedures. To address this knowledge gap, this investigation proposed to conduct large-scale fire safety experiments in an expendable spacecraft without risk to a crew.

title: PSI record PSI-99 (SAFFIRE-II) — Research impacts / Earth benefits
text:
SAFFIRE-II — Spacecraft Fire Experiment-II (PSI-99). Microgravity Investigation; platform: Cygnus Spacecraft; hardware: Cygnus Pressurized Cargo Module  SAFFIRE; period 2016-09-30 to 2017-04-01.
Research impacts / Earth benefits: The Saffire-II experiment provides a new way to study a realistic fire on an exploration vehicle, which has not been possible in the past because the risks are too high. Instruments on an unmanned cargo vessel measure oxygen, carbon dioxide, heat, pressure and flame growth, and two video cameras provide views of the flame. Results determine microgravity flammability limits for several spacecraft materials, help to validate NASA’s material selection criteria, and how microgravity and limited oxygen affect flame size. The investigation is crucial for the safety of current and future space missions. Studying fire in small, sealed environments such as the Cygnus cargo supply vehicle benefits fire safety and prevention efforts on Earth, including inside mines, airplanes, or submarines.

title: PSI record PSI-22 (ACME E-FIELD Flames) — Objectives
text:
ACME E-FIELD Flames — Advanced Combustion via Microgravity Experiments Electric-Field Effects on Laminar Diffusion Flames (PSI-22). Microgravity Investigation; platform: International Space Station (ISS); hardware: Combustion Integrated Rack (CIR)  ACME; period 2016-11-18 to 2020-11-17.
Objectives: The objective of this investigation is to better understand the relationship between electric field voltage and chemi-ion current, analyze the dynamic response of flames to electric field changes, evaluate soot formation, and characterize stabilized near-limit lifted flames.

title: PSI record PSI-22 (ACME E-FIELD Flames) — Approach
text:
ACME E-FIELD Flames — Advanced Combustion via Microgravity Experiments Electric-Field Effects on Laminar Diffusion Flames (PSI-22). Microgravity Investigation; platform: International Space Station (ISS); hardware: Combustion Integrated Rack (CIR)  ACME; period 2016-11-18 to 2020-11-17.
Approach: The E-FIELD flames experiment investigates how electric fields influence the behavior of laminar diffusion flames in microgravity. This unique environment is ideal for isolating electric field effects from buoyancy forces.
The experiment is conducted with gas-fueled flames, both with and without a coflow of air. In the former case, the tests are conducted using the same coflow burner used by the Coflow Laminar Diffusion (CLD) Flame experiment. An electric field is generated by creating a high voltage (up to 10 kV) differential between the burner and a flat circular mesh suspended above (i.e., downstream of) the burner. Measurements, as a function of the field strength and fuel, are taken of the ion current through the flame and the flame’s response time to electric forcing. The gas-jet burner is used to create a small, focused flame for detailed ion-driven convection studies while the coflow burner surrounds the fuel jet with a weak synthetic air flow to enable flame stability and soot behavior analysis. A high-voltage copper mesh electrode positioned above the burner tip generated an electric field with controlled polarity and strength. The electric field interacts with ions generated through chemi-ionization during combustion, driving ion-driving convection and influencing flame behavior.

title: PSI record PSI-22 (ACME E-FIELD Flames) — Approach
text:
ACME E-FIELD Flames — Advanced Combustion via Microgravity Experiments Electric-Field Effects on Laminar Diffusion Flames (PSI-22). Microgravity Investigation; platform: International Space Station (ISS); hardware: Combustion Integrated Rack (CIR)  ACME; period 2016-11-18 to 2020-11-17.
Approach: tioned above the burner tip generated an electric field with controlled polarity and strength. The electric field interacts with ions generated through chemi-ionization during combustion, driving ion-driving convection and influencing flame behavior. Methane and ethylene were used as fuels and diluted with nitrogen to control flame strength. Dilution levels were varied to explore a range of combustion dynamics, from highly stable to near-extinction flames. Voltage-current curves were recorded to assess the relationship between electric field strength and chemi-ion current, revealing ion-driven convection effects. High-resolution cameras captured flame shape, luminosity, and soot distribution. Spectral imaging with filters measures chemiluminescent emissions and soot volume fraction. There were thermopile detectors to measure flame radiant emissions.
All experiments were conducted in the combustion integrated rack (CIR). Tests were administered with Glenn Research Center (GRC) directing astronaut actions. Parameters such as fuel flow rate, coflow velocity, and field polarity are were varied to isolate specific effects on ion production, flame stability, and soot behavior.

title: PSI record PSI-22 (ACME E-FIELD Flames) — Hypothesis
text:
ACME E-FIELD Flames — Advanced Combustion via Microgravity Experiments Electric-Field Effects on Laminar Diffusion Flames (PSI-22). Microgravity Investigation; platform: International Space Station (ISS); hardware: Combustion Integrated Rack (CIR)  ACME; period 2016-11-18 to 2020-11-17.
Hypothesis: The application of electric fields in microgravity environments will significantly influence laminar diffusion flames by enabling precise manipulation of flame stability, soot behavior, and combustion dynamics through ion-driven convection and chemi-ionization processes.

title: PSI record PSI-22 (ACME E-FIELD Flames) — Research impacts / Earth benefits
text:
ACME E-FIELD Flames — Advanced Combustion via Microgravity Experiments Electric-Field Effects on Laminar Diffusion Flames (PSI-22). Microgravity Investigation; platform: International Space Station (ISS); hardware: Combustion Integrated Rack (CIR)  ACME; period 2016-11-18 to 2020-11-17.
Research impacts / Earth benefits: The E-FIELD Flames research is not being conducted to serve any space applications, but it is possible that its findings could aid the development of future space-based combustion devices (e.g., for solid waste processing). The use of electric fields to control flames can reduce the production of harmful pollutants in practical terrestrial combustion. The combustion of fossil fuel is the primary human source of greenhouse gas and acid rain and furthermore creates soot, which can be beneficial but is also a health hazard. Combustion using electrical fields may also allow for more efficient combustion, reducing fuel consumption in addition to unwanted emissions.

title: PSI record PSI-107 (SPICE) — Objectives
text:
SPICE — Smoke Point In Co-flow Experiment (PSI-107). Microgravity Investigation; platform: International Space Station (ISS); hardware: Microgravity Science Glovebox (MSG); period ? to ?.
Objectives: The objective of SPICE is to better understand the complex process of combustion by observing flames in a microgravity environment aboard the International Space Station (ISS) and analogous ground experiments.

Specific objectives were:
(1) Identify the laminar smoke-point properties of non-buoyant jet diffusion flames under various co-flow conditions in microgravity.
(2) Determine the effects of burner diameter and co-flow velocity on the luminous flame lengths and smoke points.
(3) Quantify the sooting propensity of different fuels, such as ethylene, propane, and propylene mixtures.
(4) Validate the correlation between luminous flame shape and residence time under microgravity conditions.
(5) Investigate the impact of air and fuel flow rate variations on smoke point phenomena in space.

title: PSI record PSI-107 (SPICE) — Approach
text:
SPICE — Smoke Point In Co-flow Experiment (PSI-107). Microgravity Investigation; platform: International Space Station (ISS); hardware: Microgravity Science Glovebox (MSG); period ? to ?.
Approach: The experimental setup in the microgravity science glovebox consisted of an apparatus with a flow duct with integrated nozzles, cameras, and fuel delivery systems. Fuels tested included methane, ethylene, propane, propylene, and propylene mixtures. Each flame was ignited in a controlled co-flow air environment, with burner diameters of 0.41 mm, 0.76 mm, and 1.6 mm and co-flow velocities ranging from 5.4 cm/s to 65 cm/s. Fuel flow rates were adjusted to identify the smoke point, marked by the flame's transition to emitting soot. Data such as flame lengths were recorded using still and video cameras. Measurements included flame height, radiative heat losses, and co-flow air velocity distributions. In total 526 flames were studied.

title: PSI record PSI-107 (SPICE) — Hypothesis

Hypothesis: The research hypothesizes that by minimizing gravity-driven transport phenomena scientists can study the laminar smoke-point properties of non-buoyant jet diffusion flames. Flame properties are expected to differ significantly from those observed under normal gravity.

title: PSI record PSI-21 (ACME CLD Flame) — Objectives
text:
ACME CLD Flame — Advanced Combustion via Microgravity Experiments / Coflow Laminar Diffusion Flame (PSI-21). Microgravity Investigation; platform: International Space Station (ISS); hardware: Combustion Integrated Rack (CIR)  ACME; period 2006-10-01 to 2022-05-31.
Objectives: In order to provide the experimental data needed to allow rigorous testing of computational models at the extremes of the fuel dilution spectrum, we have the following objectives:
A) Characterize the behavior of weak coflow diffusion flames of methane and ethylene, as a function of velocity and fuel dilution, through measurement of flame shape, lift-off heights, temperatures and extinction limits.
B) Characterize the sooting tendencies of diffusion flames with long residence times, as a function of velocity and fuel dilution, through measurement of flame shape, gas temperatures in the soot-free portion of the flame, soot luminosity, soot temperatures, and soot volume fractions.

title: PSI record PSI-21 (ACME CLD Flame) — Approach
text:
ACME CLD Flame — Advanced Combustion via Microgravity Experiments / Coflow Laminar Diffusion Flame (PSI-21). Microgravity Investigation; platform: International Space Station (ISS); hardware: Combustion Integrated Rack (CIR)  ACME; period 2006-10-01 to 2022-05-31.
Approach: ACME CLD Flame project goals include the generation of improved computational models with improved soot sub-models that are effective for both dilute flames and sooting flames that vary from low to high soot loading levels. The enhanced time and spatial scales in a microgravity environment will be important for achieving both goals. Experimentally, we plan to study methane and ethylene diffusion flames over a wide range of test conditions. For the more dilute flames, measurements will be made of flame chemiluminesence of OH* and CH* to observe variations in lift-off height and flame shape as extinction limits are approached. The sooting tendencies of the more fuel-rich flames will be investigated using soot luminosity and laser extinction measurements to determine soot temperatures and soot volume fractions. Flame temperatures in non-sooting regions will be measured using thin-filament pyrometry. Based on observations, modifications can be made to the kinetics and soot model to match better the experimental results. If the overall agreement of the measurements and computations is good, the results of the computations can be “mined” to provide insight on species (and hence chemical processes) that cannot be measured directly using the diagnostics available for the proposed experiment.

title: PSI record PSI-21 (ACME CLD Flame) — Research impacts / Earth benefits
text:
ACME CLD Flame — Advanced Combustion via Microgravity Experiments / Coflow Laminar Diffusion Flame (PSI-21). Microgravity Investigation; platform: International Space Station (ISS); hardware: Combustion Integrated Rack (CIR)  ACME; period 2006-10-01 to 2022-05-31.
Research impacts / Earth benefits: Diffusion flames are the flame type of most practical combustion devices. The ability to predict the coupled effects of complex transport phenomena with detailed chemical kinetics in such systems is critical in the modeling of turbulent reacting flows and in understanding the processes by which soot formation and radiative transfer take place. In addition, an understanding of those factors that affect flame extinction in diffusion flames is critical in the suppression of fires and in improving engine efficiency. While normal gravity combustion studies can provide important information on combustion processes, the effects of gravitational forces often complicate the interpretation of both computational and experimental results. Momentum effects dominate most practical combustion devices, but the contribution of buoyancy forces is hard to eliminate in normal gravity. A goal of the study will be to apply sophisticated numerical tools and quantitative diagnostic techniques to the study of hydrocarbon diffusion flames in a microgravity environment. This will lead to a more detailed understanding of the interaction of convection, diffusion and chemistry under momentum-dominated conditions.
