title: SPICE: Reports — SPICE 30-DayPostFlightReport
text:
Smoke Point In Coflow Experiment 
“SPICE” 
Microgravity Science Glovebox 
Increment 19-20 (30 Day Report) 
Investigators: David Urban NASA GRC, Peter Sunderland: Univ. Maryland 
Project Scientist: Zengguang Yuan, National Center for Space Exploration Research 
Project Manager: Robert Hawersaat NASA GRC 
 
I. 
Introduction 
 
A. 
Hypothesis 
The hypothesis of the SPICE investigation is that smoke point behavior 
will be observed for co-flowing flames and that it will show 
dependence on nozzle diameter and coflow velocity. 
 
B. 
Objectives of Investigation 
The objective of the SPICE experiment is to find the laminar smoke-point 
properties of nonbuoyant jet diffusion flames (i.e., the properties of the 
largest laminar jet diffusion flames that do not emit soot) for several fuels 
under different nozzle diameter/ co-flow velocity configurations. 
Luminous flame shape measurements would also be made to verify 
models of the flame shapes under co-flow conditions. 
 
C. 
Previous Mission Experience 
 
N/A 
 
D. 
Background/History of Project (Optional) 
 
The SPICE experiment was an outgrowth of the Laminar Soot Processes 
Experiment (LSP) which flew on STS 83, 94, and 107. SPICE utilized the 
design heritage and modified the hardware from the Enclosed Laminar Flames 
Experiment (ELF) which flew in the Middeck Glovebox on STS 87. 
 
II. Methods/Research Operations 
 
A.

title: SPICE: Reports — SPICE 30-DayPostFlightReport
text:
eriment (LSP) which flew on STS 83, 94, and 107. SPICE utilized the 
design heritage and modified the hardware from the Enclosed Laminar Flames 
Experiment (ELF) which flew in the Middeck Glovebox on STS 87. 
 
II. Methods/Research Operations 
 
A. 
Discussion of Method/Protocol 
 
Most tests were conducted by setting the coflow velocity, igniting the flame, 
and adjusting the fuel flow rate. Approximate smoke points were identified in 
the video by the flight crew and simultaneously by the ground support crew in 
Cleveland. Typical burn times were 60 s, and after each two such burns the 
MSG contents were flushed with ISS cabin air. After the tests the video 
record was analyzed to identify smoke point conditions. The associated 
coflow and fuel flow rates were obtained from digital data recorded in the 
video. The smoke point lengths, LSP, were obtained from the video record 
and are the measured distance from the burner tip to the tip of the luminous 
flame on the flame axis.

title: SPICE: Reports — SPICE 30-DayPostFlightReport
text:
III. Results 
 
A. 
List of Preflight, In-flight, Postflight Anomalies 
 
SPICE operated very successfully with the only significant anomaly being the 
accumulation of soot in the outlet screen which changed the flow behavior in 
the duct. This was corrected by a crew member using the vacuum to clean the 
outlet screen on June 15. 
B. 
Completeness/Quality of Data 
During Increment 18 SPICE conducted 108 test points completing its nominal 
test matrix. During Increments 19/20 SPICE conducted 155 additional test 
points the provided improved resolution of the smoke points and allowed us to 
explore further limits in the parameter space. 
C. Status of Data Analysis: The data from the down linked video have been analyzed 
for flame length and smoke point flow rate. These have resulted in a meeting apper 
and a draft journal paper. More work will be conducted with analysis of the digital 
luminance data from the Nikon. 
 
D. 
Preliminary Research Findings: 
 See attached paper below

title: SPICE: Reports — SPICE 30-DayPostFlightReport
text:
1 
2009 Fall Technical Meeting 
Organized by the Eastern States Section of the Combustion Institute 
and Hosted by the University of Maryland College Park 
October 18-21, 2009 
Laminar Smoke Points of 
Microgravity Coflow Diffusion Flames 
K.T. Dotsona, P.B. Sunderlanda, Z.–G. Yuanb, D.L. Urbanc 
aDepartment of Fire Protection Engineering, University of Maryland, College Park, MD, USA 
bNational Center for Space Exploration Research, Cleveland, OH, USA 
cNASA Glenn Research Center, Cleveland, OH, USA 
 
Laminar smoke points were measured in nonbuoyant laminar jet diffusion flames in air coflow aboard the 
International Space Station as part of the Smoke Points in Coflow Experiment (SPICE). Smoke points were found 
for ethylene, propane, propylene, and mixtures of 50 and 75% propylene by volume in nitrogen. Burner diameters 
were 0.41, 0.76 and 1.6 mm and coflow velocities varied from 5.4 – 65 cm/s. These flames afford good control over 
residence time via variations in dilution, burner diameter, and coflow velocity. Increasing coflow velocity decreases 
luminous flame lengths, but moves smoke points to higher fuel flow rates and longer luminous flame lengths. 
Smaller burners have longer smoke points for coflowing flames. These trends can be explained qualitatively by 
considering total residence time effects.

title: SPICE: Reports — SPICE 30-DayPostFlightReport
text:
ame lengths, but moves smoke points to higher fuel flow rates and longer luminous flame lengths. 
Smaller burners have longer smoke points for coflowing flames. These trends can be explained qualitatively by 
considering total residence time effects. The luminous flame lengths generally correlate with fuel mass flow rate 
divided by stoichiometric mixture fraction, although they increase slightly as air velocity decreases. 
1. Introduction 
Soot formation is an important unresolved problem in combustion science. Soot is estimated to 
be responsible for up to 50,000 premature deaths in the U.S. [1] and is believed to contribute to 
climate change and glacial melting [2]. Radiation from soot in flames allows reading by candlelight but also contributes to heat loads in engines and the spread of unwanted fires. Smoking 
flames emit carbon monoxide, which is the major cause of death in fires [3]. 
The smoke point is the condition (or length) where a flame begins to emit soot. Smoke points 
indicate the sooting propensity of a fuel in diffusion flames. In normal gravity, laminar smoke 
points have been measured for many gaseous and condensed fuels [4–9]. Laminar smoke points 
have been found to correlate with soot volume fractions [10] and radiative loss factions [11] of 
turbulent diffusion flames. Yang et al. [12] found that gas turbine soot emissions correlate very

title: SPICE: Reports — SPICE 30-DayPostFlightReport
text:
ous and condensed fuels [4–9]. Laminar smoke points 
have been found to correlate with soot volume fractions [10] and radiative loss factions [11] of 
turbulent diffusion flames. Yang et al. [12] found that gas turbine soot emissions correlate very 
well with a threshold sooting index (TSI) based on fuel molecular weight divided by the laminar 
smoke point. Smoke points have been shown to correlate with the smoke release from turbulent 
buoyant flames [13] and have been applied to developing general soot models for computational 
combustion simulations [14] and heat release measurements [15]. 
In a 1988 paper [16], Glassman predicted that smoke points would not occur in nonbuoyant gasjet flames. He based this on the assumption that residence time scales with the square root of fuel 
flow rate in normal gravity but is independent of flow rate in microgravity flames. Subsequent 
work [17] observed smoke points of nonbuoyant flames aboard a parabolic aircraft and used 
numerical predictions to show that residence time increases with flame length for nonbuoyant 
flames without co-flow. Urban et al. [18] reported smoke points of microgravity flames observed 
on a space shuttle. Microgravity smoke point measurements are difficult in parabolic aircraft

title: SPICE: Reports — SPICE 30-DayPostFlightReport
text:
2 
owing to g-jitter and in drop facilities owing to limited test times. 
Attributing smoke point behavior to total residence time helps with qualitative explanations of 
smoke point behavior but to date has not yielded successful quantitative correlations [8]. This 
may be because smoke points arise from a competition between the times available for soot 
formation and soot oxidation. Delichatsios and co-workers suggested that smoke point length is 
proportional to soot formation time [19–20]. Quantitative correlations may also be possible from 
an examination of radiative losses, which have been observed to be 20 – 30% for normal-gravity 
smoke point flames and to increase with adiabatic flame temperature [5]. 
Soot is transported in flames by convection and thermophoresis. By varying the burner diameter, 
coflow velocity, and fuel dilution, flame shape and residence times in the soot formation and 
soot oxidation regions can be changed. A decrease in coflow velocity will generally increase 
entrainment of flow towards the flame axis. 
Kent and Wagner [21] found that smoke burn out in the oxidative region of the flame ceases 
when the tip of a buoyant diffusion flame cools to approximately 1300 K. Urban et al. [22] found 
that the tip of a nonbuoyant (microgravity) flame reaches 1000 K at its smoke point. In buoyant

title: SPICE: Reports — SPICE 30-DayPostFlightReport
text:
burn out in the oxidative region of the flame ceases 
when the tip of a buoyant diffusion flame cools to approximately 1300 K. Urban et al. [22] found 
that the tip of a nonbuoyant (microgravity) flame reaches 1000 K at its smoke point. In buoyant 
flames this decrease in temperature is attributed primarily to heat conduction, while in 
nonbuoyant flames it is attributed largely to radiative quenching [23]. The radiative quenching 
effect causes a visible tip opening in nonbuoyant smoke points of flames of relatively long 
residence time [22]. 
A recent 2.5 s drop tower study by Jeon et al. [24] found that for small coflow velocities the soot 
volume fraction increases with coflow velocity. This was attributed to an increase in 
temperature. Lin and Faeth [7,25] studied the effects of coflow velocity on weakly-buoyant 
flames near the smoke point. They observed flames in normal gravity, but at low pressures to 
reduce the effects of gravity. They found that increasing the coflow velocity reduced soot 
volume fractions and increased the smoke point length. This was attributed to decreased flame 
residence time and modified soot pathlines. Refs. [7 and 24] both showed that luminous flame 
lengths decrease with increasing coflow velocity. Their burner diameters, 7 and 10 mm, 
respectively, were much larger than those considered here.

lengths decrease with increasing coflow velocity. Their burner diameters, 7 and 10 mm, 
respectively, were much larger than those considered here. 
Faeth and co-workers [25–27] applied the flame shape analyses of Spalding [28] and 
Mahalingam et al. [29] to nonbuoyant gas-jet flames to obtain

2. Experimental 
The Smoke Points in Coflow Experiment (SPICE) module was brought to the International 
Space Station (ISS) in 2008. It was operated in the Microgravity Science Glovebox (MSG) by 
various crew members in 2009. Smoke points were attempted for all fuels for fuel jet diameters 
of 0.41, 0.76, and 1.6 mm. The conditions for which smoke points were found are summarized in 
Table 1. In some cases (e.g., tests involving ethylene) the fuel supply was depleted before 
desired smoke points could be found, as the supply was limited to two 75 cc bottles of each fuel 
at gage pressures of 760 – 1440 kPa, depending on the fuel. 
 The SPICE module contains a rectangular duct that has an approximately 76 mm square cross 
section with rounded corners. A DC fan supplies coflowing air from the glovebox contents. The 
air passes through a honeycomb and screen to reduce swirl and then enters the duct. The air and

title: SPICE: Reports — SPICE 30-DayPostFlightReport
text:
ngular duct that has an approximately 76 mm square cross 
section with rounded corners. A DC fan supplies coflowing air from the glovebox contents. The 
air passes through a honeycomb and screen to reduce swirl and then enters the duct. The air and 
combustion products leave the duct through a perforated copper plate followed by a copper 
screen. The screen is 50 mm upstream of the burner discharge and the plate is 120 mm 
downstream. Fan voltage is varied to control the coflow velocity, which is measured with a hotwire anemometer between the inlet honeycomb and screen. This anemometer was calibrated in 
normal gravity using a hot-wire anemometer 36 mm downstream of the duct entrance. Fuel flow 
rate was adjusted manually and controlled with a mass flow meter. The flames were ignited with 
a hot-wire ignitor. Video was recorded with an analog color video camera and downlinked in real 
time. Still images were recorded with a 12 bit Nikon™ D100 single-lens reflex color digital still 
camera (with 3008 × 2000 pixels) with a 60 mm lens. 
Most of the tests were conducted by setting the coflow velocity, igniting the flame, and adjusting 
the fuel flow rate. Approximate smoke points were identified in the video by the flight crew and 
simultaneously by the ground support crew in Cleveland. Typical burn times were 60 s, and after

title: SPICE: Reports — SPICE 30-DayPostFlightReport
text:
he coflow velocity, igniting the flame, and adjusting 
the fuel flow rate. Approximate smoke points were identified in the video by the flight crew and 
simultaneously by the ground support crew in Cleveland. Typical burn times were 60 s, and after 
each two such burns the MSG contents were flushed with ISS cabin air. 
After the tests the video record was analyzed to identify smoke point conditions. The associated 
coflow and fuel flow rates were obtained from digital data recorded in the video. The smoke 
point lengths, LSP, were obtained from the video record and are the measured distance from the 
burner tip to the tip of the luminous flame on the flame axis. The luminous flame tips were not 
sharply defined in most images, but rather involved a transition from bright yellow to black 
across an axial distance of 2 – 5 mm. Flame height was thus measured to the point where the 
centerline grayscale intensity changed most rapidly between these yellow and black regions. This 
helped reduce the sensitivity of measured flame height to camera exposure settings. 
Smoke points were obtained for five fuels, as summarized in Table 1. Smoke points were

title: SPICE: Reports — SPICE 30-DayPostFlightReport
text:
4 
attempted with methane, but could not be obtained before the flames impinged on the plate at the 
end of the duct. Also shown in Table 1 are the ranges of various parameters for which 
microgravity smoke points were observed. 
3. Results and Discussion 
Some smoke points, propane and ethylene in particular, were identified by the onset of gradual 
(rather than sharp) dimming and reddening of the luminous flame tip in the downstream 
direction. Rounding of the tip also was associated with the smoke point. For conditions 
sufficiently above the smoke point, quenched soot could be seen leaving the flame. The brightest 
flames did not always display significant reddening or darkening near their tips, except well 
above the smoke point. This occurred for the pure propylene and propylene mixtures, and the 
smoke point was identified by the rapid transition to an open-tipped, soot emitting flame. 
The flames generally reached steady conditions within 5 s of ignition or a change in flow rate of 
fuel or air. Flames of propylene and propylene mixtures were generally more luminous than 
those of methane, ethylene, and propane, attributed to their higher propensity to form soot. The 
smoke point transition was more abrupt in the propylene-based fuels than for propane or 
ethylene. Periodic flame motion was observed in some flames, especially those with high coflow,

title: SPICE: Reports — SPICE 30-DayPostFlightReport
text:
opane, attributed to their higher propensity to form soot. The 
smoke point transition was more abrupt in the propylene-based fuels than for propane or 
ethylene. Periodic flame motion was observed in some flames, especially those with high coflow, 
long length, and low fuel velocity, and is attributed to non-uniform coflow. This effect was small 
and did not prevent clear measurement of flame length. 
Figure 1 shows images for representative flames near their smoke points. Two sequences are 
shown, and in both the smoke point occurs between the third and fourth flames. In the top 
sequence, coflow velocity decreases from left to right at constant fuel flow rate. This increases 
luminous flame length and reduces the smoke point leading to soot emission. The luminous 
length decreases in the fourth image owing to incomplete combustion. In the bottom sequence 
fuel flow rate is increased at constant coflow velocity, increasing flame length as expected. As 
seen in Fig. 1, luminous length is more sensitive to changes in fuel flow rate than to changes in 
coflow velocity.

title: SPICE: Reports — SPICE FinalReport
text:
ii 
 
Smoke Point in Co-flow Experiment (SPICE) 
Abstract 
The laminar smoke point is the condition (and the luminous flame length) where a flame begins 
to emit soot. Smoke points indicate the sooting propensity of a fuel in diffusion flames. In normal 
gravity, laminar smoke points have been measured for many gaseous and condensed fuels. 
Laminar smoke points have been found to correlate with soot volume fractions and radiative loss 
fractions of turbulent diffusion flames. SPICE project measured laminar smoke points in nonbuoyant laminar jet diffusion flames in co-flowing air aboard the International Space Station. 
Fifty-two smoke points were found for ethylene, propane, propylene, and propylene/nitrogen 
mixtures. Burner diameters were 0.41, 0.76, and 1.6 mm and co-flow velocities varied from 5.4 – 
65 cm/s. These flames afford extensive control over residence time via variations in dilution, 
burner diameter, and co-flow velocity. Increasing co-flow velocity decreases luminous flame 
lengths, but moves smoke points to higher fuel flow rates and longer luminous flame lengths. 
Smaller burners have longer smoke points for co-flowing flames. These trends can be explained 
qualitatively by considering total residence time effects. The luminous flame lengths generally 
correlate with fuel mass flow rate divided by stoichiometric mixture fraction, although they

title: SPICE: Reports — SPICE FinalReport
text:
ints for co-flowing flames. These trends can be explained 
qualitatively by considering total residence time effects. The luminous flame lengths generally 
correlate with fuel mass flow rate divided by stoichiometric mixture fraction, although they 
increase slightly as air velocity decreases. The measured smoke point lengths were found to 
correlate with burner diameter to the –0.91 power times coflow velocity to the 0.41 power. The 
measurements allow estimates of pseudo threshold soot indices (TSI) for microgravity diffusion 
flames, indicating an unusually high sooting propensity for propane in microgravity. A model of 
residence times in coflowing flames is developed, and although residence time helps explain 
many of the observations, it does not correlate the measured smoke points. The measurements 
yielded estimates of sooting propensities of the present fuels in microgravity diffusion flames. 
 
Acknowledgments 
 
The authors acknowledge G.M. Faeth for conceiving this work, the SPICE engineering team, and 
the astronauts that conducted the tests (M. Barratt, E.M. Fincke, S.H. Magnus, and K. Wakata). 
The SPICE project was conducted through the ISS Exploration Research Project of the 
Exploration Technology Development Program. The support of this program is also

INTRODUCTION 
 
SPICE project, from it was rewarded in 1997 to it was conducted onboard ISS in 2009, covered 
more than a decade time span. During these years, the project experienced a few cycles of active and 
inactive status. A brief project history is given below. SPICE project was awarded on December 3, 
1997 by the Microgravity Science and Application Division of NASA Headquarters to Professor 
Gerard M. Faeth of the University of Michigan for his proposal titled as Laminar Smoke Point 
Properties of Nonbuoyant Round-Jet Diffusion Flames in response to NASA’s 1996 Solicitation for 
Glovebox Investigations issued in late 1996. The original proposal of Professor Faeth was meant to 
be a supplement to the Laminar Soot Processes Experiment which was a combustion project under 
NASA Grant No. NAG3-1245, conducted onboard STS-73 and STS-94 in 1997. In the awarding 
letter, the experiment was planned to be carried out onboard STS-107, for which the launch date was 
then scheduled in May 2000. From December 1997 to the end of 1999 was the first phase of the 
project. In this period, the experiment was planned to be conducted in the Middle Deck Glove Box 
of a Space Shuttle and the SPICE hardware was fabricated and assembled in GRC. Various project 
reviews necessary for the flight project, were completed. In addition, significant efforts on science

title: SPICE: Reports — SPICE FinalReport
text:
nned to be conducted in the Middle Deck Glove Box 
of a Space Shuttle and the SPICE hardware was fabricated and assembled in GRC. Various project 
reviews necessary for the flight project, were completed. In addition, significant efforts on science 
side were made to explore proper camera settings for different flame conditions by conducting 
reduced gravity experiment in parabolic flight on board the KC-135 aircraft. From the end of 1999 to 
March 2002, the project was inactive. The second phase of the project was from March 2002 to

Soot formation in hydrocarbon-fueled flames is an important unresolved problem in combustion 
science. Soot is estimated to be responsible for up to 52,000 premature deaths annually in the U.S.1 
and is believed to contribute to climate change and glacial melting.2 Radiation from soot in flames is 
beneficial in many applications but also contributes to unwanted heat loads in engines and the spread 
of fires. Carbon monoxide emitted by smoking flames is the major cause of death in fires.3 
Knowledge of Soot formation is needed for developing computational combustion.

title: SPICE: Reports — SPICE FinalReport
text:
2 
 
The differences between soot processes in buoyant and nonbuoyant laminar jet diffusion flames can 
be seen by comparing their soot production regions as plotted in Fig. 1. Soot formation in diffusion 
flames generally is limited to fuel-equivalence ratios, φ, in the range 1-2, which are marked on the 
plots. Unlike gases, which both convect and diffuse, soot mainly convects with the flow velocity so 
that it moves along the streamline. For buoyant flames, the dividing streamline generally is inside 
the soot formation region so that most of the soot initially forms near the flame sheet, where φ, =1, 
and then moves radially inward toward cooler regions having higher fuel concentrations. The soot 
formation process for nonbuoyant flames is completely different: most of the soot initially forms 
near the cool core of the flame, where φ is close to 2, and is drawn directly toward the flame sheet. 
Results from an MSL-1 combustion project, the Laminar Soot Processes (LSP), revealed that the 
smoke height phenomenon in microgravity can be substantially different form that seen in normal 
gravity. The removal of buoyancy induced acceleration can cause the smoke point phenomenon to 
be dominated by radiative heat losses for conditions of low overall flame velocity. Under these 
conditions the flame extinguishes at the flame tip allowing soot to be emitted.

title: SPICE: Reports — SPICE FinalReport
text:

be dominated by radiative heat losses for conditions of low overall flame velocity. Under these 
conditions the flame extinguishes at the flame tip allowing soot to be emitted. In spite of this effect, 
it is still possible to have flames that either emit soot along all stream lines or do not emit soot 
anywhere, for conditions where radiation losses do not dominate.

Soot path lines through buoyant and non-buoyant flames 
 
The information of smoke-point properties and flame shapes is needed to improve our understanding 
of heat and mass transfer mechanisms for different flame conditions. Unfortunately, while the 
laminar smoke-point properties of buoyant jet diffusion flames at normal gravity are well known, 
corresponding information for nonbuoyant flames is limited and questionable. Thus the insights of 
soot generation and oxidation processes under microgravity conditions are critical to devise better 
fire safety strategy in spacecraft needed for long term space travels and other space exploration 
activities. In addition, the improved understanding of soot processes in laminar flames will help us, 
by analogy, to gain better understanding of soot processes in practical turbulent flames.

by analogy, to gain better understanding of soot processes in practical turbulent flames. 
 
 
The objectives of the SPICE experiments is to find the laminar smoke-point properties of nonbuoyant jet diffusion flames for several fuels under different nozzle diameter/co-flow velocity 
configurations. Luminous flame shape measurements would also be made to verify models of the

flame shapes under co-flow conditions. In particular, the experiments are planned to be conducted 
under the following conditions: six types of fuels: methane, ethylene, propane, propylene, 75% 
propylene mixed with 25% nitrogen in moles, and 50% propylene mixed with 50% nitrogen in moles; 
three nozzles: 0.4, 0.8 and 1.6 mm ID and two air velocities: 100% and 50% of the maximum air 
flow velocity (near 50cm/s). The operation procedures are as such that the air velocity is set first, 
then start the fuel flow and ignite the flame. Fuel flow rate is adjusted until the smoke point is 
reached. Thus, for each combination of a fuel and a nozzle size, two smoke point fuel flow rates are 
obtained. One is under 100% air velocity and the other is under 50% air velocity. Then in the case of 
50% air velocity, the fuel flow rate is reduced to 50% of the smoke point fuel flow rate to get a flame 
length with that fuel flow rate.

B. Air velocity distribution in the flow duct 
An important feature of SPICE is that it has air co-flow surrounding the flames. SPICE is the first 
experiment that studies soot processes of laminar jet diffusion flame under long term microgravity 
condition with air coflow. Because the velocity distribution in or near the flame is complicated by 
the varying gas property and thermal expansion, the coflow air velocity can only be specified in far 
field and the inlet of the flow duct as boundary conditions of the flame under investigation. For this 
reason, the information of air velocity distribution before igniting of the flame is needed. The air 
velocity was measured with an anemometer at different locations in the flow duct at different fan 
speed.

SPICE FLIGHT TESTS 
The actual SPICE tests were conducted in SMG in twelve sessions from February 14, 2009 to June 
23, 2009. In each session, the SPICE science team and engineering team were in the TeleScience 
Center (TSC) in GRC to support the tests conducted on MSG. Real-time flame images were 
available as long as air-to-ground communication channel was available. In addition, the team was 
able to communicate with the astronaut who conducted the experiment to answer questions or to 
clarify any ambiguities. 
 
Most tests were conducted by setting the coflow velocity, igniting the flame, and adjusting the fuel 
flow rate.

shorter. This leads to plenty unused fuel for new test points. The entire test matrix and measured 
flame data are listed in Appendix A. 
 
The flames generally reached steady conditions within 5 s of ignition or a change in flow rate of fuel 
or air. Flames of propylene and propylene mixtures were generally more luminous than the others, 
attributed to increased soot volume fractions. Periodic flame motion was observed in some flames, 
especially those with high air velocity, large burners, and long flames, and is attributed to coflow 
perturbations. This increased slightly the uncertainties in smoke points for these conditions. 
 
TEST RESULTS 
Smoke points were attempted for all fuels. The conditions for which smoke points were found are 
summarized in Table 1. In some cases (e.g., tests involving ethylene) the fuel supply was depleted

TEST RESULTS 
Smoke points were attempted for all fuels. The conditions for which smoke points were found are 
summarized in Table 1. In some cases (e.g., tests involving ethylene) the fuel supply was depleted 
before all desired conditions could be tested, as the supply was limited to two 150 cc bottles of each 
fuel at gage pressures of 760 – 1440 kPa. Smoke points were attempted with methane, but could not 
be obtained before the flames impinged on the copper plate at the end of the duct. 
 
 
 
Some smoke points (particularly for propane and ethylene) were identified by the onset of gradual 
dimming, reddening, and rounding of the luminous flame tip. Conversely, the brightest flames 
(particularly for propylene and propylene mixtures) normally did not display significant dimming 
and reddening near their tips, except when much longer than their smoke points. For these flames, 
smoke points were identified by the rapid transition to open-tipped flames. Open-tipped flames are 
common in microgravity when smoke points are far exceeded4 and are associated with flame 
extinguishment along the centerline and soot that escapes in an annular shell. For conditions 
sufficiently above the smoke points, quenched soot could be seen leaving the flames despite the dark 
background in the video.

Figure 17 shows images for representative flames near their smoke points. Two sequences are 
shown, and in both, the smoke point occurs between the third and fourth images. In the top row, 
coflow velocity decreases from left to right at a constant fuel flow rate. This increases luminous 
flame length and leads to soot emission in the fourth image. The luminous length decreases in the 
fourth image owing to flame extinction and extensive reactant leakage. In the bottom row, fuel flow 
rate is increased at a constant coflow velocity, increasing luminous lengths. The luminous lengths of 
the flames in Fig. 17 are more sensitive to changes in fuel flow rate than to changes in coflow 
velocity. For a jet diffusion flame, the fuel flow rate is the limiting factor of the flame length because 
there is almost unlimited amount of oxidant (air in this case) available. This is why the flame length 
is more sensitive to the change of fuel flow rate. 
 
 
 
In Fig. 18 the measured smoke point lengths are plotted with respect to coflow velocity. For a given 
choice of fuel and burner diameter, an increase in coflow velocity generally increases the smoke 
point length. This behavior is attributed to decreased residence times and radiative losses as coflow 
velocity increases, and is an important issue for further consideration. The slope of the correlations 
in Fig.

Also shown in Fig. 18 are smoke points of microgravity flames in still air.5 The limited smoke points 
at different diameters actually increase with burner diameter. When the present measurements are 
extrapolated to zero coflow velocity, the dependence on burner diameter diminishes. Normal gravity 
smoke points are also generally found to have only a weak dependence on burner diameter.5,6 
However, testing in normal gravity8 has shown that coflowing normal gravity smoke points for 
propylene decrease with increasing burner diameter for the present range of diameters. The present 
smoke points generally were repeatable. An exception was the tests with the 0.41 mm burner (for 
which only propylene smoke points were possible). Testing on different days yielded different 
smoke points for this burner. 
 
The sooting propensity of the present fuels, identified from the smoke point lengths for fixed burner 
diameter and coflow velocity, generally increases from propane to ethylene, to 50% propylene, to 
75% propylene, and to propylene. This is consistent with normal gravity results in the same 
apparatus.7 The only exception was that, for the 0.76 mm burner, ethylene has a longer smoke point 
length than propane. The lower density of ethylene results in a decreased residence time, but this is 
unlikely to explain such a long smoke point relative to that of propane.

DISCUSSION 
 
Although it is convenient to classified all flames, laminar vs. turbulent and diffusion vs. premixed, 
into two categories based on their soot emission conditions, i.e., soot emitting flames and non-soot 
emitting flames, the conditions delineating the two or the conditions of onset of soot emission are 
difficult to define. Up to date, these conditions have been documented solely based on experimental 
observations. Many efforts have been made to develop a universal method of defining the onset of 
soot emission, i.e., smoke point, conditions, in terms of primary parameters of the flame. But none of 
these efforts has been quite successful yet. The primary parameters of the flame mentioned here refer 
to parameters used to set the flame, not those generated by the flame. The primary parameters of jet 
diffusion flames include fuel type, fuel and oxidizer supply rates, ambient temperature and pressure, 
and configuration of the device where the flame takes place, such as nozzle diameter and dimensions 
of the combustion chamber. The flame temperature, gas velocity and species distributions as well as 
flame shapes and derived parameters such as heat generation and heat loss, are the parameters 
generated by the flame which is not considered as primary parameters. If a method that relates

title: SPICE: Reports — SPICE FinalReport
text:
rature, gas velocity and species distributions as well as 
flame shapes and derived parameters such as heat generation and heat loss, are the parameters 
generated by the flame which is not considered as primary parameters. If a method that relates 
smoke point to those primary parameters were found, we would be able to predict whether a flame 
emits soot or not based on the planned flame conditions. In the course of pursuing such a universal 
method, a number of surmises of the mechanism of soot emission have been proposed to associate 
smoke point with certain flame generated parameters. Those surmises served as a middle step in 
hoping to help further development of the aforementioned method. The first surmise, and least 
controversial, is that smoke points occur when soot temperature drops below a critical temperature 
prior to soot burnout. This temperature is about 1300 K in normal gravity8,9 and 1000 K in 
microgravity.10,11 The second is that smoke point occurs when radiative loss fraction reaches 0.2 – 
0.4 for normal-gravity flames12-16 or 0.4 – 0.6 for microgravity flames.17 Since the radiative fraction 
of heat loss increases with fuel flow rate, smoke point will occur as the fuel flow rate is higher than

point correlates to the ratio of luminous length divided by stoichiometric length. This ratio increases 
with flow rate. Once it reaches about 2, smoke point occurs.15,18,19 The last surmise suggests that 
smoke point correlates with the centerline flame residence time. This is the most complex8-11,17,18,2024 surmise because flame residence time affects the soot processes in twofold. An increase in 
residence time can lead to soot emissions by increasing the time available for soot formation. 
Because this generally also increases the time available for soot oxidation, it has been proposed that 
smoke points are associated with conditions where the time available for soot formation exceeds that 
for soot oxidation to certain extent.21 This is difficult to prove because to evaluate the flame 
residence time requires the velocity distribution alone the centerline and the flame length, both of 
which are resulted flame parameters, not readily available from primary parameters of the 
experiment. In addition, the soot formation time and oxidation time are conceptually defined. 
Practically, these times are not measurable and they might be overlapped, i.e., for the same soot 
aggregate, adding and oxidizing carbon particles may happen simultaneously. Because of these

title: SPICE: Reports — SPICE FinalReport
text:
ation time and oxidation time are conceptually defined. 
Practically, these times are not measurable and they might be overlapped, i.e., for the same soot 
aggregate, adding and oxidizing carbon particles may happen simultaneously. Because of these 
difficulties and ambiguities, the fame residence time theory cannot be proved or disproved 
rigorously. However, these obstacles do not prevent us from checking the residence time theory 
against the observed smoke point data with the help of some approximated velocity distribution and 
flame length information. More detailed discussion of this effort can be found in the publications 
resulted from the SPICE project listed in Appendices B through F. The results showed that although 
residence time is helpful in understanding the present smoke points, it does not yield quantitative 
correlations. 
 
 
CLOSING REMARKS 
Smoke points of 55 microgravity gas-jet diffusion flames in coflowing air were measured in earth 
orbit. The conditions emphasized small burners and the effects of coflow velocity. These flames 
allow extensive control over residence time, which is important in smoke point phenomena. The 
major conclusions are as follows: 
1. An increase in coflow velocity increases the smoke point length. 
2. A decrease in burner diameter increases the smoke point length. 
3.

major conclusions are as follows: 
1. An increase in coflow velocity increases the smoke point length. 
2. A decrease in burner diameter increases the smoke point length.

fuel and/or coflow velocities yield increased smoke point lengths. 
4. The sooting propensities of the present fuel mixtures in microgravity increase according to 
ethylene < propane < 50% propylene < 75% propylene < propylene. This is the same as in 
normal gravity except for the exchanged positions of ethylene and propane. 
5. Consistent with past theory and experiments, luminous length at the smoke point is 
proportional to fuel mass flow rate. However there is a slight increase in luminous length as 
ua / uf decreases. 
6. Although residence time is helpful in understanding the present smoke points, it does not 
yield quantitative correlations of smoke points.

title: PSI-115: Reports — NNX17AF08A FinalReport
text:
1
Executive Summary
This work examines how microgravity conditions on spacecraft change the development of smoke
aerosol relative to smoke on Earth.
We perform simulations of particle formation and growth with
the goal of capturing smoke dynamics similar to those realized in experiments performed aboard the
International Space Station. The simulations provide detailed information about fluid/thermal/particle
interactions that cannot be acquired experimentally on orbit. A surrogate material, dibutyl pthalate, is
expelled from a hot surface in a rectangular chamber while ambient air is blown through the domain,
convecting the developing smoke downstream. The study considers two flow rates, two geometric configurations, and the isolated effects of gravitational particle settling and thermophoresis. In Earth gravity,
buoyancy produces asymmetries in all fields of interest and amplifies vapor-to-particle conversion near
room temperature surfaces at the upper boundary of the simulation domain. Gravitational settling removes large particles from the aerosol, limiting the maximum particle size to ∼40 µm and the mode
particle size to ∼5 µm. Without buoyancy or settling, the microgravity smoke plume is spatially symmetric and contains very large particles (> 40 µm). A bimodal particle size distribution results in microgravity

title: PSI-115: Reports — NNX17AF08A FinalReport
text:
particle size to ∼40 µm and the mode
particle size to ∼5 µm. Without buoyancy or settling, the microgravity smoke plume is spatially symmetric and contains very large particles (> 40 µm). A bimodal particle size distribution results in microgravity
when prominent recirculation occurs behind the hot vapor source. The distribution is comprised of large
particles (> 20 µm) associated with long residency time, vapor rich, high temperature recirculation, and
smaller particles (< 10 µm) that originate farther downstream of the hot vapor source. A distinct large
particle mode does not appear in microgravity flows that do not have prominent high temperature recirculation, although the aerosol still contains large particles. Without recirculation, the mode particle
diameter in microgravity is ∼10 µm, or approximately twice that of terrestrial smoke. Results show that
future experiments should carefully consider and quantify surface interactions and the presence of hot,
recirculating vapor, in order to control geometry-dominated features of the particle size distribution.
A manuscript based on this work will be submitted to the journal Aerosol Science & Technology. The
final document, when accepted, will be provided to NASA.

title: PSI-115: Reports — NNX17AF08A FinalReport
text:
2
Introduction
Gravity affects the evolution of aerosols by introducing buoyancy and particle settling. Buoyant convection modifies the time-temperature history of the aerosol, as well as the spatial distribution of particles,
condensing vapor, and thermal energy. Gravity also causes the settling of large particles out of the
aerosol, provided the chemistry and vapor concentrations allow for the generation of large particles
with appreciable settling velocities. These factors combine to increase particle residency times in high
temperature, vapor rich regions in microgravity systems relative to terrestrial or Earth gravity systems
(Urban et al., 1998, 2005). As a result, smoke particles produced in microgravity tend to be larger than
those produced on Earth (Ku et al., 1995, Urban et al., 1998). Measurements suggest microgravity
smoke particles to be 2 −8 times larger than terrestrial smoke particles (Urban et al., 2005). Moreover,
large particles (not only smoke particles) persist in microgravity, with mass concentrations of particles
with diameter > 100 µm measured at ten-times that of a nominal terrestrial environment (Liu et al.,
1991). Total particulate mass concentrations are also more than five times greater in microgravity (Liu
et al., 1991). Understanding gravitational effects is of practical interest because it assists in the design

title: PSI-115: Reports — NNX17AF08A FinalReport
text:
terrestrial environment (Liu et al.,
1991). Total particulate mass concentrations are also more than five times greater in microgravity (Liu
et al., 1991). Understanding gravitational effects is of practical interest because it assists in the design
of mission-critical smoke detection systems for use in microgravity environments, including the International Space Station (Mulholland et al., 2015); systems developed and calibrated for terrestrial use may
not perform correctly in microgravity because of inappropriate particle size sensitivities (Urban et al.,
2005).
The present work uses numerical simulation to explore the influence of gravity on pyrolysis smoke
growth from a fundamental perspective. We simulate the formation and growth of dibutyl-phthalate
(DBP) particles in Earth gravity and microgravity environments. We utilize direct numerical simulation
via a Navier-Stokes nodal approach. The smoke originates from pyrolysis vapor expelled from a heated
sample in a geometry similar to that considered in the SAME experiments (Mulholland et al., 2015). The
intention of this effort is to quantify the differences between microgravity and Earth gravity smoke, and
to identify the fluid dynamic mechanisms that cause the differences. This study considers two crossflow velocities of sufficiently low speed that buoyancy cannot be neglected in the presence of gravity.

title: PSI-115: Reports — NNX17AF08A FinalReport
text:
ween microgravity and Earth gravity smoke, and
to identify the fluid dynamic mechanisms that cause the differences. This study considers two crossflow velocities of sufficiently low speed that buoyancy cannot be neglected in the presence of gravity.
Simulations are presented to assess the dependence of particle size distributions on thermophoresis,
particle settling, and flow geometry. The paper is organized as follows: we introduce the simulation and
modeling methodology, followed by a description of the flow geometry and the parameter space under
consideration; we then examine differences in the wake geometry attributable to buoyancy for the lower
of two flow speeds; next, we present and discuss instantaneous scalar fields as a means to describe
particle accumulation and growth in the buoyant and non-buoyant wakes that form downstream of the
hot vapor source; after developing an understanding of how the particle fields interact with the fluid
dynamics for the low speed cases, we consider the effects of thermophoresis, particle settling, flow
geometry, and the higher flow speed; we conclude with a discussion of the results, summarize findings
relevant to future experimentation, and outline directions for future work.

Results
4.1
FLOW CONFIGURATION
We simulate the formation and growth of DBP particles in air flowing over a heated sample that expels
DBP vapor. The simulation mimics the smoldering or pre-conflagration stage of a fire studied in experiments performed aboard the ISS (Mulholland et al., 2015). A schematic of the computational domain is
shown in Fig. 1. Room temperature air enters a long chamber and flows over a heated rectangular sample. Vapor released from the sample nucleates into particles that grow and are subsequently collected
downstream for analysis. The flow is laminar and steady, allowing the two-dimensional representation
to present physical characteristics largely representative of the SAME experiments (Mulholland et al.,
2015). DBP is used as the surrogate material because its properties are known and its use in modeling
is well-established (unlike the materials used in the SAME experiments).
4.2
PHYSICAL CONDITIONS
Constant fluid properties for air and DBP are provided in Table 1, and variable DBP properties are
provided in Table 2.
The enhancement factor required for the nucleation expression, Eqn. (20), is
defined for DBP as cnuc = 3.2 × 10−4 (Nguyen et al., 1987, Pyyk¨onen and Jokiniemi, 2000).
The thickness of the heated DBP source serves as the reference length scale, Lo = 0.0044 m (illustrated
in Fig.

The thickness of the heated DBP source serves as the reference length scale, Lo = 0.0044 m (illustrated
in Fig. 1), which is representative of the length scale in the SAME experiments (Mulholland et al.,
2015). The air enters from the left with velocity Uo and temperature To = 300 K. We consider two
inlet velocities: Uo = 0.08 m/s, the velocity considered in the SAME experiments, and a slightly faster
flow of Uo = 0.10 m/s. The upper and lower boundaries are impermeable, no-slip, iso-thermal surfaces
(Twall = To). The heated rectangle is also no-slip, has a fixed temperature of Ts = 473.2 K, and releases
DBP vapor at a constant mass flux of q′′ = 8.4 × 10−5 kg/m2 · s. The mass flux has been selected to be
representative of the mass loss data presented by Mulholland et al. (2015). Zero-derivative conditions
are imposed for all species and particle fields at the inlet and outlet. The gravitational acceleration is
considered at terrestrial (go = 9.81 m/s2) and microgravity (go = 0 m/s2) conditions.
The inlet velocities and the gravitational accelerations considered represent four cases with varying
Reynolds and Froude numbers. A summary of the simulations performed at the two flow speeds and

All assumptions utilized in this work are listed below.

perfect gases with constant properties defined in Table 1.

convective speed imposes a large computational burden. The computational challenge is often
remedied with a Boussinesq approximation, but this approach is not valid in the presence of large
density variations. Additionally, an elliptical solve for pressure is computationally intractable for the
number of iterations required to resolve the particle time scales. We instead use a scaled dynamic

The velocity field controls the convection of thermal energy, condensible species vapor, and particles.
Vorticity ω, defined as the curl of the velocity vector
ω = ∇× u,

Figure 8 shows the particle number densities for Cases 1MG and 1EG at downstream measurement

The Case 1MG distribution contains particle diameters ranging from hundreds of nanometers to tens

1EG contains a larger number density than Case 1MG for all particle sizes < 20 µm, and Case 1EG
contains no particles > 40 µm – these large particle settle out of the system. Case 1EG contains orders
of magnitude more particles < 5 µm than Case 1MG.

EFFECT OF PARTICLE SETTLING
In order to isolate the effects of particle settling, we modify Case 1EG by neglecting the settling mechanism (by setting uss⋆
j,k = 0). This case is referred to as Case 1EG–NS, where NS stands for “no settling”.
Figure 9 compares size distributions for Case 1MG, Case 1EG, and Case 1EG–NS at measurement
plane x′ = 26 at time t = 7 seconds. The Case 1EG–NS distribution is considerably wider than the other
cases. It contains particles ranging in size from nanometers to 100 µm. Case 1EG–NS also contains

two local maxima in the particle size distribution, much like Case 1MG and unlike Case 1EG. Eliminating
the settling mechanism has expanded the size distribution to include both smaller and larger particles,
and has also introduced a new local maximum in the size distribution near 35 µm.
4.8
EFFECT OF THERMOPHORESIS
Figure 10 shows particle number densities at time t = 7 seconds for Case 1MG in panel (a) and Case
1MG-NT in panel (b) (where NT stands for “no thermophoresis”). When thermophoresis is active, as in
panel (a), particles do not appear adjacent to the surface of the heated vapor source; the temperature
gradient is large normal to the surface, and thermophoresis forces the particles out of this region.
When thermophoresis is inactive, particles are able to remain near the hot surface. In this region, the
temperature is sufficiently high to cause evaporation. Small particles are able to diffuse out of the wake,
resulting in lower particle number densities inside the Case 1MG-NT wake than the Case 1MG wake.

Summary
We have simulated smoke formation and growth in microgravity and Earth gravity to examine how
buoyancy and particle settling affect thermal/fluid/particle interactions and the resultant smoke particle
size distributions. The simulated geometry emulates the SAME experiments performed aboard the
International Space Station (Mulholland et al., 2015). Dibutyl pthalate (DBP) vapor is released from a
heated rectangular sample, which serves as a surrogate for the smoldering material used in the SAME
experiments.
Large particles (> 30 µm) are present in the wake region downstream of the heated vapor source, and
large particle number densities (∼1010 m−3) occur inside the wake vortices. The wake contains large
particle number densities because dividing streamlines prevent the particles from being convected away,
and the particles continue to grow as condensation consumes all available DBP vapor. The particles
simultaneously grow via coagulation. Downstream of the wake, two parallel particle streams contain
high number densities of both large and small particles. No particles are present far downstream with
diameter < 400 nm because nucleation only occurs for a short distance downstream of the heated vapor source. The particle size distributions contain local maximums near dp = 5 µm and dp = 35 µm for
both flow speeds.

title: PSI-115: Reports — NNX17AF08A FinalReport
text:
es are present far downstream with
diameter < 400 nm because nucleation only occurs for a short distance downstream of the heated vapor source. The particle size distributions contain local maximums near dp = 5 µm and dp = 35 µm for
both flow speeds. The faster flow conditions present a slightly larger wake but this does not manifest
as a meaningful difference in particle size distribution. Thermophoresis prevents particles from contacting the heated surface, which has been demonstrated by turning off the thermophoresis mechanism.
Without thermophoresis, particles contact the heated vapor source and undergo evaporation. With respect to the particle size distribution, this has the effect of decreasing the number of large particles and
increasing the number of small particles – this supports an assertion that the wake is responsible for
producing the largest particles in the system.
When gravity is present, all fields become asymmetric due to buoyant convection. Upward convection
in the faster flow brings DBP vapor into close proximity with the cool upper surface, resulting in locally
high nucleation rates near the upper wake vortex and the upper surface. Large particle number densities (∼1011 m−3) are present along the upper surface, and slightly lower number densities are present
in the upper wake vortex. Comparably few particles are present in the lower wake vortex, where the

nd the upper surface. Large particle number densities (∼1011 m−3) are present along the upper surface, and slightly lower number densities are present
in the upper wake vortex. Comparably few particles are present in the lower wake vortex, where the
diameter of average mass is maximized. Downstream of the wake vortices, gravitational settling eliminates all particles with diameter > 35 µm. Unlike the microgravity case, the 8 cm/s Earth gravity case is
not bimodal, with a single local maximum at dp = 5 µm. Without particle settling, a bimodal distribution
results with two local maximums at particle diameters comparable to the microgravity case. Rotating the
heated vapor source 90◦dramatically reduces the wake volume, and no particles appear in the small
wake. Rotating the heated vapor source does not affect the Earth gravity case as significantly as the
microgravity case. Increasing the flow speed from decreases the prominence of buoyancy, delays interaction with the upper surface until further downstream, widens the particle size distribution to include
particles on the nanometer scale, and introduces a second local maximum to the PSD near dp = 30 µm.
Microgravity smoke presented in this study contains larger particles than terrestrial smoke. When the
microgravity PSD is bimodal, the larger mode contains particles with dp > 35 µm, while the terrestrial

title: PSI-115: Reports — NNX17AF08A FinalReport
text:
nd local maximum to the PSD near dp = 30 µm.
Microgravity smoke presented in this study contains larger particles than terrestrial smoke. When the
microgravity PSD is bimodal, the larger mode contains particles with dp > 35 µm, while the terrestrial
PSD contains effectively zero particles in this size range. Alternatively, the microgravity PSD can be unimodal with a mode diameter of dp = 10 µm – roughly twice that of the terrestrial case. Results exhibit
three primary mechanisms that differentiate the microgravity and Earth gravity smoke: (1) different recirculation geometries and volumes modify the time-temperature-concentration history of the aerosol in
regions of high temperature and high vapor mass fraction; (2) particle settling eliminates large particles
from Earth gravity smoke, which reduces the maximum particle size and modifies aerosol development
by changing coagulation and condensation rates of the remaining particles; (3) buoyant convection can
transport condensible species toward relatively cool surfaces, increasing vapor-to-particle conversion.
Each of these factors tend to increase the size of particles in microgravity relative to Earth gravity. However, each of these factors is also highly material- and geometry-dependent: (1) the wake dynamic
becomes unimportant if nucleation occurs far downstream of the wake, or if there is a time dependent

cles in microgravity relative to Earth gravity. However, each of these factors is also highly material- and geometry-dependent: (1) the wake dynamic
becomes unimportant if nucleation occurs far downstream of the wake, or if there is a time dependent
flow without a stable recirculation region; (2) particle settling is irrelevant if the condensing species forms
particles that are too small to settle (the DBP considered in this work forms large particles); (3) if smoke
is produced in an open environment, there may not be cool surfaces nearby to increase nucleation
rates. In these situations, microgravity and Earth gravity smoke are hypothesized to be more similar. In

11
Extinction Diameter
Comparison of measured and predicted hot and cool flame extinction diameter for different 
initial droplet diameter for the three n-alkane fuels (atmospheric air) 
•
 High temperature combustion is strongly governed by the small species kinetics – all three fuels share 
nearly identical values of HF extinction diameter for the same do
•
The LTC differs with carbon number as each involve reactions associated with the carbon number of the 
fuel and the large intermediates produced. The overall rates of isomerization of radical-O2 adducts 
controlling rate of degenerate chain branching rate increase from C7 to C12
•
The CF extinction is dictated by the increase in decomposition of •O2QnOOH for all three fuels.

title: PSI-117: Presentations — Extinction Characteristics TFarouk
text:
12
Extinction Characteristics: Pressure Dependence
Evolution of FSR, Kb and Tmax for n-dodecane droplets 
for different pressure (do = 4.00 mm, air)
•
For pressure ≤ 1.0 atm, two stage combustion – hot 
and cool flame extinction. 
•
At 1.25 atm, multi-cycling of hot-cool-hot-cool flame 
transition. 
•
At 3.0 atm, the system transitions to a stable “Warm” 
flame. 
•
Cool flame temperature increases with pressure and 
results in a hot flame reignition. 
•
“Warm” flame is dictated by NTC kinetics and 
competition for OH between hydrocarbon and 
oxygenated hydrocarbon fragments.

text:
15
Extinction Diameter: Pressure Dependence
Comparison of predicted and measured de,HF and de,CF as a 
function of operating pressure for of n-dodecane droplets burning 
in air. (do = 4.00 mm).
•
Both hot and cool flame extinction diameter has a 
non-linear dependence on pressure. 
•
de,CF decreases as pressure is increased, and is 
absent at 3 atm as the droplet burns to completion 
following a “Warm” flame combustion
•
The de,CF is most sensitive to:
•O2QnOOH → •OQn`OOH + OH
•O2QnOOH → QnOOH + O2

title: PSI-117: Presentations — Extinction Characteristics TFarouk
text:
16
• Two-stage hot-cool flame burning mode transitions are demonstrated to exist for the three 
fuels, and the maximum flame temperature at which transition to the second stage occurred 
was universally found to be ~ 1200K. 
• Hot flame characteristics of all three fuels indicate that predicted extinction phenomena are all 
very similar.
• Cool flame extinction properties are significantly affected by the n-alkane molecular weight, 
and the chain length of the n-alkane has significant effect on the cool flame reactivity - larger nalkane exhibited more robust cool flame (i.e., higher temperature) and hence smaller extinction 
diameters.
• Universally, de,CF for each fuel varies linearly with initial droplet diameter, but unlike de,HF these 
relationships do not collapse to a single function.
• n-Dodecane droplet combustion reveal a strong dependence of observations on ambient 
pressure. Single, two-stage hot-cool flame combustion transitions to a multi-cycle combustion 
behavior at ambient pressures above one atmosphere, and eventually into a hot - “Warm” flame 
transition.

title: PSI-117: Presentations — Oscillatory Cool Flame TFarouk
text:
 Dynamics of near-limit cool flame burning of isolated submillimeter (Do = 
0.5 mm) n-C7H16 droplet is numerically studied.
Reduced ambient O2 mole fraction (10%) is considered to facilitate nearlimit condition.
Under selective O3 seeding (5%), the droplet briefly attempts to initiate 
stable cool flame before entering continuous oscillatory cool flame burn.
Local depletion of O2 (<13.5%) near the droplet initiates the pulsing 
behavior with initial small fluctuation in flame temperature.
The oscillation is found to increase in magnitude with time, and at each 
successive cycle.
Dynamic interaction of degenerate chain branching and chain propagation 
/ termination reaction classes of QOOH (within NTC region) is responsible 
for the observed oscillation.
Continuous fuel leakage through the flame location assists the oscillation 
to grow in radial direction with time.

discretized first in space and then integrated in an automated fashion as a set 
of coupled ordinary differential-algebraic equations in time.
Spatial discretization is performed according to a node-centered finite 
volume scheme with a second order accuracy.
The innermost liquid node is centered at the origin, providing the required 
no-flux condition.
The discretized mass flux is represented on cell interfaces and not cell 
centers, in the manner traditionally referred to as a staggered grid to avoid 
oscillatory solutions.
Numerical integration of the final set of discretized equations is performed 
using a backward difference formula with a variable order of up to fifth order 
and a variable time step utilizing a fully implicit multipoint interpolation.

vi 
ABSTRACT
The primary scientific explorations of this thesis work are to better understand (a) 
microgravity fire-suppression of untested extinguisher, (b) combustion kinetic model 
refinement of renewable fuel butanol (C4H9OH) isomers, and (c) directly induced cool 
flame dynamics of higher n-alkane fuels from an isolated small droplet combustion 
perspective employing computational fluid dynamics with comprehensive chemical 
kinetics. The chronological development of the research direction shifts from a relatively 
small fuel like methanol (CH3OH) to heavier straight paraffinic fuel n-decane (n-C10H22). 
The first installment of the thesis is directed towards answering the feasibility of thennewly considered fire suppressant xenon (Xe) for microgravity space application by the 
National Aeronautics and Space Administration (NASA). Methanol was used as model 
fuel to assess the combustion behavior under xenon-rich environment. The 
comprehensive analysis revealed that xenon promotes longer burning time and higher 
flame temperature compared to existing other diluents/extinguishers and can support hot 
flame with much lesser oxygen content than its counterparts. The exceptionally low 
thermal diffusivity of xenon is identified to be responsible for the significantly higher 
peak gas temperature and prolonged burn time. This detailed analysis clearly debilitates

lesser oxygen content than its counterparts. The exceptionally low 
thermal diffusivity of xenon is identified to be responsible for the significantly higher 
peak gas temperature and prolonged burn time. This detailed analysis clearly debilitates 
the potential of xenon as a next-generation fire-suppressant for microgravity applications 
and helped NASA in safeguard financial investment for International Space Station (ISS) 
experiments using xenon.

vii 
The second installment of the thesis outlines the efforts directed towards 
improving the gas phase kinetic model of butanol isomers based on droplet combustion 
experiments and computations. This is a unique contribution where the traditional gasphase experiment/theory-driven kinetic model is further refined in light of critical 
recommendations from the droplet combustion analysis. The comprehensive kinetic 
model of Sarathy et al. (Combust. Flame, 2012) is one of the two widely used model for 
butanol isomers which has been extensively validated against homogeneous gas phase 
experiments. The numerical simulation of the butanol droplet combustion experiments at 
atmospheric conditions predicted the faster burning rate and larger flame diameter using 
the above model. An exhaustive perturbation analysis is carried on chemical, 
thermodynamic and transport parameters influences (while simultaneously isolating their 
cross-influences) to pinpoint the root cause of faster burning tendency of the model. The 
synthesized results from this huge variable-matric perturbation revealed that the isomerspecific species transport parameters were culpable, and recommendations were made to 
update those Lennard-Jones potential parameters. Once updated, the computational 
predictions significantly improves for the Sarathy et al. model based on the feedback 
from droplet combustion.

The final segment of the thesis discusses the direct initiation of cool flame 
combustion for submillimeter-sized higher n-alkane droplets (n-heptane and n-decane) 
for possible terrestrial experiments without the necessity of radiative extinction as 
frequently encountered onboard the ISS experiments. It has been found that the 
dimensionality of the droplet (Do = 0.5 mm) statistically reduces the possibility of 
achieving direct cool flame burn for the droplet by simply varying the ignition energy

initiation. Therefore, it was conceptualized that a combination of a reduced ignition 
source and induction chemistry modulation may hold the possibility of direct initiation of 
cool flame for n-C7H16 and n-C10H22 even in ground-based drop tower experiments. To 
facilitate this idea, we numerically investigate the droplet combustion under selective 
ozone (O3) augmented ambient where O3 serves as an induction chemistry modulator 
through its liberation of atomic O via molecular decomposition. The available atomic O 
then reacts with the surrounding fuel producing OH radical, and eventually water and 
heat. This latter heat input acts as a secondary thermal feedback to the droplet surface 
maintaining steady surface burning rate which then stabilizes the cool flame very near the 
droplet surface. It was found that the fuel physical properties, especially flash point, play 
a decisive role in determining the nature of the initial cool flame dynamics and the ozone 
requirements. Higher flash point fuel (here, n-C10H22) is likely to undergo initial dumped 
cool flame oscillation than its lower value counterpart (n-C7H16) and will require higher 
O3 loading under identical ambient. In the near-limit condition, such directly introduced 
cool flame fails to attain a steady burn and enters into a continuously evolving oscillatory 
cool flame.

PREFACE
This thesis reports the combustion behavior of sphero-symmetric small droplets 
for two different classes of fuels (oxygenated alcohols and n-alkanes) under diversified 
ambient conditions with the individual unique objective for each study. The research 
outcomes from this dissertation work were timely published in the leading combustion 
field-specific journals. The author prepared the thesis chapters 3-7 (in consultation with 
the thesis adviser) from those published articles with necessary amendments following 
the guidelines from the graduate school of the University of South Carolina, SC, USA. 
As a consequence, chapter relevant thorough background information from literature is 
provided at the beginning of each chapter. However, an abridged critical review of the 
droplet combustion literature is also included in the 1st chapter to complement the 
rationale of this Ph.D. work. It should be noted that the necessary approval from the 
publishing agencies and collaborators were sought in advance for this dissertation. The 
list of correlated chapters and the associated published article can be found on page 11.

1.1 PROBLEM STATEMENT 
The efficient conversion of fossil fuels to useful energy has been an active area of 
research ever since the development of steam engine by Sir James Watt and the postindustrial revolution [1]. Since then, fossil fuels have incredibly the preferred choice of 
energy production in the form of ‘shaft output’ from the prime movers (i.e., engines, gas 
turbines, propellers, boilers and so on). Consequently, it is anticipated that the fossil fuels 
(gaseous and condensed phase) will also remain the automatic choice of ground, marine 
and aviation transportation systems for forth-coming future [2]. Such a prolific use of fossil 
fuels is primarily due to their extraordinary energy density irrespective of any defined 
metric (unit mass or volume basis) as illustrated in Figs. 1.1 and 1.2. Therefore, despite the 
resurgence of renewable energy sources in recent times (solar, wind, tidal, biomass etc.), 
combustion technology will remain the principal source of energy conversion for centuries. 
 
 
Figure 1.1 Comparison of energy content per unit volume for different fossil fuels and battery types 
(normalized against the conventional gasoline). Courtesy- United States energy information 
administration (https://www.eia.gov).

However, the boon of combustion technology is not a singular entity and is often 
rationally criticized for contributing to the harmful emissions, posing detrimental effects 
on the environment as well as human health. Therefore, modern combustion technology 
simultaneously aims for higher conversion efficiency and lower perilous emission to tackle 
the ever stringent regulatory constraints [4, 5]. In relation to the fuel combustion, its 
ignition, flame development, and pollutant formation are inevitably interconnected. 
Therefore, the fundamental insights regarding the flame dynamics and species evolutions 
(including the harmful ones) are typically studied in standardized combustion and/or 
oxidation settings at desired thermodynamic states (P, T). Historically, such fundamental 
endeavors are carried out extensively using shock tubes [6], flow reactors [7], jet-stirred 
reactors [8], rapid compression machines [9], burner stabilized premixed flames [10] and 
opposed diffusion flame burners [11]. Although these test facilities are far from practical 
ideality for combustion devices, they offer unique opportunities to individually study

due to their simplified flow field, the detail kinetic analysis is possible for these zero- or 
one-dimensional problems. While these experimental platforms and associated kinetic 
analyses serve as the foundational stage for the combustion research, they have two major 
concerns- (a) the studies have to be conducted in gas phase reactant mixtures, and (b) they 
are either steady state [7, 8, 10, 11] with transport effect, or transient in nature [6, 9] 
ignoring altogether the transport effect. Therefore, there exists a natural gap in studying the 
fuel combustion considering both the unsteady flame dynamics and the transport effect. 
The investigation of isolated single fuel droplet combustion in absence of (under 
significantly reduced) gravity offers a unique opportunity to probe liquid fuel combustion 
under unsteady transport dependent environment [12]. With such an advantageous 
canonical configuration, the physical problem becomes classical Stefan flow problem [13] 
where enthalpy and species transports are one-dimensional in radial coordinate. 
Computationally, such a facile reacting fluid domain can be modeled with detailed kinetics 
[14, 15], even to validate associated submodels, e.g., radiation model [16, 17], transport 
model (multicomponent vs. mixture average) [18] and water dissolution model [15, 1921].

[14, 15], even to validate associated submodels, e.g., radiation model [16, 17], transport 
model (multicomponent vs. mixture average) [18] and water dissolution model [15, 1921]. 
Interestingly, although one-dimensional droplet combustion may appear simple in 
configuration, it has relevance to the complex spray environment by incorporating moving 
boundary effects, unsteady heat conduction and mass diffusion in the droplet and 
surrounding gas, variable properties (dependent on temperature and composition), phase 
equilibrium at the interface, radiation dynamics, and a detailed kinetic mechanism for the 
combustion process. Traditionally, isolated droplet combustion studies (with or without the 
gravity) are conducted to understand the fuel ignition, burning rate characteristics, flame

conventionality to apply droplet combustion approach, namely- (a) fire extinguishment, (b) 
kinetic model validation and improvement, and (c) new combustion technology study. This 
thesis work is dedicated to exploring these less-ventured pathways where computational 
droplet combustion can enhance the understanding of liquid fuel combustion. 
 
1.2 LITERATURE REVIEW 
 
Study of single isolated or array of isolated droplets has existed nearly seven 
decades since the pioneering work of G.A.E. Godsave [25, 26]. These initial investigations 
were primarily empirical in nature, therefore covering a wide range of fuels, e.g., benzene, 
tertiary butyl benzene, decalin, n-heptane etc. Along the line, Kumagai and coworkers were 
the forerunners in studying the combustion behavior of isolated droplet under reduced 
gravity environment [27, 28]. These investigators are the first to conduct research on 
spherical diffusion flames in absence of gravity and formulated a theoretical framework to 
study it numerically. In an independent study, Goldsmith and Penner [29] improved the 
simplified model of Godsave and also performed extensive experimental investigations 
[30] to delineate the role of increased ambient oxidizer, pressure and temperature on 
burning rate.

simplifying assumptions can lead up to 20% error in predictions [33]. In contemporary 
time, researchers also engaged continuous photography and video recording techniques 
[34] to understand the dynamics of droplet combustion. As the importance of droplet 
combustion became more prominent from spray perspective, researchers like Hottel et al. 
[35] experimentally pursued the combustion behavior of different heavy fuels. 
The pivotal works of the fifties (i.e., till 1960) played an instrumental role to 
motivate the researchers to study droplet combustion with multifaceted research objectives. 
Combustion of the droplet and its subsequent burning behavior has been studied for rocket 
combustor application [36], high-pressure systems [37-39], denotation configuration [40], 
super-critical condition [41], evaporation model development [42] and for the ignition and 
extinction of droplets [43, 44]. Kassoy and Williams are the first to propose a theoretical 
formulation accounting for variable property effect on droplet combustion along with finite 
rate chemistry [45], and showed that numerical predictions improved significantly over 
constant fluid property approach.

decoupling the role of external convective perturbation. Concurrently, Aldred and 
coworkers [49] experimentally explored the transient dynamics of relatively smaller 
droplet combustion with a conclusion of the inadequacy of the-then existing theoretical 
models. In the form of theoretical treatment, Law [50] proposed an asymptotic analysis of 
ignition and extinction of liquid fuel droplet which was then further improved to account 
the internal mixing considering the unsteady effect of multicomponent droplet [51]. Based 
on this contributing works, Law and Sirignano [52, 53] developed fully transient droplet 
combustion model. Crespo and Linan [54] also deployed asymptotic analysis to explore 
the effect of unsteady effects of droplet combustion and evaporation. In pursuit of 
developing more realistic theoretical models, Law et al. [55] improved their previous 
formulations incorporating the convective effect to unsteady multicomponent model. By 
the late 1970s, an emulsion of water-fuel mixture received attention across the combustion 
communities due to its relevance to practical application, and it was venture as a binary 
mixture under droplet configuration [56-58].

works lead by F.L. Dryer at the Princeton University were the first to deploy computational 
fluid dynamics (CFD) in analyzing sphero-symmetric droplet combustion invoking 
detailed kinetics [69, 70]. These authors have successfully demonstrated the necessity of 
detailed kinetics in reproducing the experimental targets against reduced- or micro-gravity 
tests [71]. At this point in time, a careful synthesis of four decades of droplet combustion 
research (1950s-1990s) illustrates that the research thrust was first initiated by the 
empirical terrestrial experimentation (with or without gravity) which simultaneously led to 
the theoretical development of isolated droplet combustion phenomena. Subsequently, the 
role of chemistry was included in numerical consideration through single-step finite rate 
chemistry, and finally the development of CFD analysis with detailed kinetics. 
Beginning in the early nineties (the 1990s), the research direction with isolated 
droplet combustion shifts from global observational and/or fundamental targets to 
individualistic physical phenomena base understanding. To accommodate such objectives, 
methanol (CH3OH) was a generic choice of fuel due to its simplified chemistry and nonsooting tendency [16, 19-21, 72-81].

of this literature review, and is well documented in the review articles of Aggarwal [23] 
and Sirignano [24], and in respective chapters hereafter. However, a careful reexamination 
of all these major studies shows that the isolated droplet combustion can be further 
deployed to harness deeper insight for (a) fire suppressant effectiveness, (b) 
improving/refining detailed chemistry to complex fuels, and (c) oscillatory behavior of low 
temperature driven cool flames. This existing knowledge gap was the main intrinsic 
motivation to pursue this dissertation work in the field of isolated droplet combustion 
employing high fidelity CFD code with detailed kinetics. 
 
1.3 SCOPE AND ORGANIZATION OF THE THESIS WORK 
 
Since the seminal works of Godsave [25, 26], attention for isolated droplet has been 
given exclusively for large diameter droplets (order of several millimeters, 
analytical/experimental/computational) including the experiments conducted onboard the 
international space station [89]. To facilitate a gravityless environment for large diameter 
droplets, testings were primarily conducted in either space shuttle experiments or in the 
ISS as a terrestrial test site would demand very high drop tower free-fall height. To the

droplets, testings were primarily conducted in either space shuttle experiments or in the 
ISS as a terrestrial test site would demand very high drop tower free-fall height. To the 
contrary, smaller droplets (Do < 1.0 mm) require much less drop hight, thus opening the 
opportunity to do the testing in ground-based facility avoiding the expansive space-based 
testing [94]. This thesis work focuses on the numerical analysis of small diameter droplet 
combustion for a variety of practical fuels to extend the potentiality of droplet combustion 
in understanding the fire dynamics, reaction kinetics, and cool flame combustion.
