instability, and soot formation. 
 
The tests conducted on 19254 (near the end of Increment 60) revealed that a quasi-steady 
flame could be attained for extended duration at low flow rate, i.e., 3 cc/s for 20% 
C2H4/80% N2 (on a volume basis). The flame was shut down by the automated system 
because the burner reached a cut-off temperature of 250°C. Although the flame 
oscillated near the end of the test, it was likely due to influence of the burner tube. 
Comparisons with computation simulations will help to clarify the involved processes. For 
higher flow rates, e.g., 5-10 cc/s, with the same mixture, radiative extinctions were 
observed. Generally, the flames showed unstable behavior near the burner tube prior to 
extinction, likely because of lack of fuel mixture and heat loss in that region. Other

title: ACME s-Flame: Reports — s Flame final report 20210729
text:
ACME/s-Flame Final Report (2021) 
 
29 July 2021 
65 
 
mixtures, e.g., 25% C2H4/75% N2 and 30% C2H4/70% N2, also showed radiative extinctions 
at higher flow rates. For some cases, the pyrometry fiber interacted with the flame, 
allowing determination of temperature in on-going analyses. Soot was observed only 
during ignition, which went away as the flame established itself. To assess whether these 
nitrogen-diluted ethylene flames are non-sooty or sooty, cases were run where mixtures 
were ignited and established at low flow rates (e.g., 3 cc/s) with low ethylene contents 
(e.g., 25-30% C2H4) and then ramped to high flow rates (e.g., 5-10 cc/s) with higher 
ethylene contents (e.g., 40-50% C2H4). The flames all radiatively extinguished, but no 
sooting was observed. Observations of such radiative extinction behavior at high flow 
rates is an achievement because such phenomenon was not observed in our groundbased studies, given the limited microgravity durations. Radiative reabsorption extends 
flame size at extinction. In ISS testing, radiative extinction has been found to be a 
common event, which was predicted computationally, but not observed previously for 
our flame conditions. 
 
The 19256 tests (in Increment 60) were aimed at examining kinetic extinction. Similar to 
the radiative extinction cases, sufficient microgravity duration is needed to observe

title: ACME s-Flame: Reports — s Flame final report 20210729
text:
mputationally, but not observed previously for 
our flame conditions. 
 
The 19256 tests (in Increment 60) were aimed at examining kinetic extinction. Similar to 
the radiative extinction cases, sufficient microgravity duration is needed to observe 
kinetic extinction because a near steady flame needs to be established first, before ramp 
down in flow rate to find properly the chemical kinetic extinction limit. High flow rate 
cases (e.g., 13.5 cc/s, 15 cc/s) showed asymmetrical flames which radiatively 
extinguished. Flow rates were lowered so that quasi-steady flames could be established 
before ramp down in flow rate. The 15% C2H4 mixtures were not strong enough to sustain 
a quasi-steady flame at 3 cc/s before ramp down. However, for stronger mixtures, i.e., 
20-30% C2H4, very nice flames were established at 3 cc/s; and kinetic extinctions were 
observed during ramp down before reaching 1 cc/s. Radiative extinctions for ramp up 
cases were also examined. Similarly, for stronger mixtures, i.e., 20-30% C2H4, very nice 
flames were established at 3 cc/s; and radiative extinctions were observed during ramp 
up before reaching 8 cc/s. 
 
Testing on 19304 investigated 45% CH4/55% N2 mixtures issuing into an air atmosphere. 
The results indicated that the flow rates specified by the fuel MFC (0.5 slpm) were in the 
regime of kinetic extinction.

title: ACME s-Flame: Reports — s Flame final report 20210729
text:
uring ramp 
up before reaching 8 cc/s. 
 
Testing on 19304 investigated 45% CH4/55% N2 mixtures issuing into an air atmosphere. 
The results indicated that the flow rates specified by the fuel MFC (0.5 slpm) were in the 
regime of kinetic extinction. Quasi-steady flames could not be established. Furthermore, 
larger flow rates could not be provided by the MFC, so observations of radiative extinction 
could not be achieved. Even with a larger capacity MFC, characteristically larger flames 
would be expected to be asymmetric. As such, nitrogen-diluted methane flames were 
planned to be reexamined in increased oxygen atmosphere, i.e., 30% O2/70% N2. 
 
Consequently, the 19308 tests investigated nitrogen-diluted methane flames in 30% 
O2/70% N2 atmosphere. Various methane concentrations from 45% down to 15% were 
examined. For 45% CH4/55% N2, relatively long duration flames of ~15 s and ~10 s were 
established at flow rates of 2 cc/s and 3 cc/s, respectively. At larger flow rates of 5 and 
9.4 cc/s, the flames expanded to large radii and then extinguished. These flames 
appeared to demonstrate radiative extinction. Reduction of flow rate from 2 cc/s to 1 
cc/s resulted in extinction during ramp down, indicating kinetic extinction. For 30%

title: ACME s-Flame: Reports — s Flame final report 20210729
text:
ACME/s-Flame Final Report (2021) 
 
29 July 2021 
66 
 
CH4/70% N2, flow rates of 3, 5, and 10 cc/s produced flames that expanded to extinction 
(assumed radiatively); while reduction of flow rate from 3 to 1 cc/s resulted in presumably 
kinetic extinction during ramp down. For 25% CH4/75% N2, flow rates of 5 and 10 cc/s 
yielded flames that expanded to extinction. For 20% CH4/80% N2, constant flow rate of 
10 cc/s created a flame that expanded until extinction (assumed radiatively); while 
reduction of flow rate from 10 cc/s to 1 cc/s resulted in wavering extinction during ramp 
down, suggesting kinetic extinction. For 15% CH4/85% N2, flames were ignited, but 
extinguished very quickly. These tests of 19308 suggest that they could manifest both 
radiative and kinetic extinction for the conditions specified. 
 
The 19352 tests examined various concentrations of H2 (45%-70%) diluted with N2 issuing 
into air. The installed fuel MFC had a maximum output of 0.1 slpm, which unfortunately 
provided a less-than-sufficient flow range where its use may have precluded the study of 
radiative extinction corresponding to larger flame sizes. Imaging the diluted hydrogen 
flames was a challenge, especially since the hobj image files from the ACME DataCam 
were mis-formatted. Furthermore, little could be seen in the analog ops imaging, e.g.,

title: ACME s-Flame: Reports — s Flame final report 20210729
text:
xtinction corresponding to larger flame sizes. Imaging the diluted hydrogen 
flames was a challenge, especially since the hobj image files from the ACME DataCam 
were mis-formatted. Furthermore, little could be seen in the analog ops imaging, e.g., 
where it, like the DataCam and Cool Flames Investigation (CFI) intensified camera, cannot 
image the ultraviolet OH* flame emission (at 310 nm). Analysis of images from the Low 
Light Level Ultraviolet (LLL-UV) camera and its OH* filter is ongoing. And as one might 
expect, little could be seen with the CFI intensified camera using its broadband CH2O filter. 
Quasi-steady flames seem to be present at low flow rates (e.g., 2.4 cc/s for 70% H2), as 
inferred from PMT, pyrometry fiber emission, and burner temperature observations. 
Kinetic extinction seems to occur as the flow rate is ramped down. There were various 
problems with the IPSU and some tests aborted. Using the 100% H2 bottle with a higher 
flow rate MFC was later performed for tests of 20024 (see below), which was a make-up 
test day added because of the mis-formatting of the DataCam image files. 
 
The tests conducted on 20006, using the 44.4% H2/55.6% CH4 bottle, examined 20% 
H2/25% CH4/55% N2 mixtures issuing into air. Flames extinguished, some with wavy 
oscillating behavior prior to extinction. However, it seems that even for very small flow

title: ACME s-Flame: Reports — s Flame final report 20210729
text:
tests conducted on 20006, using the 44.4% H2/55.6% CH4 bottle, examined 20% 
H2/25% CH4/55% N2 mixtures issuing into air. Flames extinguished, some with wavy 
oscillating behavior prior to extinction. However, it seems that even for very small flow 
rates, e.g., 2 cc/s, extinction was by the radiative mechanism during flame 
expansion. There was too little parameter room in terms of flow rate and burner size to 
identify conclusively kinetic extinction during ramp down for these mixtures. In short, 
radiative extinction (with local flame extinction and re-ignition seemed to occur prior to 
ultimate extinguishment) during flame expansion after ignition was observed. However, 
it is unclear whether ramping down the flow rate resulted in kinetic extinction. Detailed 
analyses of the data are needed. The various cameras seemed to capture the tests well. 
 
The 20013 tests, which used the 66.7% H2/33.3% CH4 bottle, mainly investigated 30% 
H2/15% CH4/55% N2 mixtures issuing into air. Radiative extinction was difficult to identify 
conclusively because flames with larger flow rates, e.g. 15 cc/s, seemed to last, although 
with patchy extinction areas, until time out. Larger flow rates could not be examined 
either because of limited MFC range or distorted flame shape cause by burner limitations 
at high flow rates. Also, kinetic extinction during ramp down could not be identified

67 
 
conclusively, as some flames seemed to extinguish because they were "going into the 
burner." 
 
The 20024 tests using the 100% H2 bottle repeated and augmented conditions for those 
of 19352 where the 0.1-slpm fuel MFC range was too low to examine radiative extinction 
and the analog and intensified cameras did not pick up the flame images at all or well. 
Here, the 0.5-slpm fuel MFC was used and only a fused silica filter was used for the Cool 
Flames Investigation (CFI) intensified camera. 45%-15% H2/N2 balance mixtures were 
investigated. The flames at high flow rates, e.g., 10 cc/s, did not extinguish, appearing 
quasi-steady until time out. The pyrometry fibers glowed, perhaps making good flamestructure measurements, which will be evaluated subsequently. The flames seemed to 
extinguish during ramp down, but further analysis is needed to assess kinetic extinction. 
 
The tests conducted on 20029 used 50% C2H4/50% N2 and repeated and augmented 
conditions of 19256, when the images were not good. Again, the results indicated both 
kinetic and radiative extinction phenomena under corresponding conditions. However, 
no sooting flames were established, necessitating 100% C2H4 and an enriched oxygen 
atmosphere to facilitate sooting behavior in possible future tests.

kinetic and radiative extinction phenomena under corresponding conditions. However, 
no sooting flames were established, necessitating 100% C2H4 and an enriched oxygen 
atmosphere to facilitate sooting behavior in possible future tests. 
 
The 20132 tests kicked off a round of tests with helium-diluted fuel and oxidizer. The 
ambient was 21% O2 and 79% He. The fuel was composed of 25% H2, 20% CH4, and 55% 
He. Using He as inert made igniting the mixture much more difficult compared to that for 
the N2 inert cases of Round 1, using the same ignition parameters. The reason is believed 
to be due to the 6X higher value in thermal conductivity of He versus that of N2. As a 
result, ignition parameters were varied, e.g., with a longer preheat time and higher 
power, to achieve ignition for the He-diluted mixtures and ambient. The tests produced 
flames at 3, 5, 7, and 10 cc/s that expanded outwardly quickly and extinguished. For 5, 7, 
and 10 cc/s, the flames seemed to disappear and 're-ignite' with a "flash" before final 
extinction. We are currently investigating the flash phenomenon. Moreover, the 
radiation mechanism is not conclusive, as it appears different than for the N2-diluted 
cases. We did not have a chance to examine lowering of flow rates to assess kinetic 
extinction. 
 
The 20136 tests examined 20% H2/25% CH4/55% He issuing into 21% O2/He. For 5 cc/s

title: ACME s-Flame: Reports — s Flame final report 20210729
text:
s not conclusive, as it appears different than for the N2-diluted 
cases. We did not have a chance to examine lowering of flow rates to assess kinetic 
extinction. 
 
The 20136 tests examined 20% H2/25% CH4/55% He issuing into 21% O2/He. For 5 cc/s 
and 7 cc/s, the mixture ignites but immediately extinguishes, with almost no observable 
flame-front expansion. For 10, 13, 15, and 17.5 cc/s, the mixtures ignite, expand quickly, 
and extinguish. We believe that the extinction mechanism is radiative and will compare 
with computational simulations. For the cases with a ramp down in flow rate, the flames 
seemed to extinguish before ramp down. Thus, we were not able to assess purely kinetic 
extinction. Ignition parameters were varied to investigate thresholds for igniting the 
mixture for different flow rates. Only flow rates above 7 cc/s showed flame-front 
expansion leading to extinction, with 17.5 cc/s showing a flash or wavering of the flame 
before final extinction.

The tests conducted on 20142 investigated 30% H2/15% CH4/55% He issuing into 30% 
O2/He. Elevated oxygen was approved for study, since ignition and extinction limits in 
previous testing were affected by the high thermal conductivity of He. For 5, 7, 10, 15, 
13, and 16.5 cc/s flow rates, nice flames were established that expanded to 
wavy/oscillating extinction at the end, indicative of radiative extinction. For the cases 
with a ramp down in flow rate, the flames seemed to extinguish during the ignition flow 
rate stage before ramp down. Thus, we were not able to assess kinetic extinction. 
 
The 20155 tests examined 45% H2/55% He issuing into 30% O2/He and 21% O2/He. 
Previous tests using He as inert had shown that much larger energy and power are needed 
to ignite the mixtures. For the 30% O2/H2 atmosphere, the tests produced flames at 10 
and 14 cc/s (MFC limit of 1 SLMP) that expanded after ignition, but were extinguished by 
the automated protocol because the burner reached the 250°C temperature limit before 
any self-extinction could occur. The flames were not too large at the end. Presumably, 
the thermally-conductive He diluent facilitates heat transfer to the burner. For the cases 
with a ramp down in flow rate, i.e., starting at 10 and 14 cc/s and ramping down, the

title: ACME s-Flame: Reports — s Flame final report 20210729
text:

the thermally-conductive He diluent facilitates heat transfer to the burner. For the cases 
with a ramp down in flow rate, i.e., starting at 10 and 14 cc/s and ramping down, the 
flames seemed to self-extinguish during ramp down. Flow rate at 5 cc/s results in flames 
that only existed briefly. Extinction at this lower flow rate is probably due to heat loss to 
the burner, rather than pure kinetic extinction. Ramp down from 14 cc/s towards 5 cc/s

needed. Tests at 21% O2/He atmosphere were limited. Fuel flow of 5 cc/s showed flash

expand to self-extinction.

and 4 cc/s, the mixtures flashed at ignition, and extinguished almost immediately. It was 
not clear whether extinction was due to kinetic extinction or heat loss to the burner. At

case with a ramp down in flow rate could not conclusively identify kinetic extinction. 
More analysis is needed. Tests at 21% O2/He atmosphere needed even more energy and 
power for ignition. At 5, 7, 10, and 15 cc/s, flames ignited with soot, and expanded quickly 
to extinction. 
 
The 20164 tests began study of ethylene-based flames, where 20% C2H4/80% He issued 
into 30% O2/He and 21% O2/He atmospheres. For 5 cc/s, the flame expanded and 
remained quasi-steady until the burner limit temperature (250°C) was reached. At 6, 7, 
10, and 15 cc/s, the flames expanded to extinction, with the higher flow rates (i.e., 10 and 
15 cc/s) exhibiting sooty ignition. Fuel flow of 5.5 cc/s seemed to correspond to a 
condition where the onset of oscillating extinction was simultaneous with the burner 
reaching the 250°C temperature limit. For the cases with a ramp down in flow rate, the 
flames seemed to extinguish during ramp down, but heat loss to the burner may be the

title: ACME s-Flame: Reports — s Flame final report 20210729
text:
ACME/s-Flame Final Report (2021) 
 
29 July 2021 
69 
 
mechanism of extinction. Although 13 tests were conducted with the 21% O2/He 
atmosphere, ignition was not achieved. 
 
The tests performed on20170 investigated 25% C2H4/75% He issuing into 30% O2/He and 
21% O2/He. At 5 and 5.5 cc/s, nice blue chemiluminescent flames were ignited, but 
eventually were cut off because of the burner temperature limit being reached. At 6 cc/s, 
a nice blue flame was ignited which expanded slowly to extinction. At 7, 10, and 15 cc/s, 
sooty ignition occurred, but as the flames expanded, the soot went away, eventually 
resulting in radiative extinction. By ramping the flow rates up, starting at 5 cc/s, soot at 
ignition was minimized, and the flames could expand to extinction. Ramp down of the 
flow rate resulted in almost immediate extinction. For tests at 21% O2/He atmosphere, 
cases at 5, 10, and 15 cc/s resulted in flames that expanded quickly to extinction. Less 
soot was present at ignition compared with that for the 30% O2/He atmosphere cases. 
Consistent ignition was not always achieved for the same conditions, which is puzzling. 
 
Testing on 20176 explored 30% C2H4/70% He issuing into 30% O2/He and 21% O2/He. At 
5 cc/s, a long duration flame was established that eventually reached the burner 
temperature limit.

title: ACME s-Flame: Reports — s Flame final report 20210729
text:
ot always achieved for the same conditions, which is puzzling. 
 
Testing on 20176 explored 30% C2H4/70% He issuing into 30% O2/He and 21% O2/He. At 
5 cc/s, a long duration flame was established that eventually reached the burner 
temperature limit. At 6, 7, 10, and 15 cc/s, the flames were sooty at ignition, but the soot 
dissipated; and they expanded to extinction. Ramping up the flow rates, starting at 5 cc/s, 
minimized soot at ignition and resulted in flames that slowly expanded to extinction. For 
tests at 21% O2/He atmosphere, cases at 5, 10, and 15 cc/s resulted in flames that 
expanded to extinction. At 4 cc/s, the flame lasted a while before eventual extinction. 
The 3 cc/s case did not ignite. Ramp down of the flow rate seemed to result in flames 
that extinguished quickly before the protocol could ramp down the flow rate. 
 
The last testing of Round 2, which was a makeup of 20155, occurred on 20190, with 45% 
H2/55% He issuing into 30% O2/He and 21% O2/He. For both oxygen concentration 
environments, flow rates resulting in expanding flames lasted for a while, but were cut 
off by automated protocol before self-extinction when the burner temperature limit was 
reached. As for cases where the flow rates were ramped down, extinction detection was 
observed for both oxygen concentration environments. We are currently analyzing the

title: ACME s-Flame: Reports — s Flame final report 20210729
text:
omated protocol before self-extinction when the burner temperature limit was 
reached. As for cases where the flow rates were ramped down, extinction detection was 
observed for both oxygen concentration environments. We are currently analyzing the 
data to determine if extinction was kinetic or due to heat loss to the burner. A last set of 
tests were conducted with a reduced oxygen concentration atmosphere, i.e., 17.5% 
O2/82.5% He. Some cases indicated that radiative and kinetic extinction were possibly 
observed. 
 
In summary, selected preliminary findings from this testing include: 
o Cases run for nitrogen-diluted methane and ethylene flames and in air seemed to 
indicate kinetic extinction at low flow rates and radiative extinction at high flow 
rates. As previously mentioned above (and in our report for the preceding 
increment pair), such phenomena were not observed in our ground-based 
research, given the limited microgravity durations. Nevertheless, comparisons 
with computational simulations are needed to assess better the extinction 
behavior.

o Cases run for nitrogen-diluted hydrogen flames seemed to show kinetic extinction 
at ramp down. However, for the mass flow rates that could be accommodated, 
radiative extinction was not observed. 
o Cases run for nitrogen-diluted hydrogen/methane mixture flames manifested 
extinction, which are presumed to be radiative. However, kinetic extinction at low 
flow rates could not be identified. More analyses of the data are needed. 
o Cases for helium-diluted cases shifted the extinction limits with respect to the 
nitrogen-diluted cases. In general, kinetic extinction was difficult to observe for 
the conditions examined. More analyses are needed to assess instability near the 
flame limits, which was predicted to occur computationally.

Appendix G. ISS Operations per the Payload Weekly Science Summary 
This section is from Dennis Stocker’s log of ACME operations. 
 
s-Flame round 1, featuring nitrogen dilution 
 
2019 
Week 21: July 26 – August 1 
On GMT 206, we performed the final test points for the first round of testing for ACME Flame Design. Test 
points were performed using ethylene fuel (sometimes diluted) in a chamber environment of air (21% 
oxygen, 79% nitrogen at 1 atm). The flames for these tests were short-lived and non-sooty—unlike the 
flames from the tests at higher oxygen concentrations. The goal of Flame Design is to improve our 
understanding of soot processes so that flames can be “designed” to be soot free. 
 
To prepare for the start of ACME s-Flame (Structure and Response of Spherical Diffusion Flames), Christina 
Koch replaced the bottles on CIR Manifolds #2 and #4 on GMT 211. While monitoring the bottle pressures, 
it was noted that the pressure of the bottle at Manifold #4 was slowly decreasing. The rack was powered 
down, and Nick Hague and Luca Parmitano both helped with troubleshooting operations. Currently, a 
forward plan is being developed. 
 
Week 22: August 2 - 8 
On GMT 219, Luca Parmitano replaced the CIR Manifold #4 bottle, which was losing pressure while 
installed and the valve opened, with a known good bottle.

title: ACME s-Flame: Reports — s Flame final report 20210729
text:
leshooting operations. Currently, a 
forward plan is being developed. 
 
Week 22: August 2 - 8 
On GMT 219, Luca Parmitano replaced the CIR Manifold #4 bottle, which was losing pressure while 
installed and the valve opened, with a known good bottle. While monitoring, the known good bottle 
maintained its pressure! Next week, we plan to continue transitioning to the next ACME experiment, sFlame (Structure and Response of Spherical Diffusion Flames). 
 
Week 23: August 9 - 15 
On GMT 225, Christina Koch configured the ACME Chamber Insert and the CIR Combustion Chamber to 
support the next ACME experiment, s-Flame (Structure and Response of Spherical Diffusion Flames). 
 
 
Week 27: September 6 - 12 
On GMT 254, the first test points were performed for ACME s-Flame (Structure and Response of Spherical 
Diffusion Flames) with 13 spherical flames ignited. This investigation is the fifth to be conducted as part 
of the ACME project, which features studies of burner-stabilized flames of gaseous fuels. s-Flame’s goal is 
to advance our ability to predict the structure and dynamics, including extinction, of both soot-free and 
sooty flames—where today’s testing was focused on soot-free flames. Without the buoyant flows created 
by Earth’s gravity, flames in microgravity are typically spherical, which allows the analysis to focus on the

title: ACME s-Flame: Reports — s Flame final report 20210729
text:
extinction, of both soot-free and 
sooty flames—where today’s testing was focused on soot-free flames. Without the buoyant flows created 
by Earth’s gravity, flames in microgravity are typically spherical, which allows the analysis to focus on the 
combustion chemistry and details of the transport phenomena. 
 
CAPTION TO VIDEO, WHICH IS NOT INCLUDED IN THIS LOG 
In this test point video, a non-sooty (blue) flame is ignited with a retracting hot-wire igniter, where 
the gaseous fuel is flowing from a porous spherical burner. After ignition, the flame grows slightly 
as a result of the diminishing oxygen gradient. An array of 14-micron ceramic fibers is then moved 
toward the flame, where the temperature of the flame can be determined from the color of the 
fiber’s glow—where yellow is hotter than orange, and orange is hotter than red. While only a 
single fiber can be seen at first, a second becomes visible when the flame suddenly gets bigger

title: ACME s-Flame: Reports — s Flame final report 20210729
text:
ACME/s-Flame Final Report (2021) 
 
29 July 2021 
76 
 
and engulfs the first fiber. The diluted ethylene flow to the burner was abruptly increased and 
made to be more fuel rich. As a result, the flame needed to grow to reach enough oxygen to burn 
all the fuel. 
 
Throughout the test, the spherical flame is open near the burner’s tube because of heat loss. As 
the flame grows, the opening around the tube increases (while the flame weakens and dims). The 
flame edge then pulls away from the burner tube and leaves just a small portion of the spherical 
shell. This large hole in the flame shell allows for fuel and air mixing and the flame momentarily 
reestablishes and brightens before it extinguishes. 
 
Week 28: September 13 - 19 
On GMT 256, 16 spherical flames were successfully ignited for ACME s-Flame (Structure and Response of 
Spherical Diffusion Flames). Even though ethylene’s double bond tends to make it a sooty fuel, these 
nitrogen-diluted ethylene flames were all non-sooty (except for during ignition). For each test point, the 
harp-like array of 14-micron ceramic fibers was used to determine temperatures in or near the flame, 
while an array of thermocouples was used to measure the spread of the thermal field from the flame. 
 
ACME Flame Design Images 
 
These two images are of the same flame at nearly the same time. The image on the left is a false-colored

title: ACME s-Flame: Reports — s Flame final report 20210729
text:
the flame, 
while an array of thermocouples was used to measure the spread of the thermal field from the flame. 
 
ACME Flame Design Images 
 
These two images are of the same flame at nearly the same time. The image on the left is a false-colored 
image. The porous spherical burner can be seen in the middle of the flame. The flame shell surrounds the 
burner except at the fuel supply tube, which causes the flame to locally quench because of heat loss. A 
glowing ceramic fiber can be seen above the flame, where the fiber’s glow is used to determine the local 
temperature by comparison of the red, green, and blue color planes in a measurement technique known 
as pyrometry. The faint lines at the top of the flame suggest that the fiber may have locally quenched the 
flame even though it was above the flame. 
 
The image on the right is from an intensified camera looking at the emission from the excited molecule 
CH*, which emits a photon of blue 431-nm light when it drops to a lower energy state in a process referred 
to as chemiluminescence. The location of the burner sphere is noticeable due to the diminished light in 
the middle of the flame. The opening in the flame shell due to the burner’s tube is also noticeable. The

title: ACME s-Flame: Reports — s Flame final report 20210729
text:
ACME/s-Flame Final Report (2021) 
 
29 July 2021 
77 
 
apparent opening in the top of the flame may be caused by the fiber array arm, which, in this camera’s 
view, blocks the flame. 
In microgravity, flames aren’t supplied oxygen through buoyant convention. As a result, low-momentum 
flames like these in a quiescent (still) atmosphere tend to be quite weak and self-extinguish. Microgravity 
is an extremely useful for environment for this experiment since a key objective is to study flame dynamics 
and extinction. 
 
Week 29: September 20 - 26 
On GMT 266, Luca Parmitano replaced the ACME Fuel Controller and the bottles at CIR Manifold #2 and 
CIR Manifold #4. These changes support the next ACME s-Flame test points, which will be in a chamber 
environment of air (21% oxygen, 79% nitrogen at 1 atm) and will use diluted methane fuel at faster flow 
rates. 
 
Week 5: October 25 - 31 
On GMT 297 on the back of the CIR Optics Bench, Jessica Meir removed a failed hard drive from the FCF 
Image Processor and then replaced the FCF Image Processor. On GMT 301, the CIR was powered up and 
a checkout of the new FCF Image Processor was successful. We returned to performing test points later 
in the week! 
 
Week 6: November 1 - 7 
On GMT 304 and 308, 30 spherical flames were successfully ignited for ACME s-Flame (Structure and 
Response of Spherical Diffusion Flames).

title: ACME s-Flame: Reports — s Flame final report 20210729
text:
Processor was successful. We returned to performing test points later 
in the week! 
 
Week 6: November 1 - 7 
On GMT 304 and 308, 30 spherical flames were successfully ignited for ACME s-Flame (Structure and 
Response of Spherical Diffusion Flames). These tests burned methane fuel diluted with nitrogen in 
atmospheres of 21% and 30% oxygen (with a balance of nitrogen). Methane is the primary component of 
natural gas. These test points focused on determining where the radiative heat loss or velocities are too 
high for the flame to be sustained, which are known as the radiative and convective extinction limits. 
Radiative heat transport is much more important under microgravity conditions because the hot gases 
don’t buoyantly rise from the flame. 
 
ACME s-Flame Images 
 
This figure shows three flames of 45% methane burning in 30% oxygen. The gaseous methane fuel flows 
from the porous sphere of the burner, which is visible in the flame’s center. The flow of fuel increases 
from left to right, which increases the size of the flame. The burner’s fuel supply tube is visible below the 
sphere. The flame loses heat to this tube causing an opening, which typically grows with time as the flame 
weakens. In the flame on the right, the opening is comparatively small, which signifies a stronger flame.

In the left and center images, the glow of a 14-micron ceramic fiber is visible above the flame. Where the 
fiber is visibly glowing, the flame’s temperature at that point can be determined via color-ratio pyrometry, 
which uses a color camera characterized for that purpose. The faint glow of a second fiber further from 
the flame can be seen at the top of the center image. When the image on the right was captured, the fiber 
array was not yet inserted into the flame. 
 
Week 8: November 15 - 21 
On GMT 323, Drew Morgan replaced the bottles at CIR Manifold #2 and CIR Manifold #4 to support ACME 
s-Flame test points using pure hydrogen fuel in air (21% oxygen, 79% nitrogen at 1 atm). 
 
Week 12: December 13 - 19 
On GMT 347, Drew Morgan replaced the ACME Bypass and Fuel Controllers to support the ACME s-Flame 
(Structure and Response of Spherical Diffusion Flames) test points on GMT 352, which flowed nitrogen 
and fuel at slower flow rates. 
 
Ten flames were successfully ignited on GMT 352. These tests were conducted with nitrogen-diluted 
hydrogen fuel making the flames very faint. The CIR is equipped with an intensified camera, which images 
these very faint flames by visualizing the ultraviolet emission of the OH molecule (at 310 nm) as it drops 
to a lower energy level. This process is known as chemiluminescence.

Week 14: December 27 - January 2

(Structure and Response of Spherical Diffusion Flames) test points with faster nitrogen and fuel flow rates.

Week 15: January 3 - 9 
On GMT 006, 17 flames were successfully ignited for ACME s-Flame (Structure and Response of Spherical 
Diffusion Flames), which uses spherically-symmetric diffusion flames to investigate fundamental 
processes, such as flame extinction. These tests were conducted with a mixture of hydrogen (20%), 
methane (25%), and nitrogen (55%) ejected from the porous spherical burner into a chamber atmosphere

title: ACME s-Flame: Reports — s Flame final report 20210729
text:
ric diffusion flames to investigate fundamental 
processes, such as flame extinction. These tests were conducted with a mixture of hydrogen (20%), 
methane (25%), and nitrogen (55%) ejected from the porous spherical burner into a chamber atmosphere 
of air (21% oxygen, 79% nitrogen at 1 atm). The dim, soot-free flames exhibited local quenching due to 
radiative heat loss and reignition, which sometimes occurred repeatedly. In these cases, the dynamic parts 
of the broken flame sometimes appear to dance around the burner. 
 
CAPTION TO VIDEO, WHICH IS NOT INCLUDED IN THIS LOG 
In this test point video, a non-sooty (blue) flame is ignited with a retracting hot-wire igniter. The 
harp-like array of 14-micron ceramic fibers moves in from the left to a fixed position. The glow 
from the fibers allows for a good estimation of the local temperature. The flame starts “dancing,” 
where it partially quenches due to radiative heat loss and the remaining flame stretches and 
circles around the burner through a repeated combination of quenching and reignition. The fuel

title: ACME s-Flame: Reports — s Flame final report 20210729
text:
ACME/s-Flame Final Report (2021) 
 
29 July 2021 
79 
 
and oxygen, which are normally separated by the flame, mix where the flame quenches, making 
the local gas more flammable. 
 
Week 16: January 10 - 16 
On GMT 013, 22 flames were successfully ignited for ACME s-Flame (Structure and Response of Spherical 
Diffusion Flames), which is a record number of sustained flames in a single day of testing for all the ACME 
experiments! Like the tests performed on GMT 006, these tests burned a mixture of hydrogen, methane, 
and nitrogen but with a greater hydrogen concentration relative to the methane concentration. Even 
though these flames were less dynamic than the “dancing” flames from GMT 006, they did break apart 
and create flamelets. The flamelets were about 1 cm across and were shaped like curved bands or circles 
rather than spheres or ellipsoids. 
 
 
This figure shows four different tests from GMT 013, where the flow rate of the hydrogen/methane fuel 
increases from left to right while the nitrogen flow rate remains constant. The burner, with its supply tube 
and porous sphere, is opposite the flame. The fuel and nitrogen both flow from the burner sphere into a 
chamber atmosphere of ~19% oxygen and nitrogen at a pressure of ~1 atm. 
 
The bright horizontal lines in each flame are the glowing 14-micron ceramic fibers, where that glow can

title: ACME s-Flame: Reports — s Flame final report 20210729
text:
flame. The fuel and nitrogen both flow from the burner sphere into a 
chamber atmosphere of ~19% oxygen and nitrogen at a pressure of ~1 atm. 
 
The bright horizontal lines in each flame are the glowing 14-micron ceramic fibers, where that glow can 
be used to determine the flame’s temperature. As the fuel flow rate increases, the flames become larger 
and separate flamelets form. For these tests, the flow rate was increased to explore flame stability and

CAPTION TO VIDEO, WHICH IS NOT INCLUDED IN THIS LOG 
In this test point video, helium-diluted ethylene fuel is ignited with a low fuel flow rate to limit 
the soot produced with ignition. After ignition, the flow rate is tripled in a smooth ramp, so that 
the flame response can be observed. As expected, the flame quickly grows, where it must expand 
to reach enough oxygen to consume all the fuel. 
 
Before the fuel flow rate has completely tripled, the flame retreats from the burner’s fuel supply 
tube because of heat loss—creating a hole in the flame near the tube. This hole allows for 
increased mixing of the ethylene and oxygen, which are normally separated by the flame shell. 
This mixing causes the flame to momentarily reestablish around the burner tube with a bright 
flash of light. Mixing again leads to another flame flash, after which the flame fully extinguishes. 
The fuel flow rate did completely triple before the flame extinguished. 
 
Although not visible in the video, the measured OH* and CH* chemiluminescence was relatively

title: ACME s-Flame: Reports — s Flame final report 20210729
text:
g again leads to another flame flash, after which the flame fully extinguishes. 
The fuel flow rate did completely triple before the flame extinguished. 
 
Although not visible in the video, the measured OH* and CH* chemiluminescence was relatively 
constant throughout this test with the important exceptions of ignition and the bright flashes of 
light prior to extinction. In contrast, the measured chemiluminescence declined with time in 
similar tests with constant fuel flow rates. OH* and CH* are molecules at an elevated energy state 
which emit a photon of a specific wavelength as their energy level drops a level. The CH* emission 
is the source of most of the blue in a hydrocarbon flame, while the OH* emission is in the 
ultraviolet. ACME uses the latter measurement as an indicator of ignition and extinction because 
it is insensitive to the hot-wire igniter and hot burned gases. 
 
Using this unique microgravity data, the s-Flame investigation seeks to test and improve 
computational models, which may enable improvements to practical combustion on Earth.

Appendix M. Summary of the ISS data collection 
The s-Flame data is all digital and includes both image and non-image data, where this is true for the other 
ACME experiments. To be clear, there was no collection of soot or other physical samples that were 
subsequently transported to the ground. 
 
The s-Flame image data includes images from the following cameras: 
1. ACME DataCam, used with a clear fused-silica ‘filter’ and various zoom and focus settings (but 
those settings were consistent within each individual test) 
2. CFI intensified camera, used with CH*, formaldehyde, and UV fused silica filters, but where only 
a single filter was used in each test 
3. Low Light Level Ultraviolet (LLL-UV) camera, equipped with an OH* filter 
4. High-Bitdepth Multispectral (HiBMs) camera, equipped with a red filter corresponding to the 
opposing CIR illumination package, which was sometimes left off 
The raw DataCam images are in a Halcon Iconic Object (hobj) format, while the images from the CFI, 
HiBMs, and LLL-UV cameras are provided in a Tagged Image File (tif) format. In contrast, the analog video 
was recorded on the ground in a Transport Stream (ts) format. 
 
The key non-imaging data from a test is a comma-delimited file that is described in detail in the Software 
Interface Design Description (ACME-DOC-010 Rev. D).

The data is generally explained through 2 excerpts from the Software IDD, i.e., 
Software Interface Design Description, ACME-DOC-010 Rev C (August 2016) 
 
 
8. Output Files 
 
 
4. Internal Interfaces (which includes Tables 15-17*) 
*where Table 17 describes channels A0-4 of the DNx-AO-333 analog output board as discussed in 8.1 below. 
 
8.0 
Output FILES 
8.1 
Data Output File 
Data output files are created using the SystemOpenTestPoint command which creates a file named and stored at 
/payload/sci/testpointName_x/testpointName_x_data.csv, where testpointName is the parameter received in the 
SystemOpenTestPoint command and _x is optional to avoid duplicate files, where x = 1,2,3, etc. 
The file contains a two-line header. The first line has the date and time, documentation of the setup received in a 
SystemDefineSetup command, and the PMT gains. The second line has the column headings for the subsequent rows of data. The 
text of the column headings is defined by the Diagnostics/Header registry entry or the Diagnostics/BreHeader entry depending on 
whether the SystemDefineSetup command experimentType parameter was BRE or not. The column headings should match the data 
which is the following: 
- 
A timestamp in the format HH:MM:SS:mmm, where mmm is milliseconds. 
- 
11 channels of analog input from the cube DNx-AI-207 board in the order shown in Table 1. 
-

8.2 
Message Log File 
Software messages are logged to files named and stored at /payload/logs/YYYY-MM-DD_hh-mmACME.log, where YYYY 
is year, MM is month, DD is day of month, hh is hour, and mm is minutes. The date in the name is when the log file is 
created, soon after software startup. 
Each message line in the file begins with a timestamp and a logging category. The timestamp is of the format YYYY-MMDD DDD hh:mm:ss:mmm, where DDD is day of the year, mmm is milliseconds, and the rest are self-explanatory. See 
section Error! Reference source not found. for information about the logging category and how to filter them out if 
desired. 
8.3 
Command Log File 
The message log file, section 8.2, includes messages showing commands received and their parameters. Command log 
files contain only the details of each command received. The files are named and stored at /payload/logs/YYYY-MMDD_hh-mmACMECommands.log. The format is for each command received a timestamped line of text with the 
command name followed by timestamped lines of text showing each parameter name and parameter value, including 
header information.

text:
ACME-SORD-001.A Science Ops Requirements Document 
 
2011-10-18 
Any text in italics is a comment and not a requirement. 
 
4 
 
Science Summary 
The Advanced Combustion via Microgravity Experiments (ACME) project is now under 
development with a set of four independent experiments which are each focused on 
advancing combustion technology through fundamental research. The current ACME 
experiments are specifically directed at addressing energy and environmental concerns. 
The overall goals are to improve our understanding of (1) combustion at fuel lean 
conditions where both optimum performance and low emissions can be achieved, (2) 
combustion of fuels with increased hydrogen content which could enable reduced 
greenhouse emission, (3) soot control and reduction, (4) oxygen enriched combustion 
which could enable practical carbon sequestration, and (5) use of electric fields for 
combustion control. Unlike the Flame Extinguishment Experiment (FLEX), ACME is not 
focused on the advancement of spacecraft fire safety technology, although it is likely 
that some ACME findings will be relevant. While distinct, the experiments share several 
significant traits. The principal unifying feature of the ACME experiments is their use of 
gaseous fuels (e.g., methane and ethylene) rather than liquid or solid fuels. With this in

doc_id: psi:PSI-23/PSI-23_Science Documents_ACME Science Operation Requirements revA 20111018.pdf
title: ACME s-Flame: Science Documents — ACME Science Operation Requirements revA 20111018
text:
will be relevant. While distinct, the experiments share several 
significant traits. The principal unifying feature of the ACME experiments is their use of 
gaseous fuels (e.g., methane and ethylene) rather than liquid or solid fuels. With this in 
common, the experiments will be conducted within the Combustion Integrated Rack 
(CIR) through the use of a single modular insert. In addition to the fuel state, the current 
set of ACME experiments all use laminar, non-premixed (i.e., diffusion) flames for their 
studies. To simplify analysis, these flames are either one or two dimensional, 
depending upon the experiment. 
 
A general goal of the current ACME experiments is to gain fundamental understanding 
that can enable improved efficiency and reduced emissions in practical combustion 
processes, for example through the development and verification of models for chemical 
kinetics and transport processes in computational simulations. In addition to enhanced 
performance, improved modeling capability can lead to reductions in the time and cost 
for combustor design. In summary, microgravity investigations of non-premixed flames 
could lead to eco-friendly combustion systems providing our nation with green power for 
the future. 
 
Coflow Laminar Diffusion Flame (CLD Flame) 
Research, especially including that already conducted in microgravity, has revealed that

doc_id: psi:PSI-23/PSI-23_Science Documents_ACME Science Operation Requirements revA 20111018.pdf
title: ACME s-Flame: Science Documents — ACME Science Operation Requirements revA 20111018
text:
xed flames 
could lead to eco-friendly combustion systems providing our nation with green power for 
the future. 
 
Coflow Laminar Diffusion Flame (CLD Flame) 
Research, especially including that already conducted in microgravity, has revealed that 
our current predictive ability is significantly lacking for flames at the extremes of fuel 
dilution, namely for sooty pure-fuel flames and dilute flames that are near extinction. 
The general goal of the Coflow Laminar Diffusion Flame (CLD Flame) experiment is to 
extend the range of flame conditions that can be accurately predicted by developing and 
experimentally verifying chemical kinetic and soot formation submodels. The 
dependence of normal coflow flames on injection velocity and fuel dilution will be 
carefully examined for flames at both very dilute and highly sooting conditions.

title: ACME s-Flame: Science Documents — ACME Science Operation Requirements revA 20111018
text:
ACME-SORD-001.A Science Ops Requirements Document 
 
2011-10-18 
Any text in italics is a comment and not a requirement. 
 
5 
 
Measurements will be made of the structure of diluted methane and ethylene flames in 
an air coflow. Lifted flames will be used as the basis for the research to avoid flame 
dependence on heat loss to the burner. The results of this experiment will be directly 
applicable to practical combustion issues such as turbulent combustion, ignition, flame 
stability, and more. 
 
Electric-Field Effects on Laminar Diffusion Flames (E-FIELD Flames) 
An electric field can strongly influence flames because of its effect on the ions present 
as a result of the combustion reactions. The direct ion transport and the induced ion 
wind can modify the flame shape, alter the soot or flammability limits, direct heat 
transfer, and reduce pollutant emission. The purpose of the Electric-Field Effects on 
Laminar Diffusion Flames (E-FIELD Flames) experiment is to gain an improved 
understanding of flame ion production and investigate how the ions can be used to 
control non-premixed flames. Outside reviewers concluded that the experiment “… will 
contribute to our critical understanding to our knowledge of combustion processes in the 
presence of electric fields.” The experiment will be conducted with a simple gas-jet

doc_id: psi:PSI-23/PSI-23_Science Documents_ACME Science Operation Requirements revA 20111018.pdf
title: ACME s-Flame: Science Documents — ACME Science Operation Requirements revA 20111018
text:
premixed flames. Outside reviewers concluded that the experiment “… will 
contribute to our critical understanding to our knowledge of combustion processes in the 
presence of electric fields.” The experiment will be conducted with a simple gas-jet 
flame, where an electric field will be generated by creating a high voltage (up to 10 kV) 
differential between the burner and a flat circular mesh above (i.e., downstream of) the 
burner. Measurements, as a function of field strength and fuel dilution, will be made of 
the ion current through the flame and the flame’s response time to electric forcing. 
 
Flame Design 
The primary goal of the Flame Design experiment is to improve our understanding of 
soot inception and control in order to enable the optimization of oxygen enriched 
combustion and the “design” of non-premixed flames that are both robust and soot free. 
An outside review panel declared that Flame Design “… could lead to greatly improved 
burner designs that are efficient and less polluting than current designs." Flame Design 
will investigate the soot inception and extinction limits of spherical microgravity flames, 
created in the same manner as for the s-Flame experiment. Tests will be conducted 
with various concentrations of both the fuel (i.e., ethylene or methane) and oxygen in 
order to determine the role of the flame structure on the soot inception.

doc_id: psi:PSI-23/PSI-23_Science Documents_ACME Science Operation Requirements revA 20111018.pdf
title: ACME s-Flame: Science Documents — ACME Science Operation Requirements revA 20111018
text:
mes, 
created in the same manner as for the s-Flame experiment. Tests will be conducted 
with various concentrations of both the fuel (i.e., ethylene or methane) and oxygen in 
order to determine the role of the flame structure on the soot inception. The effect of 
the flow direction on soot formation will be assessed by studying both normal flames 
and inverse flames, where in the latter case an oxygen/inert mixture flows from the 
spherical burner into a fuel/inert atmosphere. The Flame Design experiment will 
explore whether the stoichiometric mixture fraction can characterize soot and 
flammability limits for non-premixed flames like the equivalence ratio serves as an 
indicator of those limits for premixed flames.

2011-10-18

6 
 
Structure and Response of Spherical Flames (s-Flame) 
The purpose of the Structure and Response of Spherical Flames (s-Flame) experiment 
is to advance our ability to predict the structure and dynamics, including extinction, of 
both soot-free and sooty flames. The spherical flame, which is only possible in 
microgravity, will be created through use of a porous spherical burner from which a 
fuel/inert gas mixture will issue into the CIR chamber. Flames will be ignited at nonsteady conditions and allowed to transition naturally toward extinction. Tests will be 
conducted with various inert diluents, in both the fuel and chamber atmosphere. The 
fuel gases include hydrogen and methane for soot-free flames, and ethylene for sooty 
flames. One experiment objective is to identify the extinction limits for both radiative 
and convective extinction (i.e., at high and low system Damkohler numbers, 
respectively). Another objective is to determine the existence, onset, and nature of 
pulsating instabilities that have been theoretically predicted to occur in such flames with 
fuel/diluent mixtures that are above a critical Lewis number. 
 
 
INTRODUCTION 
The ACME project currently includes four distinct experiments and will tentatively include

doc_id: psi:PSI-23/PSI-23_Science Documents_ACME Science Operation Requirements revA 20111018.pdf
title: ACME s-Flame: Science Documents — ACME Science Operation Requirements revA 20111018
text:
ilities that have been theoretically predicted to occur in such flames with 
fuel/diluent mixtures that are above a critical Lewis number. 
 
 
INTRODUCTION 
The ACME project currently includes four distinct experiments and will tentatively include 
even more in the future. Therefore, it is critical that the project adopt a flexible approach 
to experiment control. This flexibility can be achieved through a set of explicit, and 
generally predefined and verified, functions which can be selected, repeated as needed, 
and ordered to create a variety of overall experiment sequences. Functions can include 
variable parameters, e.g., flow rate(s), providing additional flexibility. Furthermore, 
experiments can be run via either operator or software control. This approach to 
operational (ops) control is similar to the ordered stringing of beads to make a necklace, 
where each bead represents a function, and where each bead’s characteristics (e.g., 
color, shape, size) represent its function and the associated variable parameters. The 
approach is further explained in section 1 of this document, i.e., General Requirements. 
 
As defined herein, the control functions almost always occur in a serial fashion, but 
multiple operations may occur simultaneously. For example, sequential functions may 
in turn activate non-imaging and imaging data acquisition, the CIR illumination package,

doc_id: psi:PSI-23/PSI-23_Science Documents_ACME Science Operation Requirements revA 20111018.pdf
title: ACME s-Flame: Science Documents — ACME Science Operation Requirements revA 20111018
text:
erein, the control functions almost always occur in a serial fashion, but 
multiple operations may occur simultaneously. For example, sequential functions may 
in turn activate non-imaging and imaging data acquisition, the CIR illumination package, 
and fuel flow such that all are active at the same time. While these are operating, a 
timed function can also occur, e.g., translating the TFP fiber array. Normally, only a 
single timed function will be operative at a time, given their serial arrangement. 
However, there is at least one critical exception, namely the automated detection of 
extinction, where that function should normally always be active following ignition when 
the burner reactant(s) are flowing. Note that extinction detection requires

measurement filtering over time (e.g., time averaging) to avoid the false detection that 
could result from signal noise. 
 
The following requirements provide a great deal of operational control, allowing for 
stepped, stair-cased, ramped, rectangular-wave, and triangular-wave changes in the 
flow or electric field potential (i.e., voltage), and ramped or triangular-wave translation of 
the TFP fiber array. Examples of such control are shown graphically in Appendix A. 
Provisions are included for operator control to allow for determination of, or operation at 
(or near), limit conditions such as soot inception, lifting, and extinction.

FUNCTIONAL REQUIREMENTS 
The functions are tentatively identified as being instant or timed (or sometimes general) 
and are categorically associated with either CIR or ACME operations. Key associated 
requirements from ISRD sections 1-3 are also cited at the end of each functional 
requirement, but specific citations are not provided for ISRD section 4. 
 
1. [CIR & ACME] General Requirements 
1.1. [general] ACME shall provide flexible experiment control based on explicit 
functions which can be selected, repeated as needed, and ordered (like colored 
beads on a string) to create a variety of overall experiment sequences. Where 
possible, flexibility shall be provided within the individual functions by allowing 
the specification of relevant parameters (like the flow rate, or by analog the size 
of the bead). Flexibility is critical for avoiding limitations that could hinder 
operations or limit ACME science. For example, the SOFBALL experiment 
(STS-83, STS-94, and STS-107) initially had a hard shutoff at 5 minutes 
because it was fully expected that the flames would extinguish by that time. 
However, that assumption was found to be faulty and the tests terminated while

title: ACME s-Flame: Science Documents — ACME Science Operation Requirements revA 20111018
text:
OFBALL experiment 
(STS-83, STS-94, and STS-107) initially had a hard shutoff at 5 minutes 
because it was fully expected that the flames would extinguish by that time. 
However, that assumption was found to be faulty and the tests terminated while 
flames were still burning diminishing the scientific return. The test duration could 
not be extended until a subsequent spaceflight. Flexible experiment control will 
also enable future ACME experiments which differ operationally from the current 
set of ACME experiments. 
1.2. [general] During at least combustion, ACME shall be capable of operations by 
either automated software control or operator control. ACME shall furthermore 
be capable of both automated and operator control within a single test, but 
where automated and operator control are not required simultaneously. 
Software control allows for a higher fidelity of time control (e.g., as can be 
important for some experiments or tests), while operator control allows a human 
response to downlinked measurements, which can be especially valuable when 
trying to either identify or test at (or near) limit conditions, e.g., for soot inception, 
lifting, or extinction. 
1.3. [general] ACME shall provide for automated software control through sequences 
of functions that are each either instant (i.e., without a duration) or timed, i.e.,

of functions that are each either instant (i.e., without a duration) or timed, i.e., 
with a variable duration that is a parameter of that function. 
1.4. [general] ACME shall be capable of software upgrades, i.e., capable of 
developing and using new operational functions, for ISS operations after the 
ACME hardware has already been delivered to the ISS. The purpose for this 
requirement is to support future, and as of yet undefined, ACME experiments. 
1.5. [general] ACME shall not prevent the possible implementation of future closedloop software functions, where control of some parameter(s) (e.g., gas flow) is 
based on one or more non-imaging measurements, e.g., temperature, thermal 
radiation, chemiluminescent emission. This requirement only applies to control

1.6. [general] Unless otherwise specified, ACME shall be capable of carrying out 
operational functions while simultaneously doing any specified subset or all of 
the following in a time-constant manner: (1) acquiring imaging and non-imaging

hardware), there could also be simultaneous monitoring for out-of-range 
measurements (e.g., chamber pressure or temperature) that could initiate an 
alert or automatically shut down the test. 
1.7. [general] ACME shall provide a detailed time log of commands issued (i.e., 
functions enacted) for each test conducted. This will aid in the analysis of 
results, e.g., to determine whether a flame naturally extinguished (where 
extinction detection would lead to automated termination of the burner flow) or

2. [CIR & ACME] Pause Functions 
2.1. [timed] ACME shall be capable of pausing for a specified duration between 
functions, where it shall be possible to specify a duration in the range of at least 
0.01 to 999.99 s, with a precision of 0.01 s or less, where a precision smaller 
than 0.0001 s is probably more than adequate. Pauses of specified duration, 
especially when short, can or should be controlled by software. This function 
has a single parameter: the specified duration. 
2.2. [general] ACME shall be capable of pausing for a specified duration between 
functions, where it shall be possible to specify a duration in the range of at least 
10 s to 99 minutes, with an uncertainty of no more than the larger of (a) 5 s or 
(b) 10% of the specified duration. Long pauses can be operator controlled, 
where the operator initiates the start and end through separate instant functions. 
This function has a single parameter: the specified duration.

3. [CIR & ACME] Hardware Set Up Functions 
3.1. [general] ACME shall be capable of installing and removing specified CIR or 
ACME hardware at specified positions external to the CIR chamber, where the 
hardware shall include (at a minimum) all of the following or any specified subset 
thereof: ACME avionics package, the GCIP, CIR and ACME imaging packages, 
IPSUs, the CIR illumination package, gas bottles, and a filter cartridge. 
3.2. [general] ACME shall be capable of installing and removing specified ACME 
hardware at specified positions on the ACME chamber insert assembly, where 
the hardware shall include (at a minimum) all of the following or any specified 
subset thereof: burner, igniter tip (associated with the burner), electric field 
components (including the electrode mesh, high-voltage power supplies, and 
associated electronics), mass flow controllers, Thin Filament Pyrometry (TFP) 
fiber array, far-field thermocouple array, and the Photomultiplier Tube (PMT) 
array.

4.1. [general] ACME shall be capable of venting the CIR chamber atmosphere to a

4.2. [instant] ACME shall be capable of activating and deactivating the scrubbing of 
the CIR chamber atmosphere, i.e., circulating it through a specified filter 
cartridge without venting. Such scrubbing will allow for reuse of the chamber 
atmosphere, where the upmass requirement for gas bottles is dominated by the 
gas used to fill the chamber. Furthermore, only a very small fraction of the

4.3. [general] ACME shall be capable of verifying that the CIR chamber is sealed, 
i.e., gas tight. This is important for safety following any operation in which the 
chamber is opened. 
4.4. [general] ACME shall be capable of adding specified gas to the CIR chamber to

pressure. Per the baselined ACME requirements, the initial total pressure (not

APPENDICES 
There are no requirements in the appendices; they are only provided for design 
reference. 
A. Variation Examples 
B. CLD Flame (2 example sequences) 
C. E-FIELD Flames (3 example sequences) 
D. Flame Design (1 example sequence) 
E. s-Flame (1 example sequence) 
 
The sequences in Appendices B-E are based on the baselined ISRD and are not meant 
to be a complete list, but are simply examples of possible likely operations for each 
experiment. Even neglecting pre-ignition and post-extinction operations, each 
experiment may have several different operational sequences, and at least one 
example is provided here for each experiment. 
 
The provided examples are quite similar, especially in the pre-ignition and postextinction operations. In other words, the principal differences are typically related to 
the control of the flow, TFP fiber array, or the electric field. However, other operations 
are certainly possible in any section of the operations. 
 
 
 
Appendix A: Variation Examples 
This section provides depictions of major ways in which the three ACME gas flows, TFP 
array position, and electric field potential can be varied. Note that the TFP array cannot

text:

Appendix A: Variation Examples 
This section provides depictions of major ways in which the three ACME gas flows, TFP 
array position, and electric field potential can be varied. Note that the TFP array cannot 
be moved instantaneously so the stepped and rectangular wave functions are not 
applicable. And while relatively abrupt changes in flow are possible (at least in the gasjet burners), it should be understood that the control will not be accurate during rapid 
transitions because of the limited response time of the Mass Flow Controllers. Finally, 
note that while time durations are generally shown as either 0 or 10 seconds in the 
presented examples, this was done as a convenience and the functions allow for 
durations of varying values. Finally, it should be emphasized that these are just 
examples, where a careful review of the function requirements will reveal additional 
details.

Appendix C: E-FIELD Flames 
E-FIELD Flames: ISRD Table 4.2.1 
Voltage Sweep Procedure 
Time 
A. Prepare Chamber 
 1. Fill chamber (with N2 for coflow; O2/N2 for gas jet) 
 2. Select fuel/diluent mixture 
B. Initiate Experiment 
 1. Initiate data acquisition 
 2. Initiate gas flows 
 3. Ignite flame and retract igniter 
 4. Allow 10 seconds settling time 
 5. Set the desired voltage (initially to 0V) 
 6. Initiate high voltage power supply 
C. Measurements1 
 1. Wait 0.3 seconds for flame to settle 
 2. Collect data over 0.5 seconds 
D. Step 100V (assuming approx. 5ms ramp) 
E. Repeat steps C & D until (+/-) 5kV or flame blowout 
F. Pause in Experiment 
 1. Stop gas flows/extinguish flame (zero ion current)

Appendix D: Flame Design 
Flame Design: ISRD Table 4.3.1 
Operational Sequence for Flame Design Spherical Flame Tests 
 
Action 
Approx. 
Time 
1. Ensure that 6.4 mm spherical burner is installed. Preflow the burner fluent gas 
at the composition of the upcoming test point to flush the plumbing system. 
2. Establish chamber conditions. These consist of a set point pressure and 
species compositions, as specified in the test matrix. Conditions are obtained in 
four ways: from cabin air (desired); from the preceding test; from scrubbing and 
replenishing; or from a complete evacuation and recharge. 
3. Allow chamber contents to reach equilibrium. A hold time of 5 minutes is 
required for quiescent, isothermal, and well-mixed conditions. 
4. Take reference images (if applicable). Establish framing rates for video 
cameras. Begin color imaging. Begin monitoring measurements. After 15 s, 
commence fluent flow, ignite flame, and retract ignitor. 
Perform either Steps 5, 6, and 8 OR Steps 7 and 8. 
5. Soot inception limit. Allow the flame to pass its soot-inception limit. 
Continuously record temperature distributions. 
6. Radiative extinction. Detect radiative extinction with a PMT or with near realtime video.

ps 5, 6, and 8 OR Steps 7 and 8. 
5. Soot inception limit. Allow the flame to pass its soot-inception limit. 
Continuously record temperature distributions. 
6. Radiative extinction. Detect radiative extinction with a PMT or with near realtime video. Continuously record temperature distributions. At uplinkable time 
(estimated 3 s) after extinction, reduce flow rate by uplinkable amount (estimated 
50%) for uplinkable time (estimated 5 s) to confirm extinction. If the flame 
reappears, return to the initial flow rate and return to the beginning of Step 6. 
Otherwise terminate the fluent flow. 
7. Kinetic extinction. After an uplinkable time (estimated 10 s), decrease fluent 
flow rate linearly in time such that flow rate becomes zero at uplinkable time 
(estimated 30 s) after ignition. Detect kinetic extinction with a PMT or with near 
real-time video. Continuously record temperature distributions. At uplinkable time 
(estimated 3 s) after extinction detection, increase flow rate by uplinkable amount 
(estimated 100%) for uplinkable time (estimated 5 s) to confirm extinction. If the 
flame reappears, return to the initial flow rate and return to the beginning of Step 7. 
Otherwise terminate the fluent flow. 
8. Record reference images (if applicable). After 60 s terminate color imaging and 
monitoring measurements. Select data for downlink and downlink data.

text:
ACME-SRD-001.B Integrated Science Requirements Document (ISRD) 
2013-SEPT-30 
5 
 
INTRODUCTION 
 
Science Summary 
The Advanced Combustion via Microgravity Experiments (ACME) project is now under 
development with a set of five independent experiments which are each focused on advancing 
combustion technology through fundamental research. Four of the current ACME experiments 
are specifically directed at addressing energy and environmental concerns, while the fifth 
experiment addresses fire prevention, especially for spacecraft. The overall goals are to improve 
our understanding of materials flammability, combustion at fuel lean conditions where both 
optimum performance and low emissions can be achieved, flame stability and extinction limits, 
soot control and reduction, oxygen enriched combustion which could enable practical carbon 
sequestration, and the use of electric fields for combustion control. 
 
While distinct, the ACME experiments share several significant traits. The principal unifying 
feature of the experiments is their use of gaseous fuels (e.g., methane and ethylene) rather than 
liquid or solid fuels. With this in common, the experiments will be conducted within the 
Combustion Integrated Rack (CIR) through the use of a single modular insert. In addition to the

title: ACME s-Flame: Science Documents — ACME Integrated Science Requirements RevB
text:
use of gaseous fuels (e.g., methane and ethylene) rather than 
liquid or solid fuels. With this in common, the experiments will be conducted within the 
Combustion Integrated Rack (CIR) through the use of a single modular insert. In addition to the 
fuel state, the current set of ACME experiments all use laminar, non-premixed (i.e., diffusion) 
flames for their studies. To simplify analysis, these flames are either one or two dimensional, 
depending upon the experiment. 
 
With the exception of the Burning Rate Emulator (BRE) experiment discussed immediately 
below, the general goal of the current ACME experiments is to gain fundamental understanding 
that can enable improved efficiency and reduced emissions in practical combustion processes on 
Earth, for example through the development and verification of models for chemical kinetics and 
transport processes in computational simulations. In addition to enhanced performance, 
improved modeling capability can lead to reductions in the time and cost for combustor design. 
In summary, microgravity investigations of non-premixed flames could lead to eco-friendly 
combustion systems providing our nation with green power for the future. 
 
Burning Rate Emulator (BRE) 
Unlike the other current ACME experiments, the Burning Rate Emulator (BRE) experiment is 
focused on fire prevention, especially in spacecraft.

title: ACME s-Flame: Science Documents — ACME Integrated Science Requirements RevB
text:
combustion systems providing our nation with green power for the future. 
 
Burning Rate Emulator (BRE) 
Unlike the other current ACME experiments, the Burning Rate Emulator (BRE) experiment is 
focused on fire prevention, especially in spacecraft. Specifically, BRE’s objective is to improve 
our fundamental understanding of materials flammability, such as extinction behavior and the 
conditions needed for sustained combustion, and to assess the relevance of existing flammability 
test methods for low and partial-gravity environments. A flat porous burner fed with gaseous 
fuel will simulate the burning of solid and liquid fuels, where measurements are made of the 
thermal feedback (i.e., to the burner) upon which the vaporization of condensed-phase fuels 
depend. A small number of gaseous fuels (including mixtures with inert gases) will be used to 
simulate the burning of fuels such as paper, plastic, and alcohol by matching properties such as 
the heats of combustion and gasification, the surface temperature, and smoke point.

title: ACME s-Flame: Science Documents — ACME Integrated Science Requirements RevB
text:
ACME-SRD-001.B Integrated Science Requirements Document (ISRD) 
2013-SEPT-30 
6 
 
Coflow Laminar Diffusion Flame (CLD Flame) 
Research, especially including that already conducted in microgravity, has revealed that our 
current predictive ability is significantly lacking for flames at the extremes of fuel dilution, 
namely for sooty pure-fuel flames and dilute flames that are near extinction. The general goal of 
the Coflow Laminar Diffusion Flame (CLD Flame) experiment is to extend the range of flame 
conditions that can be accurately predicted by developing and experimentally verifying chemical 
kinetic and soot formation submodels. The dependence of normal coflow flames on injection 
velocity and fuel dilution will be carefully examined for flames at both very dilute and highly 
sooting conditions. Measurements will be made of the structure of diluted methane and ethylene 
flames in an air coflow. Lifted flames will be used as the basis for the research to avoid flame 
dependence on heat loss to the burner. The results of this experiment will be directly applicable 
to practical combustion issues such as turbulent combustion, ignition, flame stability, and more. 
 
Electric-Field Effects on Laminar Diffusion Flames (E-FIELD Flames) 
An electric field can strongly influence flames because of its effect on the ions present as a result 
of the combustion reactions.

title: ACME s-Flame: Science Documents — ACME Integrated Science Requirements RevB
text:
mbustion, ignition, flame stability, and more. 
 
Electric-Field Effects on Laminar Diffusion Flames (E-FIELD Flames) 
An electric field can strongly influence flames because of its effect on the ions present as a result 
of the combustion reactions. The direct ion transport and the induced ion wind can modify the 
flame shape, alter the soot or flammability limits, direct heat transfer, and reduce pollutant 
emission. The purpose of the Electric-Field Effects on Laminar Diffusion Flames (E-FIELD 
Flames) experiment is to gain an improved understanding of flame ion production and 
investigate how the ions can be used to control non-premixed flames. Outside reviewers 
concluded that the experiment “… will contribute to our critical understanding to our knowledge 
of combustion processes in the presence of electric fields.” The experiment will be conducted 
with a simple gas-jet flame, where an electric field will be generated by creating a high voltage 
(up to 10 kV) differential between the burner and a flat circular mesh above (i.e., downstream of) 
the burner. Measurements, as a function of field strength and fuel dilution, will be made of the 
ion current through the flame and the flame’s response time to electric forcing. 
 
Flame Design 
The primary goal of the Flame Design experiment is to improve our understanding of soot

title: ACME s-Flame: Science Documents — ACME Integrated Science Requirements RevB
text:
tion of field strength and fuel dilution, will be made of the 
ion current through the flame and the flame’s response time to electric forcing. 
 
Flame Design 
The primary goal of the Flame Design experiment is to improve our understanding of soot 
inception and control in order to enable the optimization of oxygen enriched combustion and the 
“design” of non-premixed flames that are both robust and soot free. An outside review panel 
declared that Flame Design “… could lead to greatly improved burner designs that are efficient 
and less polluting than current designs." Flame Design will investigate the soot inception and 
extinction limits of spherical microgravity flames, created in the same manner as for the s-Flame 
experiment. Tests will be conducted with various concentrations of both the fuel (i.e., ethylene 
or methane) and oxygen in order to determine the role of the flame structure on the soot 
inception. The effect of the flow direction on soot formation will be assessed by studying both 
normal flames and inverse flames, where in the latter case an oxygen/inert mixture flows from 
the spherical burner into a fuel/inert atmosphere. The Flame Design experiment will explore 
whether the stoichiometric mixture fraction can characterize soot and flammability limits for 
non-premixed flames like the equivalence ratio serves as an indicator of those limits for

title: ACME s-Flame: Science Documents — ACME Integrated Science Requirements RevB
text:
uel/inert atmosphere. The Flame Design experiment will explore 
whether the stoichiometric mixture fraction can characterize soot and flammability limits for 
non-premixed flames like the equivalence ratio serves as an indicator of those limits for 
premixed flames.

title: ACME s-Flame: Science Documents — ACME Integrated Science Requirements RevB
text:
ACME-SRD-001.B Integrated Science Requirements Document (ISRD) 
2013-SEPT-30 
7 
 
Structure and Response of Spherical Flames (s-Flame) 
The purpose of the Structure and Response of Spherical Flames (s-Flame) experiment is to 
advance our ability to predict the structure and dynamics, including extinction, of both soot-free 
and sooty flames. The spherical flame, which is only possible in microgravity, will be created 
through use of a porous spherical burner from which a fuel/inert gas mixture will issue into the 
CIR chamber. Flames will be ignited at non-steady conditions and allowed to transition 
naturally toward extinction. Tests will be conducted with various inert diluents, in both the fuel 
and chamber atmosphere. The fuel gases include hydrogen and methane for soot-free flames, 
and ethylene for sooty flames. One experiment objective is to identify the extinction limits for 
both radiative and convective extinction (i.e., at high and low system Damkohler numbers, 
respectively). Another objective is to determine the existence, onset, and nature of pulsating 
instabilities that have been theoretically predicted to occur in such flames with fuel/diluent 
mixtures that are above a critical Lewis number.

1.10. Ignition 
While hot-wire igniters have been effectively used in many combustion experiments, 
special care is required for ACME because of the testing with elevated oxygen (for 
the Flame Design experiment) which leads to higher flame temperatures which in 
turn could significantly shorten igniter life. Hot Surface Ignition (HSI), which is 
often used in furnaces, may be better for ACME than hot-wire ignition. 
1.10.1. The igniter shall reliably ignite all initial flow conditions. Reliable ignition shall 
be verified in 1g at the limiting (i.e., extreme) conditions in the test matrices for 
each burner within 1 s of igniter activation. For the spherical and BRE burners, 
it is suggested that the ignition occur at about 3 mm from the burner outlet. For 
the gas-jet, coflow, and BRE burners, the ignition should occur within the mixing 
layer between the fuel and oxidizer (and not centered on the burner axis).3,4,* 
1.10.2. Hydrodynamic disturbance from igniter insertion and retraction shall be 
minimized by inserting the igniter at least 30 s prior to ignition, and removing it 
from the free area within 0.5 s after ignition detection.

title: ACME s-Flame: Science Documents — ACME Integrated Science Requirements RevB

1.10.2. Hydrodynamic disturbance from igniter insertion and retraction shall be 
minimized by inserting the igniter at least 30 s prior to ignition, and removing it 
from the free area within 0.5 s after ignition detection. The igniter retraction time 
is a required example, where it shall be possible to vary that time as described in 
ACME’s Science Operations Requirements Document (SORD). The disturbance 
can be minimized through a linear rather than a sweeping retraction, and by 
limiting the speed of the retraction (because a rapid retraction could disturb the 
flame). 
1.10.3. The igniter energy output shall be variable and minimized to ensure minimal 
effects on subsequent flame behavior and avoid igniter burnout. As one example 
of implementation, the igniter should not be energized longer than required.3,* 
1.10.4. The capability to vary the ignition duration and set it to an uplinked value 
between 0 and 10 s is required.*

4. Operational Requirements 
The general science requirements are now combined in ACME’s Science Operations 
Requirements Document (SORD), but this does not eliminate the importance of this section 
of the existing ISRD in describing the general operational sequences. However, these 
operational sequences should be considered as examples where the details are subject to 
change. For example, future ground-based or ISS testing may reveal that superior results 
are achieved when the igniter is preheated before the gas flows are initiated. The times 
specified in the ISRD shall also be considered as required examples, where it shall be 
possible to vary those times as described in the SORD. Furthermore, it should be 
understood that the sequences in the ISRD don’t fully address operational details associated 
with measurements, e.g., the position or range of positions for the Thin Filament Pyrometry 
(TFP). It should also be understood that the format of this ISRD section is not consistent 
between experiments, especially in regard to description of the pre-ignition and postextinction steps. 
 
4.1. CLD Flame 
The main goal of this experiment is to evaluate flame characteristics at the extremes 
of fuel dilution: both weak, highly-dilute flames, and sooting flames up to pure-fuel 
conditions.

title: ACME s-Flame: Science Documents — ACME Integrated Science Requirements RevB
text:
